Massal selection , also called field selection, involves taking propagation material from several desirable vines in an existing vineyard or population rather than multiplying one formally identified clone. This approach can preserve a broader range of genetic diversity and may help maintain heritage or locally adapted material. Formal clonal selection, by contrast, generally involves evaluating and documenting one selected line, including its agronomic and health characteristics. Neither approach is automatically superior. Clonal material may offer greater consistency and traceability. Massal selection may preserve diversity and history, but its identity and health status can be less uniform unless the material has been carefully tested and documented. What Does This Mean in Australia? Australia uses planting material from different propagation and selection systems. Clone names and numbers should not be treated as a universal international code: their meaning can depend on the variety, collection, nursery or identification system involved. Wine Australia is developing VitiCert Australia, a national certification programme for grapevine planting material. The programme is intended to improve confidence in vine identity and health across the propagation supply chain. It launched in 2026, with the first certified cuttings expected from winter 2028. That does not mean all Australian vine material is currently VitiCert-certified. The Australian Wine Research Institute also provides DNA-based grapevine clonal identification using a verified reference database. This reflects a practical issue: names and records are important, but identity can sometimes require scientific verification. Australia also maintains and develops collections of grape varieties, clones, rootstocks and heritage material. This work supports access to planting material with better-known identity and health status while helping preserve valuable older vines. How Should Wine Drinkers Interpret Clone Information? If a producer mentions a clone, you can reasonably understand it as information about a selected planting line within a grape variety. It may help explain: why the grower chose that material; how the vines suit a particular site; when the grapes tend to ripen; how the vineyard manages crop levels; why several selections may be blended. You should not assume that a clone name or number tells you: exactly how the wine will taste; whether the wine is better; whether the material is prestigious; whether it is certified or disease-free; whether it is used throughout a region; whether it expresses terroir more strongly. A useful question is: What does this clone information add to my understanding of the vineyard? If the producer explains the clone’s role in ripening, crop level or site suitability, it may be genuinely useful. If the label simply lists a number, there may not be enough information to turn it into a reliable flavour prediction. Frequently Asked Questions Are clones genetically identical? They are highly similar vegetative descendants of one selected vine, but “identical in every way” is too absolute. Health status, propagation history, rootstock, vine age and growing conditions can all affect field performance. Is a clone the same as a variety? No. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are varieties. A clone is a selected line within one of those varieties. Is a clone the same as a rootstock? No. The clone normally refers to the fruiting part of the vine. The rootstock provides the root system beneath it. Does a clone determine a wine’s flavour? No. A clone may contribute to grape composition and wine style, but site, climate, farming, vintage, harvest timing and winemaking also matter. Does certified planting material guarantee better wine? No. Certification can improve confidence in identity and health. It does not guarantee quality, flavour or commercial success. Why might a winery mention a clone? It may be giving context about vineyard material, ripening behaviour, site suitability or the way a wine was assembled. The meaning is strongest when the producer explains the clone alongside the vineyard and winemaking choices. The Takeaway A wine grape clone is a selected vine line reproduced from one parent vine. It sits within a grape variety and is separate from the rootstock. Clones can help growers manage ripening, yield, bunch structure, vine vigour and plant health. Those choices may influence the grapes and contribute to wine style. But a clone is not a flavour shortcut. To understand the wine in your glass, consider the whole picture: the variety, the clone, the site, the season, the farming and the winemaking.

title: What Does Oak Do to Wine?
description: Learn how oak can influence wine flavour, aroma, texture and ageing, and why not every oaked wine tastes the same.
text: Highlights Oak can change wine through wood-derived flavour and through the way wine matures in an oak vessel. Possible oak characters include vanilla, spice, toast, smoke, cedar and coconut. Oak can also affect texture, tannin and perceived body. New, small barrels usually make a more obvious impression than older, larger or neutral vessels. “Oaked” does not automatically mean sweeter, better or more expensive. Barrel fermentation and barrel maturation are related, but they are not the same thing. Australian Chardonnay, Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon can all be made with oak—or without it. Quick Answer: How does oak affect wine? Oak affects wine in two main ways. First, wine extracts compounds from the wood. These can contribute aromas and flavours such as vanilla, spice, toast, smoke, char, cedar, coconut or caramel. Oak also contributes tannins that can affect bitterness, astringency and mouthfeel. Second, an oak barrel provides a particular environment for maturation. Because wood is porous, the wine can have limited, gradual interaction with oxygen. This can change colour, aroma, tannin structure and texture over time. Small amounts of oxygen may support some maturation reactions, especially in red wine, but too much oxygen can damage freshness and fruit character. So oak is not simply a flavouring. It is both a material that can contribute flavour and a vessel that can influence how wine develops. The result depends on the type of oak, whether it is new or used, the toast level, barrel size, time in contact with the wine and the wine itself. Fruit ripeness, acidity, alcohol, grape tannin, lees contact and bottle age also shape how oak is perceived. Oak flavour is only part of the story When people say a wine is “oaky”, they may be describing obvious aromas of vanilla, toast or smoke. Those impressions can come from compounds released by the wood, particularly after the inside of a barrel has been heated or toasted during manufacture. But oak influence is broader than aroma. Time in oak can also make a wine feel more textured, firm or rounded. In a red wine, oak-derived tannins may add structure or a drying sensation. In a white wine, barrel use may contribute weight or texture, particularly when combined with lees contact or stirring. These effects are not guaranteed. Oak does not automatically add body, soften every wine or improve its quality. A wine’s alcohol, acidity, concentration and grape tannins may be just as important to the way it feels in your mouth. What do new, used and neutral oak mean? New oak New oak has not previously been used for wine. It contains more extractable compounds, so it generally contributes a stronger and more recognisable oak character. A wine matured in a small new barrel may show prominent vanilla, toast, spice or smoke. That can be an intentional style, but if the oak overwhelms the fruit, the wine may feel unbalanced. Used or seasoned oak Used, or seasoned, oak has already held wine and released some of its extractable compounds. It normally contributes less obvious flavour than new oak. That does not mean it does nothing. An older barrel can still influence the wine’s oxygen environment, maturation, evaporation, lees contact and texture. It must also be carefully maintained, because poorly managed barrels can contribute unwanted taints. Neutral oak “Neutral oak” is a practical wine-industry term for a vessel that contributes little obvious oak flavour. It is not necessarily chemically or structurally inactive. A winemaker may use neutral oak when they want some of the benefits of barrel maturation without making vanilla or toast the main feature. Why barrel size matters Barrel size changes the amount of wood surface area in contact with each litre of wine. A smaller barrel generally gives a greater relative wood contact and a faster, more noticeable oak influence than a larger vessel made from comparable wood. This is why a small new barrel may produce a more obvious oak style, while a large-format oak vessel or foudre can allow slower, subtler maturation. Larger vessels are not automatically “better”, and smaller barrels are not automatically more powerful in every circumstance. Barrel age, wood, toast, fill level, cellar conditions and the wine itself all matter. What does toasting do? Toasting means heating the inside of a barrel or oak product during manufacture. Heat changes the compounds available for extraction. Different toast levels can encourage different balances of fresh wood, vanilla, spice, toast, char and smoke. A heavily toasted barrel may offer more smoky or charred impressions, while other toast choices may emphasise sweeter spice or vanilla-like characters. However, toast level alone does not predict the final wine. Contact time, barrel size, oak species, previous use and wine composition also affect the result. “More toast” is not a simple synonym for “more oak”. Barrel fermentation versus barrel maturation These terms describe different stages of winemaking. Barrel-fermented: fermentation takes place in an oak barrel. Barrel-aged or barrel-matured: wine spends time in an oak barrel after, or partly after, fermentation. Barrel-fermented and matured: both stages take place in oak. Barrel fermentation can affect the wine differently from fermenting in stainless steel and then transferring the wine to oak. It may also occur alongside lees contact, lees stirring or malolactic fermentation. This matters particularly for Chardonnay. A creamy, nutty or broad texture may reflect a combination of oak, lees and fermentation choices—not oak alone. Oak alternatives: chips, staves and inserts Winemakers can use oak products such as chips, cubes, staves or inserts to add wood-derived compounds to wine. These formats can provide oak aromas and phenolic effects, but they do not reproduce every feature of barrel maturation. A barrel combines wood contact with a vessel environment, gradual oxygen interaction, evaporation and the possibility of lees or sediment management. Oak alternatives primarily change the amount and type of wine–wood contact. Some may be used alongside controlled oxygen techniques, but they are not identical to traditional barrel ageing. Australian wine regulations recognise oak and oxygen among inputs or techniques permitted under good manufacturing practice. That does not mean a label must disclose every technical detail of the format used. Terms such as “oaked”, “barrel-aged” and “unoaked” should therefore be understood as useful style clues, not complete production records. How oak appears in Australian wine Australian producers use oak in many different ways rather than following one national oak style. Chardonnay may be barrel-fermented, matured in new or seasoned oak, made in larger-format barrels or produced without obvious oak influence. Some producers use oak and lees to build texture; others aim to preserve freshness and fruit. Shiraz may be matured in oak for structure and integration, with older barrels or larger vessels used when a producer wants subtler influence. Cabernet Sauvignon may also be matured in French or American oak, sometimes to help its firm tannins and oak character become more integrated. These are broad examples, not rules. No grape variety must be oaked, and Australian wine style is not defined by Australian-grown barrel wood. Australian wineries may use French, American, European or other oak sources, depending on the wine and the winemaker’s choices. “Australian oak” is therefore not a synonym for “oak used in Australian wine”. For broader context, see How wine is made , and explore Chardonnay or Shiraz for variety-specific examples. How to taste oak without guessing You do not need to identify an exact aroma such as vanillin or guaiacol to notice oak. Try this: Smell the wine before swirling it, then swirl and smell again. Look for the overall impression: fresh fruit, spice, toast, smoke, cedar, creaminess or a drying finish. Taste the wine and notice whether the oak feels integrated with the fruit or sits on top of it. Pay attention to texture. Does the wine feel firmer, broader, more savoury or more drying? Compare it with an unoaked example if you can. A wine with prominent oak may show obvious toast, vanilla, smoke or drying wood-related tannin. A wine with restrained oak may show more subtle spice, texture or savoury complexity, with fruit still leading. A wine with no obvious oak influence may taste fresher and more direct, although it can still have plenty of body, structure and complexity. The same aroma descriptor can come from different sources, so tasting is about forming an impression rather than solving a laboratory test. Common questions about oak Does oak make wine taste sweet? Not necessarily. Vanilla, caramel and sweet spice aromas can create a sweet impression, but oak does not automatically add sugar. A dry wine can smell sweet without tasting sweet. Does oak make wine better? No. Oak is a stylistic and structural choice. Well-integrated oak can support a wine, while excessive oak can hide fruit and freshness. Unoaked wine can be deliberate, expressive and complex. Does oak soften tannins? Oak maturation can change tannin structure and the way tannin feels, but it does not soften every wine in the same way. The outcome depends on the wine, oxygen exposure, time and other winemaking choices. Is barrel-fermented wine heavily oaked? No. Barrel fermentation may be carried out in older or larger-format barrels, or balanced through blending. The term tells you where fermentation occurred, not how strong the oak flavour will be. Is unoaked wine less serious? No. “Unoaked” usually signals an intention to preserve fruit, acidity and freshness. It says something about the winemaking approach, not the quality of the wine. Related learning How wine is made What is Chardonnay? What is Shiraz? Winemaking

title: What Does Yeast Do in Wine?
description: Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat during fermentation. Learn how yeast affects wine aroma, texture and style.
text: Highlights Yeast drives alcoholic fermentation. It consumes grape sugars and produces alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat. Yeast also creates compounds that can influence a wine’s aroma, flavour and texture. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is commonly the main yeast carrying fermentation through to completion. Cultured yeast and ambient fermentation are different winemaking approaches—not automatically better or worse. Yeast fermentation is different from malolactic fermentation, which is performed by bacteria. The finished wine reflects yeast, grapes, vintage and winemaking conditions working together. Quick Answer Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol during alcoholic fermentation. It also produces carbon dioxide, heat and many other compounds that can influence the finished wine’s aroma, flavour and texture. A simple way to think about it is: Grape sugar + yeast activity → alcohol + carbon dioxide + heat + other flavour-active compounds The process is more than a chemical conversion. As yeast works, it changes the grape juice into wine. The type of yeast, the fermentation conditions and what happens afterwards can all affect the result. Yeast does not create a wine’s entire character by itself. Grape variety, vineyard, vintage, temperature, nutrients, oxygen, vessel and maturation also matter. Yeast is the engine of alcoholic fermentation, but the finished wine reflects the interaction between the yeast, the grapes and the winemaking choices. How Yeast Makes Alcohol Grape juice naturally contains fermentable sugars, principally glucose and fructose. Yeast consumes these sugars and converts much of them into ethanol—the alcohol in wine—and carbon dioxide. Fermentation also releases heat and produces other substances, including acids, glycerol, higher alcohols and aroma compounds. That is why fermentation can change grape juice in such a dramatic way: it alters not only the alcohol level, but also the smell, texture and overall shape of the wine. The carbon dioxide usually escapes during a still-wine fermentation. In sparkling wine, winemakers retain some of it so it becomes the bubbles. This is alcoholic fermentation. It is different from malolactic fermentation , a separate process in which bacteria convert sharper-tasting malic acid into softer-tasting lactic acid. Yeast drives alcoholic fermentation; bacteria drive malolactic fermentation. Why Saccharomyces cerevisiae Matters Many microorganisms may be present in grape juice and fermenting wine. However, Saccharomyces cerevisiae is commonly the main yeast that carries alcoholic fermentation through to completion. It is useful in winemaking because it can cope with several difficult conditions: high sugar, increasing alcohol, acidity, sulphur dioxide and limited oxygen. As fermentation progresses, these conditions become increasingly stressful. Yeasts that are less tolerant may decline, while S. cerevisiae often becomes dominant. That does not mean every fermentation is made up of one yeast species. Other yeasts can contribute earlier in the process or work alongside S. cerevisiae , particularly in ambient or mixed fermentations. Cultured Yeast and Ambient Fermentation Winemakers may add a selected cultured yeast , also called a commercial starter yeast, to grape juice. This gives the fermentation a deliberate starting point and can offer greater predictability, reliability and repeatability. Alternatively, a winemaker may allow fermentation to begin with microorganisms already associated with the grapes, winery or equipment. This is often called ambient , indigenous , uninoculated or wild fermentation. The terms overlap, but they do not mean that only one special “wild yeast” is involved. Ambient fermentation can involve a changing community of yeasts and bacteria. Its variability may contribute different aromas or textures, but it can also make the fermentation less predictable. Cultured fermentation offers more control, but that does not mean it produces characterless wine. So, is one approach better? Not automatically. Australian producers use both cultured and ambient approaches, depending on the wine style, fruit, winery practice and the desired balance between reliability and microbial variation. “Wild” does not automatically mean more natural, complex or superior, just as commercial yeast does not automatically mean inferior or artificial. How Yeast Can Affect Aroma and Style Yeast produces compounds that contribute to fermentation-derived aroma. These can include fruity esters, higher alcohols, organic acids, aldehydes and sulphur compounds. Yeast can also transform compounds that came from the grapes into forms we can smell. Different yeast species and strains may therefore contribute different aromatic profiles. One fermentation might emphasise fresh fruit or floral notes, while another may show more savoury or fermentation-derived characters. The result depends on more than the yeast’s name. Temperature, nutrients, oxygen, fermentation speed, grape chemistry and the presence of other microorganisms all influence what happens. Yeast can help shape a wine’s style, but it does not determine the style on its own. A wine’s aroma also comes from the grapes, oak, extraction, maturation and other cellar processes. It would be misleading to say that yeast creates every aroma in wine. Why Fermentation Conditions Matter Yeast does not work at exactly the same speed from beginning to end. Its environment changes as sugar is consumed and alcohol rises. Temperature Temperature affects yeast activity, fermentation speed and the balance of compounds produced. Different temperature conditions can therefore contribute to different sensory outcomes. If conditions become unsuitable, fermentation may slow or stop. Nutrients Yeast needs nutrients to grow and keep fermenting. An inadequate supply can contribute to sluggish or incomplete fermentation and can affect the compounds produced during fermentation. Oxygen Yeast may need some oxygen during its growth phase, while alcoholic fermentation later proceeds largely under oxygen-limited conditions. Oxygen exposure can affect yeast health and fermentation performance, as well as the wine’s broader chemistry. Alcohol and sugar stress As alcohol accumulates, it becomes harder for yeast to remain active. High sugar, acidity, sulphur dioxide, limited nutrients and low yeast vitality can add further stress. A slow or stopped fermentation is not necessarily caused by “bad yeast”; it can result from several pressures acting together. What Happens to Yeast After Fermentation? After fermentation, inactive yeast cells can settle to the bottom of a tank or barrel as lees . Some wines remain in contact with their lees after fermentation. Over time, the breakdown of yeast cells—called autolysis—can contribute to texture and savoury, bready or biscuity characters. This is particularly relevant in some sparkling and white-wine practices, but lees contact is a separate post-fermentation choice. It is not the same as yeast actively converting sugar into alcohol. What This Means When You Taste Wine When a wine smells fruity, floral, spicy, savoury or slightly bready, yeast may be part of the story—but it is only part. You do not need to identify a yeast strain to enjoy the wine. It is more useful to understand that fermentation choices can help explain why two wines made from similar grapes may smell or feel different. Yeast, fermentation conditions and maturation can give the winemaker several ways to influence the finished style. Frequently Asked Questions Does all wine contain yeast? Yeast is involved in the production of most wines because alcoholic fermentation is normally yeast-driven. Finished wine may contain little or no active yeast, particularly after clarification, filtration or settling. Is wild fermentation better than using commercial yeast? No approach is automatically better. Ambient fermentation can bring microbial variation and potential complexity, while cultured yeast can provide greater reliability and control. The result depends on the fruit, winery and intended style. Does yeast make wine sweet? Yeast consumes fermentable sugar. If fermentation finishes with little sugar remaining, the wine may taste dry. If some sugar remains, the wine may taste sweeter. Sweetness can also be managed through winemaking decisions, so yeast alone does not explain every sweet wine. Is yeast the same as the bacteria in malolactic fermentation? No. Yeast drives alcoholic fermentation, converting sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Malolactic fermentation is a separate bacterial process that changes malic acid into lactic acid. Can yeast make wine taste different? Yes. Yeast can produce and transform aroma-active compounds, and different strains or microbial communities can contribute different aromas and textures. Grapes and the wider winemaking process remain important influences too. Continue Learning How wine is made Winemaking What is sparkling wine?

title: What Is Acidity in Wine?
description: Learn what acidity in wine tastes like, how it differs from pH, sweetness and tannin, and how variety, climate and winemaking shape freshness and balance.
text: Highlights Acidity gives wine freshness, liveliness and a mouth-watering sensation. You may notice it as tartness, similar to the effect of citrus or green apple. Acidity is not the same as sweetness, tannin, sourness or pH. A high-acid wine is not automatically better, and a low-acid wine is not automatically faulty. Grape variety, ripeness, climate, harvest timing, winemaking and ageing can all influence acidity. You can recognise acidity by noticing how much your mouth waters and how fresh the wine feels. Quick Answer Acidity in wine is the presence and effect of naturally occurring acids that make wine feel fresh, lively and mouth-watering. It is one of wine’s main structural components, working alongside sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit flavour and body. When acidity is noticeable, a wine may taste crisp, bright or energetic. It can create a tart sensation, rather like biting into a green apple or tasting citrus. A wine with less noticeable acidity may feel softer, rounder or broader. Neither style is automatically better. Acidity needs to make sense in the wine as a whole. It can keep a sweet wine from seeming heavy, give a rich white wine freshness, or help a red wine feel energetic rather than broad. But too much, too little or poorly integrated acidity can make a wine seem sharp, flat or unbalanced. How Does Acidity Feel? Acidity is easiest to recognise on the palate rather than by looking at the wine. Take a sip and notice whether your mouth begins to water. Does the wine feel refreshing and lively, or soft and broad? Does that freshness continue into the finish? Wine writers may describe acidity as: High-acid: acidity is clearly prominent. Low-acid: acidity is less noticeable. Crisp: fresh and lively, often with noticeable acidity. Soft: rounder or less obviously acidic. Flabby: an informal term for wine that seems to lack freshness or structural energy. These are descriptions, not quality scores. A crisp Riesling and a soft, full-bodied red can both be enjoyable when their acidity suits the style. Acidity can also feel like tension or energy. It gives the wine shape and movement rather than allowing it to seem static. However, the sensation is affected by temperature, sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit flavour and the person tasting it. Mouth-watering is a useful clue, not a laboratory test. Acidity Is Not the Same as Sourness or Sharpness Acidity can contribute to sourness or tartness, but the words do not mean exactly the same thing. Acidity is the chemical property and the related sensory quality. Sourness is a taste perception that may be caused by acids. Tartness is a common way of describing the fresh, sour-edged sensation acidity can create. Sharpness is an informal description. It may mean that the acidity feels especially prominent or aggressive, but it is not a precise technical term. A wine can have noticeable acidity without tasting unpleasantly sour. The final impression depends on how much acidity is present, the types of acids involved and how the acidity interacts with the wine’s other components. Acidity, pH and Titratable Acidity Wine professionals use measurements to describe acidity, but those measurements are not identical to what you experience while drinking. pH is a chemical measurement related to the strength or activity of acidity in a solution. A lower pH indicates a more acidic chemical environment, but it does not perfectly predict how sour or refreshing a wine will taste. Titratable acidity , often shortened to TA, estimates the amount of acid that can react during a laboratory titration. It is commonly expressed as grams per litre of tartaric-acid equivalent. Perceived acidity is the experience of tasting the wine: how fresh, tart, lively or mouth-watering it feels. These measurements are related, but they are not interchangeable. Sweetness, alcohol, tannin, flavour concentration and texture can all change how acidity is perceived. This is why a number on a laboratory report cannot tell you exactly how a wine will feel in your mouth. How Acidity Interacts with Other Parts of Wine Acidity does not work alone. Sweetness Sweetness can make acidity seem less prominent, while acidity can stop a sweet wine from feeling heavy or cloying. Sweetness does not remove acidity; it changes how the two are experienced together. A dry wine with noticeable acidity may seem particularly crisp. A sweet wine with both richness and refreshing acidity can feel balanced rather than syrupy. Alcohol and Body Alcohol and body can make a wine feel broader, warmer or rounder, which may make its acidity seem less obvious. A lighter-bodied wine with similar acidity may feel brisker. This is not a fixed rule. The overall impression depends on the wine’s fruit, texture and structure. Tannin Tannin is a separate sensation. It can feel drying, grippy or slightly rough, especially in red wine. Acidity feels more tart, fresh and mouth-watering. The two can appear together. A red wine with firm acidity and tannin may feel structured and energetic, while a wine with noticeable tannin but less acidity may feel drying without feeling particularly fresh. Fruit Flavour Fruit character changes how acidity is interpreted. Citrus, green apple and some red-fruit flavours may reinforce a fresh impression. Riper tropical or dark-fruit flavours can make a wine seem fuller, even when it still has substantial acidity. Ripe fruit does not automatically mean low acidity. What Influences Acidity? Several factors shape the acidity of a finished wine. Grape variety and ripeness Different grape varieties have different natural acid profiles and differ in how well they retain acidity as they ripen. As grapes ripen, sugar generally increases while some acids decline, although the pattern varies with variety and growing conditions. Harvest timing is therefore a decision about the relationship between sugar, acidity, flavour and texture. An early harvest is not automatically better, and a late harvest is not automatically low-acid. Climate and vineyard conditions Cooler conditions can help grapes retain acidity, while warmer conditions may accelerate ripening and acid loss. But climate does not determine a wine’s acidity by itself. Variety, site, vintage, water availability, vineyard management, harvest decisions and winemaking also matter. This is one reason Australian wine cannot be described as having one acidity profile. The country’s regions, elevations, varieties and climates produce a wide range of styles. Fermentation and malolactic fermentation Some wines undergo malolactic fermentation, in which sharper-tasting malic acid is converted into softer-tasting lactic acid. This can make a wine feel rounder, but it does not simply remove all acidity. The choice to use or avoid this process is one of many winemaking decisions that can affect texture and the way acidity is perceived. For more on the wider winemaking process, see How wine is made . Ageing Acidity can help a wine retain freshness as it develops, but acidity alone does not guarantee that a wine will improve or last for a long time. Ageing also depends on the wine’s other components, its style, storage and bottle condition. How Acidity Appears in Different Wines Acidity can be present in white, red, rosé and sparkling wine. White wine: acidity may be especially easy to notice because white wine usually has little tannin and is often served chilled. It can make the wine feel crisp or citrusy. Red wine: acidity helps shape the relationship between fruit, alcohol and tannin. It may be less obvious in a full-bodied or strongly tannic wine. Rosé: acidity can support a fresh, dry style and help fruit flavours feel light rather than heavy. Sparkling wine: acidity works with carbon dioxide and sweetness to create freshness and lift. These are broad observations, not rules for every bottle. Australian Examples Australian Riesling is often a clear example of acidity supporting vibrant fruit and freshness. Adelaide Hills wines are also often described in terms such as lively and crisp. Southern Highlands Sauvignon Blanc can show good acidity. These descriptions are tendencies, not guarantees. Australian wine includes everything from bright, high-acid styles to softer, fuller wines with less prominent acidity. Warm-region wines can also retain balancing acidity, depending on variety, site, vintage, harvest timing and winemaking. The important lesson is not to judge acidity from a region name alone. Even two wines made from the same variety in the same region can feel different. A Simple Acidity Tasting Exercise Try this the next time you open a bottle: Take a small sip. Let the wine move naturally across your palate. Notice whether your mouth waters. Ask whether the wine feels fresh and lively or soft and broad. Notice whether the sensation continues into the finish. If possible, compare it with another wine. Describe the acidity separately from whether you like the wine. You do not need to identify a number. “Fresh and mouth-watering” is already a useful observation. Frequently Asked Questions Is high acidity good in wine? Not automatically. High acidity can make a wine refreshing and energetic, but balance depends on how it works with sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit and body. Is acidity the same as sweetness? No. Acidity creates freshness and tartness, while sweetness creates a sense of sugar or richness. They can balance each other but are separate sensations. Is acidity the same as tannin? No. Acidity is usually felt as freshness, tartness and mouth-watering. Tannin is more often felt as dryness, grip or astringency. Are Australian wines high in acidity? There is no single Australian acidity style. Different varieties, regions, climates, vintages and winemaking choices produce different profiles. Does acidity mean a wine will age well? Acidity can help a wine retain freshness during ageing, but it does not guarantee longevity or improvement. Other components and storage conditions matter too. How can I tell if a wine has acidity? Take a sip and notice whether it makes your mouth water and feels fresh or lively. Compare it with a softer wine if you can.

title: What Is Balance in Wine?
description: Learn what balance means in wine, how acidity, sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit and texture work together, and how to recognise balance when tasting.
text: Highlights Balance is the relationship between a wine’s main elements, including acidity, sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit, body and texture. A balanced wine does not need every element in equal amounts. Balance does not mean a wine is light, mild or low in flavour. A powerful wine can still be balanced. The right balance depends on the wine’s style. Sweet, sparkling, red, white and fortified wines are not judged by exactly the same expectations. You can recognise balance by noticing whether the wine feels coherent or whether one feature—such as sharp acidity, hot alcohol or drying tannin—takes over. Balance and personal preference are different. You can recognise that a wine is balanced without liking its style. Quick answer: what does “balanced wine” mean? A balanced wine is one in which its main elements work together so that the wine feels harmonious and proportionate for its style. No single feature distractingly dominates the experience. Those elements may include acidity, sweetness, alcohol, tannin, fruit concentration, body, texture, oak, bitterness and finish. They do not need to be equal, and balance is not a numerical formula. It is an overall tasting impression. For example, a sweet wine can be balanced when its acidity provides freshness. A red wine can be balanced with noticeable tannin and alcohol if its fruit, body and acidity provide enough support. A wine can also be intense or powerful without being unbalanced. When tasting, ask: does the wine feel integrated from the first sip through the finish, or does one feature seem disconnected or overwhelming? Balance is a relationship, not an ingredient Balance is not something winemakers add to wine as a separate component. It describes how the components already present interact. Think of a wine as a small group of musical instruments. One instrument may be prominent, but the performance can still work if the parts support one another. If one instrument drowns out everything else, the result may feel less harmonious. The same idea applies to wine. Acidity may provide freshness, sweetness may add richness, tannin may provide grip, and alcohol may add warmth and weight. Fruit and body help provide the scale and substance that make those structural features feel proportionate. This is why “more” is not automatically better. More acidity, tannin, alcohol, oak or sweetness can suit one style and overwhelm another. The elements that influence balance Acidity Acidity gives wine freshness, liveliness and sometimes a mouth-watering sensation. It can help prevent a wine from seeming flat and can keep sweetness or body from feeling heavy. A sweet wine with enough acidity may taste rich but still fresh. A dry wine with prominent acidity may feel crisp and energetic. However, more acidity is not automatically better: if it seems harsh or disconnected, it may distract from the rest of the wine. Sweetness Sweetness contributes richness and palate weight. It is not inherently a sign of imbalance. In a sweet wine, acidity, fruit concentration and texture can help support that richness. In a dry white wine, the expected relationship among sweetness, acidity, fruit and body will be different. The question is not whether sweetness exists, but whether it fits the wine’s style and feels integrated. Alcohol Alcohol can contribute warmth, body and a sense of volume. It may feel comfortably integrated when the wine has enough fruit, concentration and body to support it. When alcohol becomes the main sensation—particularly as heat or burning—it may seem distracting. But warmth alone does not prove that a wine is unbalanced. It needs to be considered alongside the wine’s style and concentration. Tannin Tannin can create grip, structure and a drying sensation, especially in red wine. Firm tannin is not automatically a flaw or evidence of imbalance. A structured red may feel balanced when its fruit, acidity, alcohol and body give the tannin a suitable context. Tannin may seem less integrated when it feels aggressively coarse or leaves the mouth excessively dry compared with the rest of the wine. Tannin and acidity are different: acidity creates freshness and tartness, while tannin is mainly experienced as texture and astringency. Fruit, body and texture Fruit concentration gives a wine flavour and density. Body is the perceived weight or fullness of the wine in the mouth. Texture describes how it feels, such as smooth, creamy, firm, grippy or rough. Together, these features provide context for the wine’s structure. A bold, concentrated wine may carry noticeable alcohol or tannin without seeming unbalanced. The same apparent structural weight may feel overwhelming in a more delicate wine. Body is not identical to alcohol, sweetness or tannin, although each can influence how body is perceived. Oak, bitterness and finish Oak can contribute aroma, flavour, texture and structure. It may feel integrated when it supports the wine’s fruit and body. It may feel dominant when vanilla, toast, smoke, spice or woody bitterness obscures the wine’s other features. Bitterness can also affect the impression of sweetness and the wine’s finish. Noticeable oak or bitterness is not automatically a problem. The useful question is whether it adds detail or takes over. The finish—the sensations and flavours that remain after swallowing—can reveal whether the wine’s components stay coherent. A wine that feels harmonious at the beginning but ends with harsh heat, excessive dryness or disjointed bitterness may seem less balanced overall. Balance changes with wine style There is no single balance profile that every wine should follow. Dry wines: acidity, fruit, alcohol, body and, in many reds, tannin may be especially important. Sweet wines: noticeable sweetness can be balanced when acidity and fruit provide freshness and prevent a cloying finish. Sparkling wines: acidity, sweetness, alcohol, fruit, bubbles and texture work together. Fortified wines: higher alcohol, sweetness, oxidative flavours or bitterness need to be considered within the intended style. Red wines: tannin, acidity, alcohol, fruit concentration and oak may all contribute strongly. White and rosé wines: acidity, fruit, alcohol and texture may be prominent, with oak or skin-contact texture also relevant in some styles. Australian wine covers a wide range of styles, from dry Riesling and sparkling wine to Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, sweet wines and fortified wines. A variety, region or colour can suggest a style, but none guarantees a particular balance profile. Australian readers may encounter “balanced” in tasting notes, cellar-door conversations, bottle descriptions, restaurant lists and wine reviews. It is a sensory and evaluative description, not a regulated label category. How to recognise balance when tasting You can build on the approach in How to taste wine without turning the experience into a test. Taste before deciding whether you like it. Notice your first impression. Notice the acidity. Does the wine feel fresh, lively, tart or flat? Notice sweetness. Does it taste dry, lightly sweet or rich? Notice alcohol. Does the warmth feel integrated or distracting? Notice tannin and texture. Is the wine smooth, firm, drying or rough? Consider fruit and body. Is there enough flavour and weight to support the structure? Notice oak or bitterness. Do they add detail or dominate the wine? Pay attention to the finish. Does the wine remain coherent after swallowing? Make an overall judgement. Does one component pull the wine out of shape? A useful mental summary is: Freshness, richness, warmth, structure, weight and texture should feel like parts of the same wine—not competing sensations. You do not need to score each element or calculate a result. Balance is a conclusion about the whole experience. Balance is not the same as quality or preference Balance is important, but it is only one part of evaluating wine. Intensity, complexity, finish and the suitability of the wine to its style may also matter. These terms describe different things: Balance: whether the main elements work together. Intensity: how strongly the wine’s aromas, flavours or structure are perceived. Complexity: the range or development of its sensory characteristics. Quality: a broader judgement that may include balance, intensity, complexity, finish and other factors. Preference: whether you personally enjoy the wine. A simple, inexpensive or low-intensity wine can be balanced. A complex wine can still feel unbalanced. And a technically balanced wine may use flavours or textures you simply do not enjoy. That distinction is useful when reading reviews or speaking at a cellar door. “Balanced” does not mean “you will definitely like it”. It means the writer or taster considers the wine’s parts to be working together. Frequently asked questions Does a balanced wine need to be subtle? No. A wine can be full-bodied, concentrated, highly flavoured or tannic and still be balanced if its elements work together. Is sweet wine unbalanced? No. Sweetness can be balanced by acidity, fruit concentration and texture. Sweet wines are assessed according to their style rather than against the expectations of a dry table wine. Does high alcohol mean a wine is unbalanced? Not necessarily. Alcohol can provide warmth and body. It becomes distracting when its heat dominates the wine rather than fitting with its fruit, concentration and structure. Is balance completely objective? No. Balance is a widely used tasting concept, but tasters can disagree about whether a feature feels integrated or dominant. Sensory perception and experience vary, and style affects expectations. Can I call a wine balanced if I do not like it? Yes. Balance and preference are related but different. You can recognise that a wine is harmonious while deciding that its sweetness, tannin, oak or intensity is not for you. What should I learn next? For the wider tasting process, start with How to taste wine . You can also explore the foundations of wine through What is wine? and How wine is made .

title: What Is Biodynamic Wine?
description: Learn how biodynamic wine relates to organic farming, certification and cellar practices, and what the label can and cannot tell you.
text: Front matter Title: What Is Biodynamic Wine? Primary topic: Biodynamic wine and biodynamic viticulture Suggested description: Biodynamic wine comes from grapes grown using a farming system that builds on organic principles. Learn what biodynamic means, how it differs from organic and natural wine, and how to interpret the claim on an Australian wine label. Related live pages: What is wine? , How wine is made , Winemaking What Is Biodynamic Wine? Highlights Biodynamic wine generally comes from grapes grown using biodynamic vineyard practices. Biodynamic farming includes organic principles, plus additional preparations and whole-farm practices. Biodynamic describes how grapes are grown—not one guaranteed flavour or wine style. Biodynamic wine is not automatically natural, vegan, additive-free, low-sulphur or healthier. Some biodynamic farms use lunar or cosmic calendars, but these ideas should not be confused with established scientific effects. In Australia, a producer’s biodynamic claim and an independent certification mark are not necessarily the same thing. Quick answer Biodynamic wine is wine made from grapes grown using biodynamic viticulture : a farming system that incorporates organic requirements and adds specific preparations, compost management, biodiversity and whole-farm principles. The word mainly tells you something about the vineyard . It does not, by itself, tell you whether the wine is red or white, what it tastes like, how much alcohol it contains or how it was made in the winery. Biodynamic wine is related to organic wine, but it is not simply another word for organic. Biodynamic systems add practices such as specially prepared materials applied to vines, soil or compost. Some also use agricultural calendars based on lunar or cosmic timing. The evidence for biodynamic farming is mixed and context-dependent. Some studies report benefits for soil properties or biodiversity in particular situations, but biodynamic farming is not proven to guarantee better wine, greater sustainability or a health benefit. What does biodynamic mean in the vineyard? Biodynamic viticulture treats the farm as an interconnected system rather than viewing the vineyard as a collection of vines. In practice, this can involve: composting and careful manure management; using specific biodynamic preparations; encouraging biodiversity in and around the vineyard; integrating animals, plants, soil and compost; reducing reliance on outside inputs through closed-loop planning; and following seasonal or biodynamic timing systems. Not every biodynamic vineyard will operate in exactly the same way. The details depend on the relevant standard, certification system and producer. A useful way to understand biodynamics is to separate practice, philosophy and evidence . Using a preparation is a documented farming practice. Seeing the property as a self-contained organism is part of the farming philosophy. Claiming that a preparation or lunar calendar reliably changes vine growth is a scientific claim—and one for which evidence remains limited or mixed. How is biodynamic wine different from organic wine? Organic farming generally focuses on production methods such as restrictions on synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, along with requirements for permitted inputs and processing. Biodynamic farming incorporates organic principles but adds its own preparations and whole-farm approach. In other words: Term What it mainly describes Organic Organic farming and, depending on the claim, organic processing Biodynamic Organic-style farming plus biodynamic preparations and whole-farm principles Natural Usually a low-intervention approach to winemaking, without one universal definition Sustainable Environmental, social or economic goals whose meaning depends on the programme or claim These terms can overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A biodynamic wine may be made with conventional yeast, filtered, fined or stabilised if the applicable production rules permit it. A natural wine may use biodynamically farmed grapes, but natural-wine language does not prove biodynamic certification. What are biodynamic preparations? Biodynamic preparations are distinctive materials used as part of biodynamic farming systems. They may involve compost, manure or plant material and are prepared and applied according to a particular method or standard. The Australian National Standard for Organic and Bio-Dynamic Produce includes requirements for biodynamic preparations, including their preparation, stirring, application and equipment. For a certified operator, these requirements are part of the production system. Some biodynamic traditions also use lunar or cosmic calendars to time vineyard work. This is best understood as a practice or belief within some biodynamic systems, not as a scientifically established guarantee of better soil, grapes or wine. The preparations are important to what makes biodynamics distinct. That does not mean every claimed mechanism behind them has been scientifically demonstrated. Does biodynamic wine taste different? Not necessarily. Biodynamic farming does not create one flavour profile. The taste of a wine depends on many factors, including grape variety, region, climate, vintage, picking decisions, fermentation, maturation and other winemaking choices. A biodynamic vineyard can produce red, white, rosé or sparkling wine in many different styles. Some research has reported differences in soil, vine or wine characteristics between farming systems. However, results vary between studies and locations. It is difficult to separate the effect of biodynamic preparations from the effects of composting, reduced synthetic inputs, biodiversity or the producer’s broader management. So biodynamic wine may taste distinctive—but the label alone cannot promise that it will taste better, earthier, more expressive or more “pure”. Is biodynamic wine healthier or more sustainable? There is no sound basis for treating biodynamic wine as automatically healthier. Farming method does not determine alcohol content, calories, sulphite sensitivity, allergen status or hangover risk. Biodynamic farming may include practices that support soil activity, habitat or biodiversity in some settings. But the label alone does not prove that a wine is more sustainable overall. Water use, energy, machinery, yields, packaging, transport and disease management also matter. It is more accurate to say that biodynamics is a farming system with environmental intentions and some promising, but not universally conclusive, evidence than to call it automatically superior. What does “biodynamic” mean on an Australian wine label? For Australian domestic sales, certification is not universally mandatory for an organic or biodynamic claim. However, businesses must be able to substantiate claims and avoid misleading consumers under Australian Consumer Law. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission identifies AS 6000–2015 as a voluntary domestic standard for organic and biodynamic products. Private certification organisations may use their own standards, marks and certification scopes. Australia also has a National Standard for Organic and Bio-Dynamic Produce. It is mandatory for relevant Australian products intended for export and includes biodynamic requirements and a wine-production section. When reading a label, distinguish between: “Certified biodynamic” — look for the named certifier or certification mark. A certification logo — check which organisation issued it and what its standard covers. “Biodynamically farmed” — this may describe vineyard practice without proving certification of the finished wine. A producer’s own description — potentially meaningful, but not the same as independent certification. The Bio-Dynamic Research Institute manages the Demeter trademark in Australia and certifies operators under its stated system. A certification mark can provide useful information, but it is still worth understanding whether it applies to the grapes, the wine, or both. What biodynamic wine does not automatically mean Biodynamic wine is not automatically: natural or low-intervention; vegan; additive-free; sulphur-free or low-sulphur; unfiltered or unfined; or healthier. Certification rules may allow particular cellar additions and processing methods. If you need to know about sulphur, fining agents, filtration or dietary suitability, check the producer’s technical information rather than assuming from the word “biodynamic”. Frequently asked questions Is biodynamic wine organic? Biodynamic systems generally incorporate organic requirements and add further practices. However, the exact certification claim depends on the relevant standard and certifier. Is biodynamic wine the same as natural wine? No. Biodynamic mainly describes vineyard farming. Natural usually refers to a low-intervention approach to winemaking, and the term does not have one universal definition in Australia. Is biodynamic wine always certified? No. Domestic certification is voluntary, although claims must be substantiated and must not mislead. A certified claim and a producer’s own description should be treated as different forms of information. Does biodynamic wine contain no sulphites? No. Biodynamic status does not automatically mean sulphite-free. Check the wine’s technical information if this matters to you. Should I buy biodynamic wine? If the farming approach interests you, look for a clear description of the producer’s practices and any named certification. Then choose the wine by its grape variety, region and style—as you would with any other bottle. Biodynamic tells you something important about how the vineyard is managed, but it does not decide whether you will enjoy the wine.

title: What Is Brettanomyces in Wine?
description: Brettanomyces, or “Brett”, is a yeast that can change wine’s aroma and flavour. Learn what Brett smells like, when it is a fault and how it differs from other wine faults.
text: Highlights Brettanomyces is a yeast associated with wine spoilage. It is often shortened to “Brett”. Brett can change a wine’s smell and flavour, sometimes producing medicinal, smoky, leathery, earthy or barnyard-like notes. A single aroma descriptor does not prove that Brettanomyces is present. Brett can suppress fresh fruit and make a wine seem muted or less expressive. Some drinkers tolerate low levels of Brett character, but higher levels are commonly considered a fault. Brett is different from cork taint, oxidation, reduction and volatile acidity. Consumers usually cannot reverse established Brett character at home. Quick answer Brettanomyces is a wine-associated yeast, particularly the species Brettanomyces bruxellensis , that can grow during winemaking, maturation or storage. It can produce volatile compounds that alter a wine’s aroma and flavour. Depending on the wine and the level present, Brett character may smell medicinal, like a bandage or antiseptic; smoky or spicy; leathery and earthy; or animal-like, sometimes described as “barnyard”, “horse” or “stable”. It may also do something less obvious: suppress the wine’s fruit, making it seem dull, muted or less fresh. Is Brett always a fault? No. Brettanomyces is generally treated as a spoilage organism, especially when it dominates the wine or obscures its intended character. However, low levels may be tolerated or even appreciated by some drinkers in some styles. There is no single point at which every wine and every person will judge it in the same way. What does “Brett” mean? “Brett” is informal shorthand, but it can mean several related things: the Brettanomyces yeast; the compounds produced by the yeast; the sensory character those compounds create; or a suspicion based on how a wine smells. These are not identical. Calling a wine “Brett-like” is a sensory description, not laboratory proof that the yeast is present. Similar earthy, leathery, smoky or savoury notes can have other causes, including reduction, oxidation, smoke taint or normal development with age. What can Brett smell and taste like? The most useful way to think about Brett is as a range of possible characters rather than one unmistakable smell. A wine affected by Brett may show: medicinal, pharmaceutical or antiseptic aromas; bandage-like or “band-aid” notes; smoky, spicy or clove-like character; leather and earthy aromas; barnyard, horsey, stable-like or animal notes; sweaty or savoury impressions. The profile depends on the yeast strain, the wine’s composition and the concentration of the compounds produced. One wine may seem mainly medicinal; another may show leather and savoury notes. A heavily affected wine may simply seem to have lost its bright fruit. This is why the word “barnyard” should be treated as a clue, not a diagnosis. Tasting vocabulary helps us describe what we notice, but it does not identify the cause with certainty. What compounds cause Brett character? Brettanomyces can transform naturally occurring compounds in wine into volatile phenols—aroma-active compounds that are easier to smell. The two most discussed are: 4-ethylphenol , often associated with medicinal, pharmaceutical, bandage-like or animal aromas; 4-ethylguaiacol , often associated with smoky, spicy, clove-like or savoury aromas. Other compounds can contribute too, so Brett character cannot be reduced to one chemical or one smell. The amount that a person notices varies with the wine. Alcohol, acidity, tannin, oak, grape variety, other aromas and the drinker’s own sensitivity can all affect perception. A level that is noticeable in a light, delicate wine may be masked or interpreted differently in a fuller wine. Is there a Brettanomyces threshold? Research reports sensory thresholds for individual compounds, but these figures vary according to the wine, the testing method and the people taking part. A chemical result also does not perfectly predict what a drinker will notice. So there is no universal Brett threshold that applies to every wine or every palate. It is better to ask: Has the wine lost its fruit and freshness? Do the medicinal, smoky or animal notes dominate? Do they fit the wine’s intended style? Do you find the wine enjoyable? A laboratory analysis can help a winery investigate a problem, but a consumer cannot definitively diagnose Brettanomyces from one aroma descriptor. Is Brett a fault or a style? Brettanomyces is commonly discussed as a wine fault because it can overwhelm fruit character and make a wine seem unbalanced. At pronounced levels, many drinkers would consider medicinal, animal-like or heavily leathery character undesirable. At lower levels, opinions can differ. Some people may accept or enjoy a subtle earthy, leathery or savoury contribution, particularly in a wine where that character does not dominate. Others may notice the same character immediately and dislike it. The important distinction is between a character that adds complexity without overwhelming the wine and spoilage that masks the wine’s fruit and structure . Neither “Brett is always bad” nor “Brett is always desirable” is a reliable rule. Where can Brettanomyces occur? Brettanomyces can be relevant during production, maturation and storage. It may persist in winery environments, equipment and porous wine-contact materials such as barrels. Wine conditions can also influence whether the yeast survives or grows. For wineries, control is mainly a matter of hygiene, monitoring and managing wine-contact materials and conditions. It is not something a producer can sensibly judge only after a bottle reaches the customer. Australian Wine Research Institute material recognises Brettanomyces as a wine-management issue across Australian wine regions. That does not mean a particular region, grape variety or producer has a special Brett problem. Brett is a wine-production challenge, not a useful basis for stereotyping Australian wine. What should you do if you suspect Brett? First, smell and taste the wine carefully in a clean glass. Avoid deciding from one word such as “leather” or “barnyard”, because those notes can have several causes. If the wine seems clearly unpleasant or significantly different from what you expected: Keep the bottle, closure and proof of purchase where practical. If possible, compare it with another bottle of the same wine. Contact the retailer or producer and describe the problem. Explain the aromas you noticed rather than insisting on a diagnosis. Decanting, chilling or leaving the wine open may change how it smells temporarily, but these actions do not reliably remove established Brett character. Consumers generally cannot reverse the underlying condition at home. Brettanomyces compared with other wine faults Cork taint: commonly associated with musty, mouldy or damp-cardboard aromas and suppressed fruit. It is a different problem from Brettanomyces. Oxidation: can produce bruised-apple, nutty, stale or cardboard-like character after excessive oxygen exposure. Reduction: may produce struck-match, rubber, cabbage or rotten-egg-like aromas. It is chemically distinct from Brett. Volatile acidity: may smell vinegary or solvent-like. It can be associated with microbial activity, but it is not the same diagnosis as Brett. Smoke taint: may show ash, burnt or campfire-like character and can overlap with some smoky Brett descriptions. Sensory overlap is real, which is another reason not to diagnose Brett from one aroma alone. Frequently asked questions Is Brettanomyces the same as cork taint? No. Cork taint and Brettanomyces can both suppress fruit, but they have different causes and commonly produce different sensory patterns. Can you smell Brett in every affected wine? No. Brett character varies. Some wines show obvious medicinal or animal notes, while others mainly seem less fruity or less fresh. Is Brettanomyces only found in red wine? No universal claim like that is supported. Brett can be relevant to wine production more broadly, although its sensory expression depends on the wine. Can aeration cure Brett? No. Aeration may temporarily change perception, but it does not reliably remove the compounds or eliminate the underlying issue. Is a wine with Brett automatically unsafe? The research supplied for this guide supports treating Brett primarily as a quality and enjoyment issue. If a wine seems faulty, contact the retailer or producer rather than relying on a home diagnosis. Related learning What is wine? How wine is made Winemaking Fault-specific related pages can be linked when their routes are confirmed as live.

title: What Is Cabernet Sauvignon?
description: Cabernet Sauvignon is a structured red grape known for dark fruit, acidity and firm tannin. Learn how its style varies and where it thrives in Australia.
text: Highlights Cabernet Sauvignon is a red wine grape variety. The name is also used for wines made mainly from that grape. It commonly produces deeply coloured, medium- to full-bodied wines. Typical Cabernet Sauvignon has noticeable acidity, firm tannin and dark-fruit flavours. Blackcurrant, blackberry, mulberry and plum are common descriptors, but every bottle is different. Climate, ripeness, oak, blending and bottle age can change the wine considerably. Most still Cabernet Sauvignon is dry, even when it tastes richly fruity. Australian examples range from elegant, cool-climate wines to fuller, more structured styles. Some Cabernet Sauvignon can age for many years, but plenty is made to enjoy now. Quick answer: what is Cabernet Sauvignon? Cabernet Sauvignon is a red wine grape variety . It is one of the world’s best-known grapes and is used to make both single-variety wines and blends. Cabernet Sauvignon wines are often medium to full bodied, with deep colour, noticeable acidity and firm or structured tannins. Tannin is the part of wine that can make your mouth feel dry or grippy. The grape commonly produces dark-fruit flavours such as blackcurrant, blackberry, mulberry and plum. That is the classic outline, but Cabernet Sauvignon is not one fixed style. A cool-climate example may taste more restrained, herbal or finely structured, while a warmer-climate wine may seem riper, fuller and richer. Oak maturation can add cedar, spice or toast, and bottle age can soften tannin and bring more savoury notes. Most still Cabernet Sauvignon is dry. In other words, it contains little perceptible residual sugar. A wine can taste of ripe blackberries or plums without being sweet. Where did Cabernet Sauvignon come from? Cabernet Sauvignon originated in south-west France. It is a natural cross between Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, although it is a distinct grape variety in its own right. Today, Cabernet Sauvignon is grown in many wine regions, including Australia. It is made as a single-variety wine and is also commonly blended with varieties such as Merlot, Shiraz or Cabernet Franc. Blending can change the wine’s balance, texture, aroma and softness; it does not make the wine “less Cabernet”. For a beginner-friendly introduction to grape varieties, visit the WineDaddy grape varieties hub . What does Cabernet Sauvignon taste like? Cabernet Sauvignon commonly has a combination of dark fruit, structure and freshness. Fruit and aroma Depending on the region, ripeness and age, you may notice: blackcurrant or cassis blackberry mulberry plum violet mint dried herbs cedar spice or savoury notes These are possibilities, not a checklist. One Cabernet Sauvignon may smell strongly of blackcurrant, while another may show more herbs, cedar or restrained black fruit. Body, acidity and tannin Cabernet Sauvignon is often medium to full bodied. Body is the sense of weight or fullness that a wine has in your mouth. It commonly has noticeable acidity , which gives the wine freshness and helps stop a rich wine from feeling flat. It also often has firm tannin , which can feel drying, grippy or slightly rough on the gums. A young, concentrated Cabernet can feel quite firm. A softer style, a blended wine or a bottle with some age may feel rounder and more approachable. This is why two wines labelled Cabernet Sauvignon can taste noticeably different. Why does Cabernet Sauvignon vary so much? The grape is only one part of the finished wine. Its style is shaped by several decisions and conditions. Climate and site Moderate climates can help Cabernet Sauvignon develop ripe fruit while retaining acidity. Warmer conditions may produce fuller body and riper fruit, while cooler conditions can result in more restrained fruit, firmer acidity or more noticeable herbal character. These are broad tendencies rather than rules. Vineyard site, vintage, harvest timing and winemaking also matter. Heat and drought stress can make it more difficult to achieve a balanced result. Ripeness and extraction Riper grapes may contribute darker, richer fruit flavours and a fuller texture. Winemakers can also influence colour, flavour and tannin through techniques such as skin contact and extraction during fermentation. More extraction can contribute to a deeper, more structured wine. The result depends on how that structure sits alongside fruit and acidity. Oak and blending Oak maturation may add cedar, toast, spice, vanilla-like notes and extra texture. Some Cabernet Sauvignon spends significant time in oak, while other examples use less oak so that the fruit remains more prominent. Blending is another way to shape the final wine. Merlot may contribute softness or mid-palate weight, while Shiraz or Cabernet Franc can alter the fruit, texture and aroma profile. The label or producer’s description may tell you whether a wine is a single-variety Cabernet Sauvignon or a blend. Bottle age Cabernet Sauvignon often has the acidity, tannin, concentration and structure needed to age well. With time, some wines develop softer tannins and more savoury, cedar-like or earthy notes. However, ageing potential is not a guarantee. Some Cabernet Sauvignon is made for earlier drinking, and not every bottle will improve after years in storage. An affordable, fresh example can be enjoyable now without needing a cellar. Australian Cabernet Sauvignon Cabernet Sauvignon is an important Australian red grape variety, and Australian examples are not all alike. Margaret River Margaret River Cabernet Sauvignon is often associated with medium- to full-bodied wines showing blackcurrant, cedar, violet and defined tannin. Some examples are blended with Merlot. Coonawarra Coonawarra is commonly associated with Cabernet Sauvignon showing concentrated blackcurrant, mulberry and plum, along with firm tannin. Mint and dried-herb notes may also appear in some examples. The region’s terra rossa soils are an important part of its regional identity, but soil should not be treated as a simple explanation for every flavour in the glass. Yarra Valley The Yarra Valley provides a useful cool-climate example. Its Cabernet Sauvignon can show elegant black fruit, with tannins ranging from soft and approachable to firm and drying. These regions are useful starting points, not rigid style labels or rankings. Australian Cabernet is made in many other areas too, so the region on the label can offer a clue without telling you everything about the wine. You can explore broader regional relationships through the Australian wine regions hub and the Yarra Valley guide . How should a beginner choose Cabernet Sauvignon? Start by considering the style you are likely to enjoy. Look for clues such as: “Medium bodied” for a less weighty style. “Full bodied” for a richer, more powerful style. “Soft tannins” if you are new to structured red wine. “Firm tannins” if you enjoy a drying, savoury grip. “Cool climate” for potentially more restrained fruit and fresher structure. “Oak matured” if you enjoy cedar, toast or spice. “Unoaked” or lightly oaked if you want more direct fruit character. These descriptions are useful guides, not guarantees. The region, vintage and producer’s approach can all change the result. Serve Cabernet Sauvignon slightly cool rather than warm. If the wine tastes tight or strongly tannic, giving it time in the glass may help it open up. More detailed serving and decanting advice belongs in dedicated WineDaddy guides. What food goes with Cabernet Sauvignon? Cabernet Sauvignon works well with rich, savoury foods because its body and tannin can match protein and substantial textures. Try it with: beef lamb darker game meats braised red-meat dishes roasted or grilled mushrooms firm cheeses Steak is a familiar match, but it is not the only one. The important idea is balance: tannin can feel smoother alongside protein-rich food, while acidity helps keep a rich pairing fresh. Cabernet Sauvignon FAQs Is Cabernet Sauvignon sweet? Most still Cabernet Sauvignon is dry. Dark-fruit flavours such as blackcurrant, blackberry and plum can taste ripe or rich without meaning the wine contains much residual sugar. Is Cabernet Sauvignon dry? Usually, yes. “Dry” refers to the amount of perceptible residual sugar, not whether the wine tastes fruity. A dry Cabernet Sauvignon can still have generous fruit flavours. Is Cabernet Sauvignon full bodied? It is often medium to full bodied, but not every Cabernet Sauvignon is heavy. Climate, ripeness, extraction, blending and oak can make a wine feel lighter, softer or richer. Is Cabernet Sauvignon very tannic? Cabernet Sauvignon is commonly associated with noticeable, sometimes firm tannin. The intensity depends on the grapes, winemaking, blending and age of the wine. Can Cabernet Sauvignon age? Some Cabernet Sauvignon can age for many years because of its acidity, tannin, concentration and structure. Many bottles, however, are made to enjoy earlier. The individual wine and its storage conditions matter. What is the simplest way to understand Cabernet Sauvignon? Think of it as a red grape that often combines dark fruit, freshness and structure . Once you know that, the region, oak and age help explain why one Cabernet Sauvignon may feel very different from another.

title: What Is Chardonnay?
description: Chardonnay is a versatile white wine grape that can make fresh, citrusy, oaky, creamy, still or sparkling wines. Learn what it tastes like and why styles vary.
text: Highlights Chardonnay is a white wine grape variety, not one fixed style of wine. It can taste fresh and citrusy, or rich, textured and creamy. Most still Chardonnay is dry, even when it smells fruity or buttery. Climate, ripeness, vineyard site and winemaking all shape its character. Oak can add toast, spice and vanilla, but Chardonnay is not automatically oaky. Malolactic fermentation can soften acidity and contribute buttery aromas. Australia produces Chardonnay in regions ranging from Tasmania and Adelaide Hills to Margaret River and Victoria. Chablis is a French region whose wines are made from Chardonnay—not a different grape. Quick Answer: What Is Chardonnay? Chardonnay is a white wine grape variety. The name also commonly refers to wine made from that grape. One reason Chardonnay is so popular is that it can make many different styles. A cool-climate Chardonnay may be light to medium-bodied, fresh and citrus-driven, with flavours such as lemon, green apple or white peach. A riper or more richly made example may be fuller and rounder, with peach, pear, melon or tropical fruit. Oak maturation, lees contact and malolactic fermentation can add texture and flavours such as toast, spice, vanilla, cream or butter. Most still Chardonnay is made as a dry wine, meaning it contains little residual sugar. That does not mean it must taste sharp or austere. Ripe fruit aromas, creamy texture, oak and alcohol warmth can create a rich or sweet impression without the wine actually being sweet. Climate is one important reason Chardonnay varies. Cooler conditions generally help preserve acidity and support fresher flavours, while warmer conditions generally encourage riper fruit and more body. Vineyard site, harvest timing and winemaking choices matter too. This is why the word “Chardonnay” on a label does not tell you one complete flavour story. Learn More What does Chardonnay taste like? There is no single Chardonnay flavour profile. It is more useful to think of Chardonnay as a broad spectrum. Fresher styles may show lemon or lime, green apple, pear, white flowers, white peach and lively acidity. They may feel light or medium-bodied, crisp and energetic. Fuller styles may show ripe peach, melon or tropical fruit, with a broader, weightier texture. If the wine has seen oak, you may also notice toast, spice or vanilla. Lees contact—the process of maturing wine with the sediment left after fermentation—can contribute extra texture and complexity. These descriptions are possibilities, not a checklist. Not every Chardonnay will taste of peach, oak or butter, and no single aroma is guaranteed by the grape. A useful beginner distinction is the difference between fruit character and winemaking influence: Fruit character can include citrus, apple, pear, peach and tropical fruit. Winemaking influence can include toast, vanilla, spice, cream and butter. The boundary is not absolute. Climate and ripeness affect fruit flavours, while winemaking can change how those flavours feel and smell. Is Chardonnay dry or sweet? Most still Chardonnay is dry. In wine language, dry refers mainly to the amount of residual sugar left in the wine—not whether it tastes fruity. A dry Chardonnay can smell like ripe peach or tropical fruit and still contain little sugar. Oak, creaminess and alcohol warmth can also make a wine seem richer or sweeter than its sugar level suggests. The specific bottle matters. Chardonnay can also be used in sparkling wine and in some sweeter styles, so the grape name alone does not guarantee a particular level of sweetness. Why can Chardonnay taste so different from bottle to bottle? Climate and ripeness Cooler conditions generally help grapes retain acidity and can support restrained citrus and stone-fruit flavours. Warmer conditions generally encourage riper fruit, more body and a richer impression. These are broad tendencies, not rules. A warm region can produce fresh wine through harvest decisions and winemaking, while a cool region can produce a textured wine through ripeness, oak or lees contact. Vineyard site Elevation, aspect, ocean influence and local temperature patterns affect how grapes ripen. Even within the same region, different sites can produce different expressions of Chardonnay. Oak Chardonnay may be unoaked, partly oaked or matured in substantial oak. Oak can add texture and flavours such as toast, spice and vanilla. Unoaked Chardonnay is often fresher and more direct, allowing fruit and acidity to take the lead. Chardonnay itself is not inherently oaky. Oak is a winemaking choice, and its influence depends on the type of oak, the vessel, the age of the barrel and the length of maturation. Malolactic fermentation Malolactic fermentation , often shortened to MLF, is a secondary biological process in which bacteria convert sharper malic acid into softer lactic acid. In Chardonnay, MLF can make the wine feel rounder or creamier and may contribute buttery aromas. Those buttery notes are associated with a compound called diacetyl. But MLF does not automatically make a Chardonnay buttery: many wines undergo little or no MLF, and the result depends on how the wine is made. Australian Chardonnay Chardonnay is Australia’s most widely planted white wine grape variety, according to Wine Australia. It is grown across a wide range of Australian climates, which helps explain the diversity of styles available here. A few regional examples show the range: Adelaide Hills: A cool, elevated South Australian region often associated with Chardonnay showing citrus, peach, freshness and texture. Margaret River: A maritime-influenced Western Australian region known for Chardonnay that can combine richness and concentration with lime-like acidity. Mornington Peninsula: An ocean-cooled Victorian region associated with restrained, medium-weight wines showing characters such as melon, white peach and citrus. Yarra Valley: A diverse Victorian region where elevation, aspect and microclimate contribute to varied, often textured Chardonnay styles. Tasmania: Important for both still Chardonnay and sparkling wine. These are broad regional tendencies, not guarantees or rankings. Australian Chardonnay includes fresh, unoaked, richly textured, oaked, still and sparkling examples. For more regional context, explore the guides to the Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula . Chardonnay can be sparkling Chardonnay is not limited to still white wine. It is also used to make sparkling wine, sometimes alongside other varieties. The production method changes the style, so a sparkling Chardonnay may taste quite different from a still Chardonnay. For a broader introduction, see What is sparkling wine? . Common Questions Is Chardonnay always oaky? No. Chardonnay may be unoaked, partly oaked or matured in oak.
