Oak can contribute toast, spice, vanilla and texture, but it is not a defining feature of the grape. Is Chardonnay always buttery? No. Buttery character can result partly from malolactic fermentation and diacetyl, but many Chardonnays are not buttery. Fresh, citrus-driven and unoaked styles may show no buttery character at all. What is the difference between Chardonnay and Chablis? Chardonnay is the grape variety. Chablis is a French wine region and appellation whose wines are made from Chardonnay. Chablis is therefore one regional expression of Chardonnay, not a separate grape. How should Chardonnay be served? Serving temperature can change how acidity, aroma and body feel, but detailed temperature guidance belongs in Wine serving temperature explained . In general, avoid serving Chardonnay extremely warm or so cold that its aroma and texture disappear. What food goes with Chardonnay? Chardonnay’s acidity, body and texture make it useful with many foods, but pairing depends on the style of the wine and the dish. Lighter styles often suit delicate food, while richer styles can handle more flavour and texture. Practical Takeaway If you are choosing or tasting Chardonnay, do not ask only, “Do I like Chardonnay?” Ask what style it is. Look for clues such as: a cooler or warmer region; fresh versus ripe fruit descriptions; unoaked or oaked production; a lighter or fuller body; still or sparkling wine. The most useful expectation is that Chardonnay is adaptable. It can be crisp and refreshing, broad and textured, or somewhere between the two.

title: What Is Cold Soak in Winemaking?
description: Cold soak is a cool, pre-fermentation period of skin contact used mainly in red-wine production. Learn how it may influence colour, aroma, flavour and tannin.
text: Highlights Cold soak is a cool period of skin contact before alcoholic fermentation begins. It is mainly used when making red wine. Winemakers use it to influence colour, aroma, flavour and texture. Cold soak may delay or limit fermentation, but it does not necessarily stop all microbial activity. The result depends on the grapes, temperature, duration and what happens afterwards. It is not the same as cold fermentation, cold stabilisation or carbonic maceration. Cold soak is a winemaking choice—not a guarantee of a darker, fruitier, smoother or better wine. Quick answer Cold soak is a pre-fermentation period when crushed red grapes or grape must are kept cool while the juice remains in contact with the skins and seeds . The cool conditions are intended to delay or limit alcoholic fermentation while extraction begins. Winemakers may use cold soak to influence the wine’s colour, aroma, flavour and tannin structure. Before alcohol is produced, the extraction environment is different from the one created during fermentation. This can change which compounds move from the skins and seeds into the juice. The effect is not automatic. Cold soak may contribute to deeper colour or more noticeable fruit character in some wines, while producing little measurable difference in others. Tannin, bitterness and astringency may also change, depending on the grape variety, ripeness, temperature, length of the soak, fruit condition and the fermentation and maceration that follow. So, in plain English: cold soak gives a winemaker another opportunity to shape a red wine before fermentation gets underway . How cold soak fits into winemaking After red grapes are crushed, the resulting mixture of juice, skins and seeds is called must . During a cold soak, the must is held at a low temperature before substantial alcoholic fermentation begins. The juice remains with the skins and seeds for a period of time. Once fermentation starts, yeast converts grape sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. That alcohol changes the conditions in which compounds are extracted from the grape solids. Cold soak therefore occupies a specific place in the process: Grapes are crushed. Juice, skins and seeds remain together. The must is kept cool before substantial fermentation. Alcoholic fermentation begins. Skin contact and extraction continue according to the winemaker’s broader choices. The wine is eventually pressed and matured. Cold soak is sometimes called pre-fermentation cold maceration or pre-ferment maceration . “Maceration” is the broader term for keeping juice in contact with grape solids. Cold soak is one particular type of maceration, defined by its timing and cool conditions. Why do winemakers use it? The main aim is to influence extraction before alcohol is present. Winemakers may be seeking changes in: Colour Red wine colour comes largely from compounds in grape skins. Cold soak may help extract colour in some circumstances, but research does not show a universal result. Vintage, grape maturity, variety, temperature and later maceration can all change the outcome. A cold-soaked wine is not automatically darker or more colour-stable than one made without the technique. Aroma and flavour Skin contact before fermentation may influence the compounds that contribute to aroma and flavour. Some winemakers use cold soak with the intention of encouraging fruit expression or adding another layer of character. However, the finished aroma is also shaped by yeast, fermentation temperature, cap management, maturation and blending. If a wine smells fruitier, cold soak may be one contributing factor—but it is rarely the only explanation. Texture and tannin Tannins contribute grip, dryness and astringency. Cold soak changes the timing and conditions of extraction, so it may affect the balance between colour, tannin and texture. This is where simple explanations become unreliable. Cold soak is sometimes described as extracting colour while limiting tannin, but studies have also found different tannin results depending on the fruit and treatment. It is more accurate to say that cold soak may alter the wine’s textural balance rather than promising softer tannins. What affects the result? Cold soak is not a single fixed recipe. Its effect can vary with: grape variety, including Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or Pinot Noir; grape ripeness and seed maturity; fruit condition; temperature; length of time; yeast activity; sulphur dioxide use; how the must is handled; the temperature and length of the fermentation that follows; and later maturation and blending. These variables matter in Australian winemaking too. Australian readers may encounter “cold soak” in discussions of Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir and other red wines, but the technique is not uniquely Australian and is not used by every producer. Research involving Australian-relevant varieties has found that results can differ with variety and climate. What might you notice in the finished wine? If cold soak has influenced a wine, you might notice a difference in colour, fruit expression, body or texture. Some wines may seem more aromatic or fruit-driven; others may show a different level of grip, bitterness or astringency. But you cannot reliably identify cold soak from one bottle. The wine’s character reflects the combined effect of the grapes, vintage, fermentation, extraction, maturation and blending. A tasting note that mentions ripe fruit or smooth tannins does not prove that cold soak was used. Cold soak compared with similar terms Cold soak and cold fermentation These are not the same. Cold soak happens before alcoholic fermentation. Cold fermentation means the alcoholic fermentation itself is carried out at a relatively low temperature. Cold soak and cold stabilisation Cold stabilisation is a later treatment applied to wine, usually by chilling it so tartrate crystals can form and be removed or reduced before bottling. It is not a grape-skin extraction technique. Cold soak and extended maceration Extended maceration usually means keeping wine in contact with skins and seeds for an extended period, often after fermentation. Cold soak happens before substantial fermentation, so the timing and extraction conditions differ. Cold soak and carbonic maceration Carbonic maceration is a different technique involving whole or mostly intact grapes in a carbon-dioxide-rich environment. It encourages intracellular fermentation. It is not simply a colder version of ordinary maceration. Frequently asked questions Does cold soak make the wine colder? Only during that stage of production. “Cold soak” describes a cool pre-fermentation process, not the serving temperature of the finished wine. Does cold soak always increase tannin? No. Tannin results vary with the grapes and the winemaking that follows. Cold soak may change the balance of tannin, bitterness and astringency, but it does not guarantee a particular texture. Does every red wine use cold soak? No. It is a common option in red-wine production, but winemakers choose techniques according to the fruit, wine style, winery facilities and desired result. Is cold-soaked wine better? Not automatically. Cold soak is a tool, and its success depends on how it suits the fruit and the rest of the winemaking process. Cold soak is best understood as one decision within a much larger chain of decisions. To place it in context, read How wine is made . You can also explore How to taste wine to think about how colour, aroma and texture appear in the glass.

title: What Is Complexity in Wine?
description: Wine complexity explained in plain English: learn how to recognise layers, development and integration, and how complexity differs from intensity, oak, age and quality.
text: Highlights Complexity is the impression that a wine offers several distinct, connected and sometimes evolving aromas, flavours and textures. It is not simply a long list of tasting-note descriptors. A wine can be intense but simple, or restrained but complex. Age, oak, price and concentration may contribute to complexity, but none guarantees it. Complexity is different from balance, length, quality and personal preference. You can look for complexity by smelling, tasting and revisiting a wine slowly. Quick Answer: What Does Complexity Mean in Wine? Complexity in wine describes the range, interaction and development of the sensations a wine offers. A complex wine may show fruit, floral, herbal, spicy, savoury, earthy or developed characteristics, with these details appearing together or revealing themselves over time. The key is not how many flavours you can name. Complexity is more about whether the wine offers several recognisable dimensions that feel connected and continue to interest you. One sip might begin with dark fruit, then reveal spice, savoury notes and a fine, lingering texture. Complexity is a sensory impression, not a direct measurement of how many chemical compounds are in a wine. It is also partly subjective: your experience can be influenced by your expectations, vocabulary, tasting context and familiarity with wine. A complex wine is not automatically better. It may be unbalanced, faulty or simply unlike your preferred style. Conversely, a straightforward wine can be clean, balanced and thoroughly enjoyable. How Can You Recognise Complexity? Start by smelling the wine before swirling. What is the first clear impression? It might be citrus, red fruit, dark fruit, flowers or herbs. Now swirl gently and smell again. Are there additional details, or has the original aroma simply become stronger? Complexity may involve a broader range of aromas rather than greater intensity alone. Take a small sip and notice what happens across your palate. Do fruit, freshness, texture, warmth or savoury flavours appear at different points? Does the finish add another dimension? After a minute or two, taste the wine again. It may seem more open or show a different emphasis. This is an observation framework, not a test with a correct number of answers. Not every complex wine changes dramatically in the glass, and a wine that changes quickly may be warming, oxidising or revealing a fault rather than becoming more complex. Useful questions include: Does the wine offer more than one clear sensory dimension? Do the aromas and flavours develop or deepen? Are the details distinct but connected? Does the finish remain interesting? Can you recognise the same characteristics on a second sip? Is the wine genuinely layered, or simply dominated by one powerful flavour? Complexity Is Not the Same as Intensity Intensity describes how strongly a characteristic is perceived. Complexity describes the range, relationship and development of the characteristics. A wine with very powerful ripe-fruit aromas may be intense but straightforward. Another wine may be quieter yet reveal subtle floral, herbal, savoury and earthy details. It can be complex without being loud. The same distinction applies to concentration. A concentrated wine can feel dense and full of flavour while still having a narrow flavour profile. Complexity does not require a wine to be full-bodied or powerful. A helpful shortcut is: Intensity asks, “How strong is it?” Complexity asks, “What else is happening, and how do the different elements develop together?” Complexity, Balance and Finish Complexity and balance can support each other, but they describe different things. Balance concerns the relationship among a wine’s major components, such as fruit, acidity, sweetness, alcohol, tannin, body and texture. Complexity concerns the range and development of the wine’s aromas, flavours and sensations. A complex wine can still feel unbalanced if alcohol, acidity, tannin or oak dominates. A simple wine can be well balanced and enjoyable without offering many layers. A long finish —the sensations that remain after swallowing or spitting—may add to a wine’s complexity. But length alone is not complexity. A single flavour that lingers for a long time is still only one main dimension. Does Oak Create Complexity? Oak can add aromas and flavours such as vanilla, toast, cedar, baking spice or smoke. It can also contribute to texture and maturation. However, obvious oak flavour is not automatically complexity. Oak may add a convincing extra layer when it fits with the wine’s fruit, freshness, structure and development. If it dominates, it can hide other details. An unoaked wine can be complex, and a heavily oaked wine can be simple. The question is whether the oak is integrated into a broader, coherent impression. Does Age Make Wine More Complex? Bottle age can add or emphasise developed characteristics such as dried fruit, leather, tobacco, earth, nuts, dried flowers or savoury notes. This is one way a wine may gain new layers over time. But an old wine is not automatically complex. Storage conditions matter, and some wines are made to be enjoyed young. A mature wine can also be tired, oxidised or faulty. Young wine is not automatically simple either: it may already show several integrated aromas, flavours and structural sensations. Age is therefore a possible contributor, not a guarantee. What Contributes to Complexity? Complexity can be influenced by many parts of a wine’s journey, including: grape variety; site, climate and vintage; fruit ripeness; blending; yeast and fermentation; malolactic fermentation; skin or stem contact; lees contact; oak; maturation; bottle age; serving temperature and aeration. These factors create opportunities for different characteristics to develop, but they do not work like a recipe. The result depends on the wine, the producer’s choices, the vintage and how the wine is served. Fermentation and maturation can add dimensions beyond fresh grape fruit. A blend may combine different components. Time in bottle may introduce developed characters. None of these automatically makes a wine complex. Australian Examples In Australia, “complex” is generally used as a descriptive tasting or review term. It is not a regulated quality classification or mandatory label category. A young Australian Shiraz might show dark fruit, spice, floral notes and firm structure. With suitable development, another Shiraz may gain savoury, earthy, dried-fruit, leather or tobacco-like characters. These are possible examples, not a fixed profile for every Australian Shiraz. Australian Cabernet Sauvignon may combine dark fruit with leafy, herbal, cedar, spicy or savoury notes, depending on its site, vintage and winemaking. Chardonnay may bring together citrus or stone fruit, lees, toast, texture and bottle development. Australian fortified wines can show layered fruit, nutty, oxidative, spicy and spirit-related characters within their own styles. None of these varieties or styles is inherently complex. Producer, vineyard site, vintage, winemaking and age all matter. Can a Simple Wine Still Be Good? Absolutely. Complexity is only one possible quality attribute, and it is not a guarantee that you will enjoy a wine. A wine may be complex but unbalanced. It may be technically impressive but made in a style you dislike. A simpler wine may be fresh, balanced, clean and exactly what you want with dinner. Try to separate three questions: What can I smell and taste? How do the elements relate to one another? Do I enjoy this wine? There is no requirement to prefer complexity. Understanding the term simply makes tasting notes and wine conversations easier to interpret. A Simple Way to Taste for Complexity The next time you open a bottle: Smell before swirling and note the obvious first impression. Swirl gently and look for additional aromas, not just a stronger version of the first one. Take a small sip and notice flavour, freshness, texture and warmth. Pay attention to the middle of the palate and the finish. Wait a minute or two, then taste again. Write down what you notice before deciding whether you like it. Ask whether the characteristics are distinct but connected. You do not need specialist vocabulary. “The fruit is joined by spice and a savoury note” is more useful than forcing yourself to identify an exact aroma. Complexity is not a competition to name the most flavours. It is the experience of discovering range, connection and development in the glass. Frequently Asked Questions Is complexity the same as having many flavours? No. Many flavours may contribute to complexity, but they need to be recognisable and meaningfully connected. A long or imaginative list of descriptors does not prove that a wine is complex. Are complex wines always expensive? No. Price does not guarantee complexity, and complexity does not establish a wine’s price or quality. Are older wines more complex? Not necessarily. Age can add developed layers to some wines, but storage, style and the wine’s condition matter. Young wines can also be complex. Does a complex wine have to be full-bodied? No. Complexity can appear in a lighter-bodied or restrained wine. Power and weight are not requirements. Can a wine be complex but not enjoyable? Yes. Complexity is different from personal preference. A wine can offer many connected dimensions while still being a style you do not like.

title: What Is Cork Taint?
description: Cork taint can mute fruit and create musty aromas. Learn how to recognise it, what causes it and what to do with an affected bottle.
text: Highlights Cork taint is a wine fault usually associated with a compound called TCA . It can smell like damp cardboard, wet newspaper, a mouldy cellar or a musty basement. The wine’s normal fruit may seem muted, flat or strangely quiet. Cork taint is not the same as cork fragments, sediment, oxidation or every unpleasant smell. It usually makes wine defective and unpleasant rather than enjoyable to drink as intended. Natural cork is a common pathway, but contamination can also come from winery materials or environments. If a bottle seems cork-tainted, keep the bottle, closure and proof of purchase where practical, then contact the retailer. Quick answer: what is cork taint? Cork taint is an unpleasant sensory fault in wine, most commonly associated with 2,4,6-trichloroanisole , usually shortened to TCA . Affected wine may smell musty or mouldy, like damp cardboard, wet newspaper or a dusty cellar. Its usual fruit aromas can seem suppressed, leaving the wine dull, flat or lifeless. The name can be misleading. Cork taint does not necessarily mean the cork looks damaged, and it does not prove that the closure alone caused the problem. TCA and related compounds can be associated with natural cork, wood-based materials, winery equipment, storage materials or contaminated environments. The practical question is often not “Can I prove this is TCA?” but “Does this bottle smell and taste so unlike the wine it should be that it seems faulty?” If it does, do not serve it as normal. Keep the bottle and closure, retain your receipt or other proof of purchase where possible, and ask the retailer how they handle suspected faulty wine. What does cork taint smell and taste like? The most familiar descriptions are: damp cardboard; wet newspaper; a mouldy cellar; a musty basement; dusty, stale or earthy aromas. Cork taint is often less like adding a single obvious “cork flavour” and more like turning down the volume on the wine. The fruit becomes difficult to smell, the palate may seem muted, and the finish can feel dull or shortened. A wine affected at a low level may simply seem strangely quiet or less expressive than expected. A stronger example is usually easier to recognise because the musty character is more obvious. These descriptions are useful clues, not a laboratory diagnosis. A musty, earthy or flat wine can have other causes, and more than one fault can occur in the same bottle. Why is TCA associated with cork taint? TCA belongs to a wider chemical group called haloanisoles . These compounds can have an odour at extremely low concentrations, although the level at which people detect or recognise them varies. That variation matters. There is no single threshold that applies equally to every person, wine or tasting situation. Perception can be influenced by the wine’s composition, the concentration of the compound, the temperature and the drinker’s individual sensitivity. Natural cork is a well-known pathway for TCA contamination. However, contamination may also involve wood, winery equipment, storage materials or cellar environments. Compounds can move between contaminated and clean materials during handling or storage. So, “corked” is best understood as consumer shorthand for a sensory condition. It is not proof that a visibly defective cork caused the wine’s problem. Can a screw-cap wine be corked? A screw-cap bottle does not have a natural cork closure to provide the usual cork-related pathway. However, TCA or a related compound can, rarely, enter through another production, storage or handling pathway. That means a screw-cap wine can show a similar musty taint, although this is not a reason to assume that screw-cap wines commonly have the problem. The important distinction is between the closure and the broader contamination pathways that can affect wine. Cork taint compared with other wine problems Unpleasant wine aromas are not all the same. These broad distinctions can help: Problem Common clues Cork taint Musty or mouldy character, damp cardboard or wet newspaper; muted fruit Oxidation Bruised or stale fruit, nutty or sherry-like notes, and reduced freshness Reduction Sulphury smells such as struck match, rubber, cabbage or rotten egg Brettanomyces Farmyard, leather, medicinal, smoky or horsey notes, depending on its level Volatile acidity Vinegar or nail-polish-remover character Cork fragments Physical pieces floating in the wine or sitting at the bottom Sediment Natural particles, colour deposits or crystals; not automatically a fault These are orientation points rather than definitive tests. For example, earthy notes may overlap between different wine issues, and a wine can have more than one problem. Cork pieces are particularly easy to confuse with cork taint. A fragment in the glass is a physical nuisance, not evidence that the wine has absorbed TCA. Likewise, sediment does not automatically mean the wine is spoiled. Is cork-tainted wine safe to drink? Research supplied for this guide supports treating cork taint primarily as a wine-quality and sensory problem. It does not support an absolute claim that every TCA-affected wine is medically harmless, nor does it establish a simple household safety threshold. For a drinker, the usual practical issue is that the wine is faulty and unpleasant rather than that it tastes normal while secretly presenting a known danger. It should not be served as intended if the fault is clear. If a wine has an unusual smell or taste and you are concerned, stop drinking it and contact the retailer or producer. Avoid treating smell alone as proof of a health risk, but do not feel obliged to finish a bottle that seems contaminated or otherwise unsafe. Can you fix cork taint at home? There is no dependable household cure that should be promised for cork taint. Aeration or decanting may change how a wine smells, but that does not mean the TCA has been removed. Chilling can temporarily alter perception without removing the contamination. Straining can remove a piece of cork, but it cannot be treated as a way to remove dissolved TCA. The most useful response is practical rather than experimental: stop serving the bottle if the fault is clear and seek a retailer or producer response. What should you do with a corked bottle in Australia? Before disposing of the wine, keep the following where practical: the bottle; the closure; the receipt, online order record or other proof of purchase; the wine’s name, vintage and batch details. Contact the retailer first and explain that the wine appears cork-tainted. The retailer may ask to inspect the bottle or closure. Australian consumer guidance says the business that sold the product is the first point of contact for a product problem, while the remedy depends on the circumstances and seriousness of the problem. Do not assume that every retailer will handle an opened bottle in exactly the same way, and do not assume that a refund or replacement is guaranteed in every case. A calm explanation and the original bottle details make the issue easier to assess. Frequently asked questions Can you taste cork? People commonly say they can “taste cork”, but cork taint is usually recognised through both smell and flavour. The strongest clues are often a musty or mouldy aroma and fruit that seems suppressed or absent. “Corked” is shorthand for the wine’s tainted sensory condition, not necessarily a literal taste of cork. Does cork taint come from the cork? Often, natural cork is the pathway. But not always. TCA and related compounds can also be associated with contaminated winery materials, wood, equipment, storage materials or environments. The cork does not need to look visibly defective. Can a screw-cap wine be corked? Yes, in the broader sensory sense, although it is uncommon. A screw cap removes the natural-cork pathway, but TCA or a related compound can potentially enter through another production, storage or handling pathway. The useful takeaway If a wine smells like a damp cellar and its fruit has gone quiet, cork taint is one possibility. Do not confuse it with cork debris, sediment or every other wine fault. If the bottle clearly seems faulty, preserve the bottle and closure, keep proof of purchase where possible, and contact the retailer rather than accepting the wine as normal. Related learning: What is wine? · How wine is made

title: What Is Fermentation? How It Turns Grape Juice Into Wine
description: Fermentation is the process in which yeast converts grape sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and flavour compounds. Learn how it shapes wine.
text: Highlights Fermentation is the biological process that turns grape sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Yeast is the main microorganism responsible for alcoholic fermentation. Fermentation also produces heat and compounds that influence aroma and flavour. Fermentation is one stage of winemaking—not a name for every cellar operation. Red, white and rosé wines can ferment in different ways, especially in their contact with grape skins. Malolactic fermentation is a separate bacterial process that changes acidity; it does not create the wine’s alcohol. Australian wineries manage fermentation differently depending on climate, grape variety, vintage and desired style. Quick Answer: What is fermentation? In winemaking, fermentation is a biological process in which microorganisms convert grape sugars into new compounds. During alcoholic fermentation , yeast consumes fermentable sugars and produces ethanol, carbon dioxide and heat. A simple way to picture it is: grape sugars → alcohol + carbon dioxide + heat That equation is useful, but incomplete. Yeast also produces other compounds that can contribute to a wine’s aroma, flavour and texture. The way fermentation proceeds can influence whether a wine tastes dry or sweet, how much alcohol it contains, which aromas it retains and how it feels in the mouth. Fermentation is central to making wine, but it is not the whole process. Crushing, pressing, skin contact, clarification, maturation and bottling are separate winemaking operations. To understand the bigger picture, see how wine is made , or explore the broader winemaking hub. What does yeast do in wine? Yeast is a type of fungus. In alcoholic fermentation, it uses sugar as an energy source and converts it mainly into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The best-known wine-fermentation yeast belongs to the genus Saccharomyces . Winemakers may deliberately add a selected yeast culture, or allow an uninoculated fermentation to begin with microorganisms already present on the grapes or in the winery environment. Neither approach is automatically better. Selected yeast can offer predictability, while an uninoculated fermentation may involve more microbial variation. Its outcome depends on the organisms present and the conditions in the ferment—not on the word “native” alone. Yeast also produces heat as it works. In a winery, temperature may therefore be monitored and managed, particularly when a vigorous fermentation could become stressful for the yeast or affect the wine’s aromas and structure. Where does fermentation fit into winemaking? Fermentation usually begins after grapes have been harvested and processed, but the exact sequence depends on the wine style. For white wine, grapes are commonly pressed before fermentation, so the yeast works mainly in juice with relatively few solids. Red wine commonly ferments as must —crushed grapes that include juice, skins and seeds. This skin contact helps extract colour, tannins and other compounds. Rosé production can follow several paths. Red grapes may be pressed early, allowing the juice to ferment with limited skin contact, or processed using another method designed to achieve a particular colour and style. These are typical pathways rather than strict rules. Skin-contact whites, sparkling base wines and other specialised styles use different arrangements. Fermentation is the biological stage, while pressing, skin contact and maturation are separate decisions that shape the final wine alongside it. How do winemakers manage fermentation? Winemakers manage the fermentation environment rather than simply letting sugar disappear. Important variables include: Temperature Temperature affects how quickly yeast grows and ferments. Cooler conditions generally slow fermentation and can help retain some volatile aromas. Warmer conditions can accelerate fermentation and increase extraction from skins and seeds in red wine, but may also increase the loss of certain aromas or place more stress on yeast. There is no single “best” fermentation temperature for every wine. The decision depends on the grapes, yeast, solids, vessel and style being made. Yeast and other microorganisms Different yeast populations can ferment at different rates and produce different aroma compounds. Saccharomyces is usually associated with completing alcoholic fermentation, while other yeasts may contribute earlier or alongside it. The microbial population can vary between vineyards, wineries, regions and vintages. That is one reason fermentation is a biological process with variation, not a completely identical factory reaction. Oxygen Alcoholic fermentation can proceed under low- or no-oxygen conditions, but oxygen is not irrelevant. The amount and timing of oxygen can affect yeast growth and the wider microbial environment. Its influence depends on the wine, the stage of fermentation and the cellar conditions. Vessel, grape solids and timing A fermentation vessel affects heat transfer, oxygen exposure and how easily the ferment can be managed. Grape solids and skin contact also change the environment in which fermentation takes place. Timing matters too. The length of fermentation and the point at which grapes are pressed or separated from solids can influence extraction, aroma and texture. These choices are why fermentation cannot be separated entirely from the winemaking decisions around it. How does fermentation change the wine? When yeast consumes fermentable sugar, the wine generally becomes less sweet. A wine described as dry has little remaining fermentable sugar compared with a sweet wine, although “dry” does not mean flavourless. Fruit aromas can remain even after much of the sugar has been consumed. This is an important distinction: sweetness and flavour are not the same thing. A dry wine can still smell and taste strongly of fruit. Fermentation also contributes to: Alcohol: ethanol is one of the principal products of sugar fermentation. Aroma: yeast metabolism produces compounds that can add to the wine’s aromatic profile. Carbon dioxide: this gas is produced during fermentation and may escape, dissolve in the wine or be retained intentionally in sparkling-wine production. Texture: alcohol, yeast-derived compounds, skin contact and fermentation conditions can all influence mouthfeel. Acidity and stability: fermentation interacts with later microbial processes and cellar decisions that affect the wine’s balance and stability. Bubbles alone do not prove which microorganism is active. Carbon dioxide shows that microbial activity is occurring, but it does not identify the dominant organism. Alcoholic fermentation versus malolactic fermentation The two processes have different jobs: Process Main microorganism Main input Main result Alcoholic fermentation Yeast Grape sugars Ethanol, carbon dioxide, heat and other metabolites Malolactic fermentation Lactic acid bacteria Malic acid Lactic acid, carbon dioxide and a changed acid profile Malolactic fermentation is the familiar wine term for a bacterial conversion that changes malic acid into lactic acid. “Malolactic conversion” is technically more precise. It does not turn sugar into alcohol. Instead, it can make acidity seem softer or less sharp, raise the wine’s pH and influence aroma and texture. It may happen after alcoholic fermentation, although winemaking practices can vary. For the full explanation, see the forthcoming guide to [what is malolactic fermentation?]. You can also explore related techniques such as whole-bunch winemaking and carbonic maceration . What is different about fermentation in Australia? Australian wine regions cover a wide range of climates, from cool maritime and elevated areas to warmer inland and continental environments. As a result, Australian wineries do not use one universal fermentation approach. Temperature management and other cellar decisions vary with the region, vintage, grape composition, winery equipment and intended style. Research into Australian wine has also found variation in yeast communities across regions, vineyards, wineries and vintages. That variation helps explain why the same broad grape variety or winemaking method can produce different results in different Australian places. Fermentation is important, but it works alongside vineyard conditions and every other stage of winemaking. Frequently asked questions Does fermentation make wine? It makes the alcohol that defines alcoholic wine, but fermentation alone does not complete winemaking. Pressing, skin contact, clarification, maturation and bottling also matter. Does fermentation always make wine dry? No. Fermentation can stop while some sugar remains, and winemakers may also make later decisions that affect sweetness. Dry means low in remaining fermentable sugar, not low in flavour. Is native yeast better than added yeast? Not automatically. Uninoculated fermentations can produce different and sometimes complex results, while selected yeast can make fermentation more predictable. Neither is universally superior. Is malolactic fermentation the same as alcoholic fermentation? No. Alcoholic fermentation is primarily yeast-driven and converts sugar into alcohol. Malolactic fermentation is bacterial and converts malic acid into lactic acid. Does fermentation determine a wine’s entire character? No. Grape variety, vineyard, climate, pressing, skin contact, maturation, oak, blending and bottling also contribute to the finished wine. The simple takeaway Fermentation is the biological engine at the centre of winemaking: yeast transforms grape sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat, while producing compounds that help shape the wine’s aroma and texture. Winemakers manage that process according to the grapes, conditions and style they want—but fermentation is only one part of the journey from grape to bottle.

title: What is fortified wine?
description: Fortified wine is wine with distilled spirit added. Learn why some styles are sweet, others dry and what Australian fortified terms mean.
text: Highlights Fortified wine is wine with distilled spirit added to increase its alcohol level. The spirit may be added before fermentation finishes or after it has finished. Early fortification usually leaves more natural grape sugar, creating a sweeter wine. Later fortification can produce a dry fortified wine. Fortified wine is not the same thing as sweet wine, dessert wine or a spirit. Fortified wines can be shaped by wood, oxygen, flor yeast and bottle maturation. Australia has a long fortified-wine history, particularly with styles from Rutherglen. Apera and Topaque are the current Australian terms associated with wines once commonly called Australian Sherry and Tokay. Quick answer Fortified wine is wine that has had distilled spirit added to it, increasing its alcoholic strength. The base wine is made through fermentation, like other wine, but the added spirit changes its alcohol level, texture, sweetness and potential for ageing. The timing of that addition matters. If spirit is added while fermentation is still under way, it can stop or inhibit the yeast. Some natural grape sugar remains, so the finished wine is often sweet. If the wine is allowed to ferment until it is dry and is fortified afterwards, the result can be a dry fortified wine. That is why fortified wine is a production category rather than a single flavour profile. It can be rich and sweet, light and dry, nutty and oxidative, or fresh and aromatic. Fortified wine is also not a spirit. A spirit is made primarily through distillation. Fortified wine begins as fermented wine and remains wine-based, even though distilled spirit has been added. How is fortified wine made? Fortified wine begins with a base wine : wine made from fermented grape juice. During fermentation, yeast converts grape sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. At a chosen point, the winemaker adds a distilled spirit, commonly grape spirit in classic fortified-wine production. This raises the wine’s alcoholic strength. The exact process varies between styles and producers. Early fortification: usually sweeter When spirit is added before fermentation has finished, the increased alcohol can stop or inhibit the yeast. The wine retains more residual sugar —sugar left in the finished wine—and is generally sweeter and fuller-bodied. Late fortification: potentially dry When fermentation is allowed to finish first, most fermentable sugar may be converted into alcohol. The wine can then be fortified after it has become dry. This produces a dry fortified style. Many Sherry styles, and Australian fortified wines made in a Sherry-like tradition, show that fortified wine does not have to be sweet. Fortified wine versus table wine, sweet wine and spirits Fortified wine describes a production method: distilled spirit has been added. Sweet or dry describes the level of perceptible sweetness. Dessert wine is a broad serving or style description, not a specific production method. Spirit describes a distilled alcoholic drink, rather than wine with spirit added. Table wine is a useful everyday term for ordinary still wine that has not been fortified, although its legal meaning can vary. A fortified wine may be sweet or dry. A sweet wine may be unfortified. And a spirit may be used to fortify wine without turning the finished drink into a spirit. The main fortified-wine families Port Port is a fortified wine from Portugal’s Douro region. It is commonly associated with sweet, fruit-driven wines, often red, although white and rosé examples also exist. Because Port is a protected geographical name, it should not be treated as a casual generic name for every sweet fortified wine made in Australia. Sherry and Apera Sherry is associated with the Jerez region of Spain and includes both dry and sweet styles. Some styles mature under a layer of flor , a film-forming yeast, while others develop through controlled exposure to oxygen. In Australia, Apera is the current protected term for qualifying Australian fortified wines made in a Sherry-like style. Madeira Madeira is known for distinctive maturation traditions involving heat and oxygen. These processes can create concentrated, nutty, dried-fruit and caramel-like flavours. Australian Muscat and Topaque Australia is especially well known for sweet fortified wines made from Muscat, including the historic styles associated with Rutherglen in Victoria. Topaque is the current Australian term for qualifying fortified wines formerly associated with the Australian use of “Tokay”. Vermouth Vermouth is an aromatised wine: it is generally fortified and flavoured with botanicals. Its use in cocktails and botanical flavouring make it a distinct subject of its own. How ageing changes fortified wine Fortification is only part of the story. Maturation can change a fortified wine just as dramatically. Some wines age in wood. Others mature with controlled oxygen exposure, contributing nutty, dried-fruit, caramel-like or savoury characters. Some styles develop under flor yeast. Others continue to develop in bottle. Spirit addition changes strength and can affect sweetness. Wood ageing changes texture and flavour. Oxygen exposure can create oxidative character. Flor ageing gives some wines a distinctive biological ageing profile. Bottle ageing may allow further development after bottling. Why fortified wine matters in Australia Fortified wine was central to Australian wine production and drinking culture through much of the twentieth century. Wine Australia describes fortified wines as the focus of the Australian industry until the 1970s, when preferences shifted towards other wine styles. That history is still visible in regions such as Rutherglen, which remains strongly associated with fortified wines including Muscat. Australian terminology has changed as geographical names and traditional terms have received greater protection: Apera replaced “Sherry” for qualifying Australian fortified wines. Topaque replaced “Tokay” for qualifying Australian fortified wines. Port is a protected geographical name associated with Portugal. How should fortified wine be served? Dry and lighter fortified wines are commonly served chilled or cool and can work as aperitifs or alongside savoury foods. Richer, sweeter styles are often served cool rather than very cold and can suit desserts, blue cheese, nuts or dried fruit. These are useful starting points, not rules. A modest pour in a small wine or fortified-wine glass is practical because fortified wines are usually served in smaller quantities than table wine. How should an opened bottle be stored? Reseal an opened bottle promptly and store it upright in a cool, dark place. Refrigeration is a sensible default because keeping the bottle cool slows chemical changes. There is no single guaranteed shelf life for every fortified wine. A style that has already spent a long time ageing oxidatively may remain enjoyable longer than a delicate, fresh or fruit-driven wine. The easiest way to remember fortified wine Was spirit added? If yes, the wine is fortified. How much sugar remains? That helps determine whether it tastes dry or sweet. How was it matured? Wood, oxygen, flor and bottle ageing can all shape its character. This prevents a common misunderstanding: “fortified” does not mean “sweet”. It tells you how the wine was made. For the wider foundation, see What is wine? and How wine is made .

title: What Is Grenache? A Beginner’s Guide to the Grape and Wine
description: Grenache is a versatile red grape known for red fruit, spice and warmth. Learn about its Australian styles, blends and growing regions.
text: Highlights Grenache is a red wine grape variety, also commonly called Garnacha in Spain. It can make red wine, rosé, fortified wine and sparkling wine, although red Grenache is the main focus here. Typical red Grenache may show strawberry, raspberry, plum, spice, white pepper, herbs or savoury notes. It is often medium-bodied and generous in alcohol, but can range from light and fresh to rich and structured. Grenache may be made as a varietal wine or blended with grapes such as Shiraz and Mourvèdre. In Australia, it has an especially strong connection with South Australia, including McLaren Vale and the Barossa Valley. Fruity Grenache is not necessarily sweet: most still red Grenache is dry. Quick answer: what is Grenache? Grenache is a red wine grape variety used to make wines in many styles. It is known for ripe berry flavours, fragrant aromas and the ability to produce generous alcohol, but it does not have one fixed personality. A lighter Grenache might taste bright, juicy and fresh, with strawberry or raspberry flavours. A richer example might feel warm, full and concentrated, with plum, spice, earth or savoury notes. Tannin and acidity also vary, so Grenache can be supple and easy-drinking or firmer and more structured. You may see the name Garnacha on a Spanish wine label. In most wine contexts, Grenache and Garnacha are different names for the same red grape variety. “Grenache Blanc” and “Grenache Gris”, however, refer to related white or grey-skinned forms and should not be assumed to taste like red Grenache. What does Grenache wine taste like? Red Grenache often has an inviting, fruit-forward aroma. Common possibilities include: strawberry and raspberry; cherry and plum; darker, ripe fruit; white pepper and other spices; dried herbs; earthy or savoury notes. The wine’s colour can be lighter or more transparent than deeply coloured reds such as Cabernet Sauvignon or Shiraz. That does not necessarily mean it is light in flavour or low in alcohol. Some Grenache wines have plenty of intensity despite their moderate colour. Grenache is often described as medium-bodied, though ripe, old-vine or more extracted examples can feel full-bodied. Alcohol can add a warming, generous sensation, while acidity provides freshness and tannin contributes grip. All three vary according to the vineyard, ripeness, crop level, harvest timing and winemaking. Is Grenache sweet? Most still red Grenache is dry. However, ripe berry flavours and warming alcohol can create an impression of sweetness or richness. This is an important distinction: fruitiness is not the same as residual sugar . A dry Grenache can taste like ripe strawberries or plums without being a sweet wine. Grenache is also used for rosé and fortified wines, where the finished style can differ considerably from a dry red. Those uses are part of the variety’s versatility, rather than evidence that Grenache has one universal flavour. Why does Grenache vary so much? A grape variety provides possibilities, not a finished wine recipe. Grenache’s final style is shaped by several decisions and conditions. Climate, ripeness and harvest Grenache buds early and ripens late, making it well suited to warmer climates with a long growing season. Riper grapes can produce fuller, more generous wines, while earlier-picked fruit may retain a fresher, brighter character. That does not mean every warm-climate Grenache tastes the same. Vineyard site, vintage and the winemaker’s decisions all matter. Crop level and vine age Grenache is vigorous and can produce heavy crops. If yields are not controlled, the resulting wine may be relatively simple. Lower yields can contribute to concentration and structure, although low yield is not automatically a guarantee of quality. Old-vine Grenache is an important part of Australia’s wine story. Older vines may produce smaller crops and are often valued for their heritage and distinctive vineyard history. But “old vine” is a useful piece of context, not a promise that every bottle will be better. Winemaking choices Winemakers can change Grenache’s texture and aroma through techniques such as whole-bunch fermentation, where some intact bunches and stems are included. Cold soaking and extended maceration may also influence colour, tannin and savoury character. Oak is optional. Some Grenache is matured in large-format or older neutral oak, which can help the wine develop texture without covering its fruit with strong new-oak flavours. Grenache as a varietal wine and in blends Grenache can be bottled as a single-variety wine, allowing its fruit, fragrance and warmth to take centre stage. It is also an important blending grape. One familiar blend is GSM , shorthand for Grenache, Shiraz or Syrah, and Mataro or Mourvèdre. The proportions vary, so GSM does not describe one fixed recipe. Grenache may contribute fruit and generosity, while the other varieties can add colour, structure, spice or savoury depth. A blended wine is not a less authentic expression of Grenache. Blending is simply another way of shaping balance and texture. Grenache in Australia Grenache has a long history in Australian wine, particularly in South Australia. McLaren Vale is strongly associated with the variety and includes old-vine vineyards. The region produces a broad range, from vibrant and juicy wines to richer, more structured examples. The Barossa Valley also has significant heritage Grenache plantings, including very old vineyards. Barossa examples may show ripe red fruit, earth, white pepper, richness and texture, but these are broad tendencies rather than rules. South Australia is an important Australian Grenache context, not the only one. The variety is grown in other Australian regions, and the label, vineyard, vintage and winemaking approach will tell you more about an individual wine than the grape name alone. When buying, you might see Grenache , Grenache Noir , Garnacha , old-vine Grenache or GSM on a label. These terms can provide clues, but they do not replace tasting the wine’s actual style. How should you serve Grenache? Serve Grenache slightly cool or at a cool room temperature, adjusting for the wine in front of you. A lighter, fresher Grenache can benefit from more chilling. A richer or more structured example may show better with less chilling. Use a normal red-wine glass and give the wine a little time to open if it seems tight. Grenache’s fruit, body and spice can work well with grilled meats, lamb, game, charcuterie, roasted vegetables and lightly to moderately spiced dishes. These are suggestions, not rules. A fresh Grenache rosé may suit a very different meal from a rich, oak-matured red. Frequently asked questions Is Grenache the same as Garnacha? Generally, yes. Grenache is the common French and English-language name, while Garnacha is widely used in Spain. The wines can still taste different because of regional climate, vineyard conditions and winemaking. Is Grenache a full-bodied wine? It can be, but many examples are medium-bodied. Ripe fruit, generous alcohol, old vines and extraction can make a Grenache feel fuller and richer. Is Grenache high in alcohol? It can be relatively generous in alcohol, especially when the grapes are harvested very ripe. Earlier-picked, cooler-site and lighter styles may feel fresher and less warming. Is Grenache low in tannin? Some Grenache is supple and relatively gentle in tannin, but it is not automatically low-tannin. Stems, skin contact, seeds, extraction and blending can create more grip. What is GSM? GSM is a blend based on Grenache, Shiraz or Syrah, and Mataro or Mourvèdre. The recipe varies between wines. What should I try if I enjoy Grenache? Start by comparing a varietal Grenache with a GSM blend. Notice how the blend changes the wine’s colour, structure, spice and texture. You can also compare a lighter, fresher style with a richer South Australian example. Related learning Explore the grape variety hub What is Shiraz? What is wine? Explore Australian wine regions What is rosé? What is fortified wine?

title: What Is Malolactic Fermentation?
description: Malolactic fermentation is a bacterial conversion that changes malic acid into lactic acid. Learn how it affects acidity, texture and aroma, why winemakers manage it, and why it matters in Australian red wine and Chardonnay.
text: Highlights Malolactic fermentation (MLF) is a bacterial conversion that changes malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide. It is different from alcoholic fermentation, which is driven mainly by yeast and produces alcohol. MLF can make acidity seem less sharp and may give wine a rounder texture. It can sometimes contribute buttery or creamy aromas, but it does not automatically make wine buttery. MLF is common in many red wines and is used selectively in white wines, including Australian Chardonnay. Winemakers may encourage, prevent or partly manage MLF depending on the style they want. Quick answer Malolactic fermentation is a stage of winemaking in which lactic-acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide. Malic acid is a naturally occurring grape acid. It can contribute to a sharper, more angular impression in wine. Lactic acid is generally perceived as softer, so MLF usually reduces the sense of sharpness and changes the wine’s acid balance. It does not remove all acidity, and it does not guarantee that a wine will taste soft or creamy. Despite its name, MLF is not the same as the alcoholic fermentation that produces wine’s alcohol. Alcoholic fermentation is mainly performed by yeast, which converts grape sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. MLF is a bacterial conversion of acid. Winemakers may allow MLF to happen naturally, use selected bacteria to manage it, prevent it, or allow it in only part of a wine. The decision depends on the grape, vintage, acidity, intended style and the wine’s need for stability. How does malolactic fermentation work? During MLF, lactic-acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide. One important wine-associated bacterium is Oenococcus oeni , although other lactic-acid bacteria can also be involved. The two main biological processes look like this: Process Main microorganism Main change Alcoholic fermentation Yeast Sugar becomes alcohol and carbon dioxide Malolactic fermentation Lactic-acid bacteria Malic acid becomes lactic acid and carbon dioxide MLF often occurs after alcoholic fermentation, although winemakers can manage the timing in different ways. The important point for wine drinkers is that MLF is not simply “a second alcoholic fermentation”. It is more precisely a bacterial conversion, even though the traditional name remains malolactic fermentation. What does MLF do to wine? It can make acidity seem less sharp MLF generally lowers a wine’s titratable acidity and raises its pH. In practical tasting terms, the wine may seem less sharp, angular or pointed. That does not mean MLF makes a wine flat. A wine can still have plenty of refreshing acidity after MLF. Its final impression also depends on grape ripeness, alcohol, tannin, residual sugar, pH and the balance of other components. This is why “softer” is best understood as a tasting description, not a guarantee. A soft-tasting wine has not necessarily undergone MLF. It may change texture Some wines that have undergone MLF seem rounder or smoother on the palate. The altered acid balance can make the wine feel less tense, while other winemaking choices may contribute to a fuller or creamier impression. MLF is only one possible influence on texture. Lees contact, oak, alcohol, blending and grape composition can also affect how a wine feels. These processes may be used alongside MLF, but they are not the same thing. It can sometimes add buttery or creamy aromas MLF can contribute to the formation of diacetyl, a compound associated with buttery, creamy, nutty or dairy-like aromas. This is one reason people often connect MLF with buttery Chardonnay. But MLF does not automatically make a wine taste like butter. The amount of diacetyl formed and retained varies with the bacteria, the wine and how it is handled. Some wines complete MLF with little obvious buttery aroma. A creamy or buttery impression may also come from oak, lees contact or a combination of influences. Aroma alone is therefore not a reliable test for whether MLF occurred. Why do winemakers use MLF? MLF is a choice, not a compulsory stage in every wine. A winemaker may encourage it to: reduce a wine’s sharper acid impression; shape the wine’s texture; develop a particular style; contribute certain aroma characteristics; or reduce the chance of an unwanted bacterial conversion happening later in the bottle. A winemaker may prevent or limit it to: preserve bright, energetic freshness; retain more of the original malic-acid character; protect a delicate aromatic style; avoid excessive softening; or avoid prominent buttery or dairy-like aromas. Sometimes only part of a wine undergoes MLF. This can help a winemaker balance freshness with texture before blending. Completing MLF may also support biological stability by reducing the amount of malic acid available for a later, unwanted bacterial conversion. However, it is not a complete guarantee of bottle stability; many aspects of wine chemistry and packaging contribute to that. Does every wine undergo malolactic fermentation? No. MLF is common in many red wines, but it is not universal. It is also used in some white wines, while others undergo only partial MLF or none at all. For Australian wine drinkers, MLF is especially relevant because it is encountered frequently in Australian red wine and selectively in Australian white wine. A historical Australian Wine Research Institute survey estimated that MLF was used in approximately 99% of Australian red table wine and 11% of Australian white table wine in its surveyed dataset. Those figures are historical survey results, not current universal statistics. Australian Chardonnay is a useful example of winemaking choice. It may be made with full, partial or no MLF. A wine with MLF may seem rounder or creamier, while one that avoids it may retain a sharper, more linear acid profile. Oak, lees contact, ripeness and other decisions also influence the result. Australian practice is not uniform. Choices vary by grape variety, vintage, winery, fruit acidity and intended style. MLF, oak and lees: what is the difference? These terms are easy to mix up: MLF is a bacterial conversion of malic acid into lactic acid. Oak maturation means wine has contact with oak, which can contribute characters such as vanilla, spice or toast. Lees contact means wine is kept with the spent yeast cells left after fermentation, which can influence texture and savoury or creamy impressions. A winemaker may use two or all three techniques in the same wine. A buttery or creamy wine does not therefore point to one process by itself. For broader context, see how wine is made , what Chardonnay is and what oak does to wine . Is malolactic fermentation good or bad? Neither. MLF is a winemaking tool, and whether it is useful depends on the wine being made. In a high-acid wine, reducing some sharpness may help create a more balanced style. In another wine, preserving that sharpness may be the goal. A winemaker may want buttery complexity in one Chardonnay but a bright, clean and linear style in another. The question is not whether MLF is inherently good. It is whether the conversion suits the wine’s intended balance, texture, aroma and stability. Can you taste whether a wine has undergone MLF? Not reliably from one sensation alone. A wine that has undergone MLF may seem less sharply acidic, rounder or more textured, and it may show buttery or creamy aromas. But those impressions can also result from alcohol, oak, lees, fruit ripeness, blending and other production choices. The most useful approach is to treat MLF as one possible explanation rather than a tasting diagnosis. If a wine tastes soft, that does not prove MLF occurred. If it tastes buttery, that does not prove oak was used—or that MLF was the only cause. Frequently asked questions Is malolactic fermentation the same as fermentation? It is commonly called a fermentation, but technically it is a bacterial conversion or decarboxylation. It is different from yeast-driven alcoholic fermentation. Does MLF make wine less acidic? It generally reduces titratable acidity and raises pH, so acidity may seem less sharp. It does not remove all acidity or guarantee a flat wine. Is buttery Chardonnay always made with MLF? No. MLF can contribute to buttery aromas through diacetyl, but oak, lees contact and other factors may also contribute. MLF does not always produce a buttery character. Does MLF happen in red wine or white wine? It is common in many red wines and is selective in white wines. Australian Chardonnay may undergo full, partial or no MLF. Can MLF happen naturally? Yes. It can occur through bacteria already present in the winery or wine, or it can be managed using selected bacterial cultures. Related learning How wine is made What is Chardonnay? What is Pinot Noir? What is Shiraz? What does oak do to wine? Winemaking

title: What Is Merlot?
description: Merlot is a red grape known for plum and dark-fruit flavours, moderate tannin and a smooth texture. Learn how its styles vary.
text: title: What Is Merlot? description: Merlot is a red wine grape variety known for its ripe fruit flavours and often supple texture. Learn what Merlot tastes like, whether it is sweet and how to choose a bottle. canonical: https://winedaddy.com.au/what-is-merlot/ What Is Merlot? Highlights Merlot is a red wine grape variety , as well as the name commonly used for wines made from it. Most still Merlot is dry , even when it tastes of ripe plum or blackberry. Merlot often has a soft, rounded texture, moderate acidity and relatively supple tannins. It can range from lighter and fresher to fuller, richer and more structured. Australian Merlot is made both as a single-variety wine and in blends, often with Cabernet Sauvignon. Merlot can suit everyday foods such as burgers, sausages, roast chicken, pizza and mushroom dishes. Quick answer: what is Merlot wine? Merlot is a red grape variety used to make red wine. A bottle labelled “Merlot” is usually a wine made primarily from that grape, although Merlot is also used in blends. Merlot commonly produces wines with plum, blackberry, black cherry and other ripe-fruit flavours. Depending on where it is grown and how it is made, it may also show chocolate, spice, herbs, cedar or savoury notes. Most Merlot is dry. Its ripe fruit flavours can make it seem rich or sweet-fruited, but fruity flavour is not the same as sweetness from residual sugar. In the glass, Merlot is often medium to full bodied, with moderate acidity and tannins that feel softer or rounder than those in many Cabernet Sauvignon wines. That is a broad tendency rather than a rule. Some Merlots are lighter, fresher or more structured. What does Merlot taste like? Merlot often tastes of ripe red and dark fruit. Plum is a common description, but you might also notice blackberry, black cherry or other berry flavours. Some examples have chocolate or cocoa-like notes. Others may show spice, herbs, cedar or savoury flavours, especially when the wine’s climate, oak maturation, blending or age contributes to its character. These descriptions are useful signposts, not promises. Merlot does not always taste the same because the grape responds to its growing conditions and winemaking choices. A warmer site and riper grapes may contribute darker fruit, fuller body and a richer texture. A cooler or maritime site may produce a fresher, more restrained wine. Oak can add flavours such as toast, vanilla, spice or cedar, while unoaked Merlot may taste more directly of fruit. Is Merlot sweet or dry? Most still Merlot is dry. This is one of the most useful things to understand about the variety. A wine can taste strongly of ripe plum or blackberry without containing much residual sugar. Fruit flavour is an aroma and flavour impression; dryness describes the wine’s sweetness level. So, if you enjoy rich, ripe fruit flavours but do not want a sweet wine, a dry Merlot may still suit you. Is Merlot full bodied? Merlot can be medium to full bodied. Body is the sense of weight or fullness a wine has in your mouth. A lighter Merlot may feel fresh and relatively delicate. A riper, warmer-climate or oak-matured example may feel broader and richer. Alcohol, extraction, blending and the wine’s overall balance also influence how full it seems. Merlot is often described as smooth, but it is worth treating that word carefully. Many examples have supple, rounded tannins, while others can be firm or structured. Tannins are compounds that create grip or dryness in the mouth. Merlot is commonly associated with softer tannins than Cabernet Sauvignon, but that does not mean every Merlot is low in tannin. Why does Merlot vary so much? Merlot’s final style is shaped by a chain of decisions and conditions: Climate and site → grape ripeness and acidity → winemaking → oak and blending → finished wine. Climate affects how quickly grapes ripen and how much freshness they retain. Vineyard site matters too: Merlot performs poorly in wet conditions and benefits from good drainage. Winemaking also changes the result. The amount of contact with grape skins can influence colour, tannin and texture. Oak maturation may add flavour and structure, while blending can change the balance between fruit, body and tannin. Merlot may be bottled as a varietal wine or combined with another grape. In Australia, it is often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon. A blend is not automatically better or worse than a varietal Merlot; it is simply another way to create a particular style. Australian Merlot Australian Merlot is not one uniform style. It is grown in warm inland areas as well as cooler or more maritime regions, so bottles from different parts of the country can feel quite different. Wine Australia’s 2024 Merlot snapshot identifies the Riverland, Riverina, Murray–Darling/Swan Hill and Coonawarra among important production contexts. Those figures describe production, not a ranking of quality. Regional examples also show Merlot’s range. Wine Australia describes Merlot in Cowra alongside dark berry, chocolate and eucalypt characters. Southern Fleurieu and Pemberton provide examples of Merlot made both as a varietal wine and in blends with Cabernet Sauvignon. The useful takeaway is simple: an Australian Merlot label gives you a starting point, not a guarantee of one fixed taste. Region, producer, vintage and winemaking all matter. How should you choose a bottle of Merlot? If you are choosing Merlot for tonight, start with the label and the style description rather than assuming every bottle will taste alike. Look for: The grape: “Merlot” indicates the principal variety named on the bottle. The region: this provides geographic context and may hint at the climate, but does not guarantee a particular style. The body: descriptions such as “medium bodied” or “full bodied” can help set expectations. The texture: words such as “soft”, “supple” or “rounded” suggest a gentler tannin impression. Oak: “oaked” or “unoaked” may indicate whether oak character is likely to be part of the style. Blending: a label naming Merlot with Cabernet Sauvignon signals a blend rather than a single-variety wine. You do not need specialist knowledge to enjoy Merlot. The WineDaddy grape-variety hub is a useful place to compare it with other familiar varieties, while what wine is provides broader context about wine itself. What food goes with Merlot? Merlot’s fruit, body and generally supple tannins make it a flexible match for everyday savoury food. Try it with: burgers or sausages; roast chicken; pizza; pasta with tomato-based sauce; meatloaf; grilled vegetables; mushroom dishes; mild to medium cheeses. These are suggestions, not rules. A lighter Merlot may suit lighter dishes, while a fuller, richer example can stand up to more substantial food. Serve Merlot slightly cool or at a cool room temperature. The ideal approach depends on the individual wine, but avoiding an overly warm serving temperature can help preserve its freshness. Merlot in one sentence Merlot is a usually dry red wine made from a versatile grape variety, commonly showing ripe fruit and a supple texture while ranging from fresh and medium bodied to rich and structured. Frequently asked questions Is Merlot always smooth? No. Many Merlots have soft or rounded tannins, but climate, ripeness, extraction, oak and blending can produce firmer, more structured wines. Is Merlot an easy-drinking wine? It can be approachable because of its fruit and supple texture, but “easy drinking” is not a guarantee. Some Merlots are more powerful, savoury or tannic. Is Merlot sweeter than Shiraz? Not necessarily. Merlot and Shiraz can both be made as dry red wines. Perceived sweetness depends on fruit ripeness, alcohol, acidity, tannin and residual sugar, not simply the grape name. Is Merlot the same as Cabernet Sauvignon? No. They are different red grape varieties, although they are sometimes blended together. A detailed comparison belongs in a separate guide. Can Merlot be blended? Yes. Merlot can be bottled on its own or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and other varieties. Blending can change the wine’s fruit, texture, body and structure.

title: What Is Natural Wine?
description: Natural wine usually means a low-intervention approach, but there is no single universal definition. Learn what the term does and does not tell you.
text: Highlights Natural wine usually means wine made with a low-intervention approach. There is no single, universally accepted definition of “natural wine” in Australia. Natural wine is not automatically organic, biodynamic, vegan, additive-free, unfiltered or sulphur-free. Native yeast, limited additions, minimal filtration and little or no added sulphur are common associations, not compulsory rules. Cloudiness, sediment and unusual aromas can occur, but they are not guarantees of quality or authenticity. The best way to understand a bottle is to look beyond the front label and check the producer’s notes. Quick answer: what is natural wine? Natural wine is generally made with a low-intervention approach. That often means the winemaker aims to let the grapes and fermentation speak for themselves, using fewer additions, adjustments and processing steps than many conventionally made wines. The difficulty is that natural wine does not have one fixed definition or universal production checklist . One producer’s natural wine might be made with organically farmed grapes, native yeast and no filtration. Another might use some different combination of farming or cellar practices. The word itself does not tell you exactly how the wine was made. Natural wine is therefore best understood as a broad winemaking movement or philosophy, rather than a grape variety, region or single flavour style. What does “low intervention” mean? Low intervention describes a relative approach: the winemaker chooses to do less at certain points from vineyard to bottle. Possible choices include: farming with organic, biodynamic or other low-input methods; allowing fermentation to begin with naturally occurring, or ambient, yeast; using fewer additions; limiting fining, which removes selected particles or compounds; using little filtration or no filtration; adding little or no sulphur dioxide. These are common natural-wine associations, not rules that every natural wine follows. “Low intervention” also does not mean “no intervention”. Growing grapes, managing fermentation, controlling temperature, choosing when to bottle and storing the finished wine all involve decisions. Native yeast is still yeast A spontaneous or ambient fermentation uses yeast naturally present on the grapes, winery equipment or in the cellar rather than relying solely on a selected commercial yeast culture. It does not mean the wine ferments without yeast. Native-yeast fermentation can create distinctive results, but it can also be less predictable. Commercial yeast is not automatically bad, and native yeast is not automatically better. They are different winemaking choices. Natural wine versus organic, biodynamic and conventional wine These terms describe different things, so they should not be treated as interchangeable. Term What it mainly describes What it does not automatically tell you Natural wine A broad, low-intervention approach to grape growing and winemaking A fixed list of practices, additives or sulphur level Organic wine Organic farming and permitted production practices under a relevant standard or substantiated claim That the wine is unfiltered, additive-free or low intervention Biodynamic wine Biodynamic agricultural practices and, where claimed as certified, a relevant certification framework That the wine follows every natural-wine convention Conventional wine A broad comparison term for more established commercial winemaking practices A single method or guaranteed flavour profile A wine can be natural and biodynamic, or organic and made with more cellar intervention than you might expect. A wine can also be described as natural without being certified organic or biodynamic. In Australia, organic claims must be able to be substantiated and must not mislead consumers. Domestic certification is not universally mandatory. Certified organic and biodynamic claims can provide useful information about the standard being followed, but the absence of certification does not by itself prove that a wine is not low intervention. Is natural wine additive-free or sulphur-free? Not necessarily. Natural wines may contain fewer additions, but “natural wine” does not establish that no additives were used. If a particular addition matters to you, look for the producer’s technical information rather than assuming from the label description. Sulphur dioxide, often written as SO₂ , is used in winemaking for antioxidant and antimicrobial protection. Some sulphites can also occur naturally during fermentation. The phrase “no added sulphur” normally means that the winemaker did not deliberately add sulphur dioxide. It does not necessarily mean the wine contains zero sulphites. Australian food-labelling rules require added sulphites to be declared in packaged food when present at or above the relevant threshold. If you are sensitive to sulphites, treat “no added sulphur” and “sulphur-free” as different claims and seek reliable product information. Why can natural wine be cloudy or unusual? A natural wine may be bottled with little filtration or no filtration. That can leave yeast, grape particles or other matter in suspension, creating a cloudy appearance or sediment at the bottom of the bottle. Cloudiness is possible, not compulsory. Clear wine can be made with a low-intervention approach, and cloudy wine is not automatically more authentic or better. Natural wine also has no single flavour profile. Depending on the grape variety, region, vintage and cellar choices, it may taste bright, fresh, savoury, earthy, fruity or highly aromatic. Some bottles can show characters associated with reduction, volatile acidity, oxidation or Brettanomyces . Those characters are not automatically faults in every taster’s view, but “natural” is not a free pass for spoilage or technical problems. Vinegar-like aromas, stale flavours or medicinal and animal-like notes may indicate issues rather than proof that the wine is more genuine. A wine can be distinctive and well made without being fault-free in the conventional sense—or it can simply be flawed. Bottle variation can also be more noticeable in wines with less stabilisation or sulphur protection, particularly if storage has been inconsistent. How should you choose and serve natural wine? If you are buying natural wine in Australia, begin with the information that matters most to you: Check the producer’s notes. Look for details about farming, yeast, filtration, fining and sulphur additions. Separate certification from philosophy. “Certified organic” and “biodynamic” answer different questions from “natural” or “low intervention”. Ask about vegan suitability. A wine described as natural is not automatically vegan, because fining practices vary. Store it carefully. Wines with limited sulphur protection can be more sensitive to heat, oxygen and poor storage. Expect variation, not a guaranteed style. Natural wine might be fresh and clean, savoury and textured, cloudy, or something else entirely. Taste without pressure. You do not have to enjoy an unusual aroma simply because it is associated with natural wine. At a winery or wine shop, a useful question is: “What did you do—or choose not to do—from fermentation through to bottling?” That usually reveals more than the word “natural” alone. Frequently asked questions Is natural wine healthier? There is no basis for treating all natural wine as universally healthier. Production method alone cannot establish a health outcome, and natural wine still contains alcohol. Does natural wine cause fewer hangovers? No reliable general promise follows from the term “natural”. Hangovers cannot be ruled out because a wine is described as natural or has no added sulphur. Is natural wine always organic? No. Some natural wines use organically farmed or certified organic grapes, but organic farming is not a universal requirement of the term. Is natural wine always biodynamic? No. Biodynamic wine is associated with a particular agricultural approach and certification framework. It may overlap with natural wine, but the terms are not synonyms. Is natural wine always vegan? No. Some wines are fined with animal-derived products, while others are unfined or use different fining materials. Check with the producer. Should natural wine be cloudy? Not necessarily. Cloudiness can result from little or no filtration, but natural wine can also be clear. Is unusual-smelling wine automatically a fault? No—but it is not automatically a virtue either. Some natural wines show unusual aromas that a drinker may enjoy. Persistent vinegar-like, stale, medicinal or animal-like characters may instead indicate instability or a fault.
