The simple takeaway Natural wine usually means a low-intervention approach, but it is not a guarantee of a particular ingredient list, farming method, appearance or flavour. In Australia, the most confident way to read the term is to treat it as a starting point, then check the producer’s specific information about farming, fermentation, filtration, fining and sulphur.

title: What Is Nebbiolo?
description: Nebbiolo is a pale-coloured but structured red grape known for high acidity, firm tannin and complex aromas. Learn how to approach it.
text: Highlights Nebbiolo is a red-wine grape variety , not a region or a single wine style. It is strongly associated with Piedmont in north-western Italy. Barolo and Barbaresco are famous wines made from Nebbiolo. Nebbiolo can look relatively pale but still have pronounced acidity and firm tannins. Common flavour and aroma associations include red cherry, rose, violet, herbs, spice, earth and savoury notes. Most conventional still Nebbiolo is dry. Australian Nebbiolo can vary from powerful and structured to fresher, more approachable or rosé styles. Quick answer: what is Nebbiolo? Nebbiolo is an Italian red-wine grape variety. It is best known as the grape used to make Barolo and Barbaresco, two important wines from Piedmont. But Nebbiolo is the grape; Barolo and Barbaresco are named wines made under particular regional rules. Nebbiolo wine is often a fascinating contrast. In the glass, it may look relatively pale or transparent compared with deeply coloured red varieties. In the mouth, however, it can feel energetic and substantial, with fresh acidity and firm tannin. Typical Nebbiolo aromas and flavours may include red cherry, raspberry, rose, violet, herbs, spice, earth and savoury notes. “Tar and roses” is a traditional shorthand sometimes associated with the grape, although not every Nebbiolo tastes exactly that way. The style varies considerably. Climate, vineyard site, harvest timing, extraction, oak maturation and bottle age can all influence the final wine. Australian Nebbiolo should not be expected to taste identical to Barolo or Barbaresco. What does Nebbiolo taste like? Nebbiolo is commonly associated with red rather than black fruit. You may notice cherry, raspberry or other red-fruit flavours, alongside floral aromas such as rose or violet. Herbs, spice, earthy notes and savoury characters may become more noticeable as the wine develops. These are possibilities, not a checklist. One Nebbiolo may feel floral and bright, while another is more savoury, earthy or firmly structured. Most conventional still Nebbiolo is dry. That does not mean it lacks fruit flavour. A wine can taste of ripe cherries while containing little perceptible residual sugar. Fruitiness and sweetness are different things. Nebbiolo may be medium- to full-bodied, depending on ripeness, alcohol, extraction, site and winemaking. Its acidity and tannin can also make it feel more substantial than its colour suggests. Why can Nebbiolo look pale but taste powerful? Colour, acidity and tannin are related to different aspects of wine, so they do not always increase together. Nebbiolo can produce a relatively transparent red or garnet appearance while still carrying plenty of structure. Its acidity gives the wine freshness and a mouth-watering lift. Its tannin creates grip, dryness or a drying sensation, particularly in a young or strongly extracted example. That combination explains why Nebbiolo can appear delicate but feel serious. Pale colour does not automatically mean a light-bodied, soft or fragile wine. Tannin is not a flavour in the usual sense. It is the sensation that can make your gums feel dry or your mouth feel grippy. With time, tannin may soften, although the result depends on the individual wine. Nebbiolo, Barolo and Barbaresco The easiest way to understand the relationship is: Nebbiolo: the grape variety. Barolo: a named Piedmontese wine made exclusively from Nebbiolo under defined production rules. Barbaresco: another named Piedmontese wine made from 100% Nebbiolo under its own regional rules. Barolo and Barbaresco are important expressions of Nebbiolo, but they do not define every wine made from the grape. Nebbiolo is also made in other Italian areas and in countries including Australia. This is similar to the difference between a grape and the place or category printed on a wine label. If you see “Nebbiolo” on a label, you are generally being told about the grape. If you see “Barolo” or “Barbaresco”, the name also refers to a defined geographical appellation. Why does Nebbiolo vary from one bottle to another? Nebbiolo is sensitive to where and how it is grown and made. A useful way to think about the chain is: Climate and site → ripeness and harvest timing → extraction and fermentation → oak and maturation → bottle age. A vineyard’s climate and site influence how the grapes ripen and how much freshness they retain. Harvest timing can affect the balance between red-fruit character, body, acidity and tannin. Winemaking also matters. More extraction from the grape skins can produce a darker, firmer style, while gentler extraction may preserve freshness and make the wine feel more approachable. Oak can add flavours such as spice, toast, vanilla or cedar, but oak is a winemaking choice rather than an unavoidable part of Nebbiolo’s flavour. Bottle age can change the wine too. Structured examples may develop more savoury, earthy, dried-flower or leathery characters as their tannins soften. Ageing potential is not a guarantee that every Nebbiolo will improve, however. Some wines are made to be enjoyed earlier. Australian Nebbiolo Australian readers may encounter Nebbiolo from regions including the King Valley, Mornington Peninsula, Yarra Valley, Adelaide Hills, McLaren Vale, Clare Valley and Beechworth. These are documented examples of Australian production or experimentation, not a ranking of the regions. Australian Nebbiolo is not one fixed style. Depending on region, site and winemaking, it may be powerful and structured, fresher and more approachable, or made as a rosé style. Some Australian educational material associates it with high tannin, pronounced acidity and the familiar “tar and roses” description. Nebbiolo remains a small Australian variety compared with the country’s major grapes. That makes it a useful reminder that a grape does not have to be familiar or widely planted to offer a distinctive wine experience. An Australian Nebbiolo may share the grape’s underlying acidity and tannin with Italian examples while expressing a different place and winemaking approach. How should you serve Nebbiolo? Serve Nebbiolo slightly cool or at a cool room temperature, adjusting for the wine’s body and structure. A young, firm example may benefit from time in the glass or careful decanting. An older bottle may need gentler handling because it could contain sediment and have more delicate aromas. The right approach depends on the bottle. Decanting is not automatically required, and every Nebbiolo does not need years in the cellar. Nebbiolo’s acidity and tannin can work well with rich meat dishes, cured meats and soft, creamy cheeses. These are suggestions rather than rules: the best pairing is one that suits both the particular wine and the meal. Is Nebbiolo a good wine for beginners? Nebbiolo can be an excellent learning wine because it demonstrates how appearance and structure can tell different stories. It may look light but feel tannic and fresh. It may taste of red fruit while remaining dry. It may also become more savoury and earthy with age. If you are new to the variety, pay attention to three things: Colour: Is it pale, transparent or more deeply coloured? Acidity: Does it make your mouth water? Tannin: Do you feel grip or dryness on your gums? You do not need to identify every aroma to understand the wine. Start with whether it feels fresh, grippy, floral, fruity or savoury. That is enough to begin building your own impression. Frequently asked questions Is Nebbiolo always tannic? Nebbiolo commonly has noticeable or firm tannin, especially in young or strongly extracted wines. But texture varies. Some examples are made to be softer or more approachable earlier. Is Nebbiolo sweet? Most conventional still Nebbiolo is dry. Red-fruit flavour does not necessarily mean sweetness. Is Nebbiolo the same as Barolo? No. Nebbiolo is the grape variety. Barolo is a named wine appellation made exclusively from Nebbiolo. What food goes with Nebbiolo? Rich meat dishes, cured meats and soft, creamy cheeses can work well with its acidity and tannin. Treat pairing suggestions as flexible rather than prescriptive. Does Nebbiolo need ageing? Some structured Nebbiolo can develop positively with bottle age, but not every example is intended for long-term cellaring. Check the individual wine and enjoy it when it tastes good to you. Learn more For the wider grape-variety family, visit the WineDaddy grapes hub . You can also read what wine is and explore how wine is made .

title: What Is Organic Wine?
description: Learn what organic wine means in Australia, how certification works and why organic does not automatically mean natural, vegan or preservative-free.
text: Primary topic: Organic wine Reading time: About 7 minutes Highlights Organic wine begins with grapes grown under organic-farming requirements. Depending on the claim and standard, organic rules may also apply to winemaking. Organic wine is not automatically natural, biodynamic, vegan, additive-free or sulphite-free. Australian wine sold domestically does not have to be certified to carry an organic claim, but the claim must be truthful and supported. “Certified organic” and “made with organic grapes” are not necessarily the same claim. Organic status does not create one particular flavour. Organic wine can be red, white, rosé or sparkling, in many different styles. The label wording and any certification mark are more useful than assumptions about what “organic” must mean. Quick Answer: What Does Organic Wine Mean? Organic wine is wine made from grapes grown according to organic-farming requirements. Depending on the wording on the bottle and the applicable standard, organic requirements may also cover cellar practices such as permitted additives, processing aids, winemaking methods and labelling. In simple terms, organic wine is about how the grapes and, in some cases, the wine are produced . It is not a grape variety or a flavour style. An organic wine might be a bright Australian Riesling, a full-bodied Shiraz, a delicate Pinot Noir or a sparkling wine. Its taste is still shaped by grape variety, region, climate, vintage and winemaking decisions. The important point for Australian shoppers is that the word “organic” can describe different levels of assurance. A bottle may be certified organic , made with organic grapes , or carry another organic-related claim that the producer must be able to substantiate. Read the exact wording rather than assuming every claim means the same thing. How Is Organic Wine Produced? Organic grape growing Organic viticulture—the organic growing of wine grapes—uses a defined production system for managing vines, soil, pests, diseases and biodiversity. Organic systems generally restrict or exclude specified synthetic agricultural inputs and allow only approved inputs or methods under the relevant standard. That does not mean the vineyard uses nothing. Weeds, pests and diseases still need to be managed, and organic growers may use permitted materials and cultivation techniques. The emphasis is on managing the vineyard as an ecosystem: maintaining soil health, supporting biodiversity, encouraging vine health and selecting inputs according to the applicable organic rules. The precise requirements vary between standards and certification schemes. That is why a short definition such as “grown without chemicals” is misleading. Everything in agriculture involves substances and processes that can be described chemically, and “organic” does not mean substance-free. Organic winemaking Some organic claims relate mainly to the grapes. Others describe the finished wine as organic or certified organic, which can involve additional rules in the winery. Those rules may cover matters such as yeast, clarification, filtration, processing aids, additives, sulphur dioxide and labelling. The details depend on the standard, certification scheme and market in which the wine is sold. This creates an important difference between: Wine made with organic grapes: a claim about the grapes used. Certified organic wine: a certification claim about the product or production system under a named standard. Organic farming claim: wording that may focus on how the vineyard was managed rather than certifying every step in the winery. These phrases should not be treated as interchangeable. Is Organic Wine Sulphite-Free? No. Organic wine is not automatically sulphite-free or additive-free. Sulphur dioxide may be used in wine for protection against oxidation and unwanted microbial activity. Sulphites can also occur naturally during fermentation. Organic standards may permit sulphur dioxide and other substances within defined conditions or limits. A “no added sulphur” claim is different from an organic claim. It means sulphur dioxide was not deliberately added; it does not necessarily mean the wine contains no naturally occurring sulphites. For Australian packaged wine, sulphites must be declared when present at or above the applicable food-labelling threshold. If this is a particular concern when you are buying wine, check the label and the producer’s technical information rather than assuming that organic means no sulphur has been used. What Does “Certified Organic” Mean in Australia? Australia has an important distinction between organic wine sold domestically and organic wine exported overseas. For wine sold within Australia, certification is not mandatory before a business makes an organic claim. However, the business must be able to substantiate the claim, and it must not be false or misleading under Australian consumer law. Many producers voluntarily use private certification bodies. A certification mark can give shoppers a clearer indication that the producer’s practices have been assessed against a particular standard. It is still worth checking which certifier is named and what the certification covers. Exported Australian organic goods operate under a more formal framework. Organic exports must be certified through an approved certifying body and meet the relevant export requirements, including government export documentation where required. Export requirements may also depend on the destination market. So, a bottle sold in an Australian shop is not necessarily certified under the same system as an organic wine prepared for export. Nor does the absence of a certification logo automatically prove that a wine was not made using organic practices. How Should You Read an Organic Wine Label? When choosing a bottle, look for four things: 1. The exact claim Does the label say “certified organic”, “made with organic grapes” or simply refer to organic farming? These descriptions can have different scopes. 2. A certification mark If certification matters to you, look for the certifier’s name or logo. An unfamiliar logo is not automatically meaningless, but its presence alone does not tell you which rules were applied. 3. Technical information A producer’s website or technical sheet may explain whether the claim covers the vineyard, the winemaking, or both. It may also provide information about sulphur dioxide and other cellar practices. 4. What the claim does not say Organic status does not automatically tell you that the wine is vegan, natural, low-intervention or free from all additives. Those are separate questions. If you want to understand the cellar decisions behind any wine—not only organic wine—our guide to how wine is made is a useful next step. Is Organic Wine the Same as Natural, Biodynamic or Sustainable Wine? No. These terms overlap, but they describe different ideas. Organic and natural wine Organic wine is connected to organic farming and, depending on the claim, regulated organic winemaking and certification. Natural wine is generally used for a broad, low-intervention approach to growing grapes and making wine. It does not have one universal definition in Australia, and a natural wine is not automatically organic or certified. Organic and biodynamic wine Biodynamic wine is associated with a distinct biodynamic agricultural system. Under Australia’s National Standard, certified biodynamic production also meets organic requirements, while adding further biodynamic requirements. That means biodynamic and organic can overlap, but “biodynamic” is not simply another word for organic. Organic and sustainable wine Sustainable wine is a broad term that may refer to environmental, social or economic practices, depending on the programme or claim. Sustainability can be a valuable goal, but the word alone does not prove organic certification. Does Organic Wine Taste Different? There is no single organic-wine flavour profile. Organic wine can be fruity, savoury, light-bodied, full-bodied, oaked, unoaked, dry, sweet or sparkling. Grape variety, Australian region, climate, vintage, harvest timing, fermentation and maturation still shape what ends up in the glass. Organic status tells you about production requirements, not whether the wine will taste “cleaner”, more expressive or better. The best way to choose is to consider the variety and style you already enjoy, then use the organic claim as additional information about how the wine was produced. Is Organic Wine More Expensive? It can be, but not always. Organic production and certification may involve additional management, labour, record-keeping, lower yields, packaging or distribution costs. Price can also reflect region, scale, grape variety and the producer’s overall approach. A higher price does not prove that a wine is organic, and an affordable bottle is not automatically less genuinely organic. Use the label wording and supporting certification or producer information instead. Practical Buying Advice If you are buying organic wine in Australia: Decide whether certified organic status is important to you. Read the exact claim rather than relying on the front label’s general impression. Look for a named certification body if certification is part of your decision. Check the producer’s technical information if you want to know about sulphur dioxide or cellar practices. Choose the variety and style you like—organic wine is not one taste category. Ask a retailer or cellar-door team what the certification claim covers if the label is unclear. The most useful question is often not “Is this wine organic?” but “ What exactly has been certified or claimed? ” Frequently Asked Questions Is organic wine healthier? Organic status is a production and labelling claim, not a health guarantee. This article does not make health claims about organic wine. Is organic wine vegan? Not necessarily. Organic certification does not automatically establish that a wine is vegan. Vegan status can depend on cellar materials such as fining agents, so check the producer’s specific statement. Is organic wine always natural? No. Organic wine can be made using a range of cellar practices. Natural wine is a separate and less consistently defined term. Can organic wine contain additives? Yes. Depending on the applicable standard, some additives and processing aids may be permitted under defined conditions. Does organic wine have to carry a certification logo? Not for every organic wine sold domestically in Australia. Domestic certification is voluntary, although organic claims must be substantiated and must not mislead. Export organic wine follows a more formal certification framework. Can organic wine be made from any grape variety? Yes. Organic describes the production method, not a particular variety. Organic wine can be made from many grape varieties and in many styles. Related Learning What is wine? How wine is made Winemaking Future guide: What is natural wine? Future guide: What is biodynamic wine?

title: What Is Oxidation in Wine?
description: Learn how oxygen can help or harm wine, how oxidation tastes and smells, and when oxidative character is intentional rather than a fault.
text: Topic: Wine oxidation Highlights Oxidation happens when wine compounds react with oxygen over time. Unwanted oxidation can make wine seem dull, flat, tired or brown. Possible aromas include bruised apple, nuts, cardboard, straw or hay. Oxidation is not always a fault: some wines are deliberately made in an oxidative style. One smell or a change in colour does not prove that a wine is oxidised. Resealing an opened bottle, limiting air exposure and avoiding heat can slow further change. Chilling may slow oxidation, but it cannot reverse established chemical changes. Oxidation is different from cork taint, reduction and volatile acidity. Quick Answer Oxidation in wine is a group of chemical changes caused by wine’s exposure to oxygen. Over time, oxygen can change a wine’s colour, aroma, flavour and sense of freshness. Unwanted oxidation may mute fresh fruit and floral aromas, make the wine taste flat or tired, and produce notes such as bruised apple, nuts, cardboard, straw, hay or sherry. White wines may become noticeably darker or browner, while red wines can lose bright fruit and develop a browner, more developed appearance. But oxidation is not automatically a fault. Winemakers sometimes manage oxygen deliberately to create a particular style. Nutty, dried-fruit, caramelised or sherry-like characters can be desirable in some fortified or traditionally matured wines. The important question is whether the change suits the wine’s intended style. You cannot diagnose oxidation with certainty from one smell, one flavour or colour alone. Normal ageing, heat damage and other wine faults can overlap with some of the same signs. What Does Oxidation Change? Wine contains many compounds that can react with oxygen. These reactions may alter: Aroma: Fresh fruit and floral notes may fade, replaced by more developed, nutty or stale characters. Flavour: The wine may lose brightness and seem dull, tired or flat. Colour: Pale wines can shift towards yellow, amber or brown. Red wines may become browner or brick-like as they develop. Freshness: The wine may feel less lively, with a shorter or less energetic finish. Structure: Oxygen-related reactions can change how a wine’s phenolic compounds and other components are perceived. The chemistry is more complicated than oxygen simply “turning alcohol into acetaldehyde”. Acetaldehyde is associated with oxidation, but several compounds and reactions contribute to the overall result. How Can You Recognise Possible Oxidation? Treat the following as clues rather than a diagnosis. White wine An oxidised white wine may show less floral or fresh-fruit aroma, along with bruised apple, nuts, cardboard, straw or hay. Its colour may become noticeably darker, amber or brown. On the palate, it may seem tired or lacking in freshness. Rosé Rosé may lose its fresh red-fruit and floral character. Its pink colour can look duller or move towards orange or brown, and the wine may seem less bright. Red wine An affected red may lose fresh berry aromas and develop dried-fruit, nutty or stale characters. Its colour may become browner, and the palate may seem less lively. Red wine is not immune to oxidation; its higher phenolic content can simply influence how the changes develop. Sparkling wine Sparkling wine may lose freshness and aromatic precision. Other storage or age-related changes can occur at the same time, so a flat or less lively bottle should not automatically be labelled oxidised. Fortified and oxidative styles A nutty, dried-fruit or sherry-like character may be intentional in some fortified or oxidative wines. The same descriptor can be welcome in one wine and a fault in another. How Does Oxygen Get Into Wine? Oxygen exposure can happen at several points: during crushing, pressing and other winemaking operations; during pumping, transfers, racking or filtration; through exposed tank or barrel headspace; during bottling and packaging; through or around the closure; during transport or storage; after the bottle is opened. In a packaged bottle, oxygen may be dissolved in the wine, present in the space above the wine—called the headspace or ullage —or associated with the closure. Once you open a bottle, air enters and the headspace can become an important source of further oxygen exposure. Time and temperature matter too. Warm storage can speed chemical change, while a longer period of oxygen contact gives those changes more opportunity to develop. Wine composition also matters: phenolics, sulphur dioxide, acidity and other characteristics influence how a particular wine responds. Is Oxidation Always a Fault? No. Some winemakers deliberately use or accept oxygen exposure to shape a wine’s character. Certain fortified and traditionally matured wines may be expected to show developed, nutty, dried-fruit or caramelised notes. In those wines, oxidative character can be part of the style rather than a defect. Oxidation becomes unwanted when it damages the qualities the wine was meant to preserve. For example, losing the fresh fruit and floral character of a young aromatic white may be considered a fault, while similar developed notes may be appropriate in a deliberately oxidative wine. So “oxidative” can describe a winemaking or maturation direction, while “oxidised” often describes an unwanted condition. Context matters. How Can You Slow Unwanted Oxidation? After opening a bottle: reseal it promptly; minimise repeated opening and unnecessary agitation; keep it in a cool, stable place; avoid prolonged exposure to direct sun, hot rooms, cars, garages and sheds; reduce the amount of air above the wine where practical. For Australian households, heat is especially worth considering during warm weather. A bottle left in a hot car or shed can change more quickly than one kept in stable, moderate conditions. There is no universal opened-bottle time limit that applies equally to every wine. Refrigeration can slow many chemical reactions and is a useful practical step, particularly for white, rosé and sparkling wine. However, cooling does not remove oxygen already absorbed by the wine and does not restore freshness that has already been lost. Screw caps and cork closures manage oxygen differently. Screw caps often provide consistent, low oxygen transmission, while natural cork performance varies. Neither closure should be described as universally superior: closure design, bottling conditions, the wine itself and storage all influence the result. Can You Fix an Oxidised Wine? Usually, not at home. Resealing and cooling can slow further change, but they cannot generally reverse established chemical oxidation. Once aroma compounds have changed and freshness has been lost, putting the wine in the fridge will not return it to its original condition. Aerating or decanting is not a reliable cure. Air may help some wines open up, but it adds oxygen and could make an already oxidised wine decline further. If a wine seems unexpectedly changed, compare it with another bottle of the same wine if possible. A single brown colour, nutty aroma or tired flavour is not conclusive proof, but a combination of signs can suggest that the wine has not travelled or been stored as intended. Oxidation Compared With Other Wine Problems Cork taint: Often associated with musty, mouldy, damp-cardboard or wet-newspaper aromas. It is not the same as oxidation. Reduction: More commonly associated with sulphury, struck-match, rubber, cabbage or rotten-egg characters. It is not simply the opposite smell of oxidation. Volatile acidity: Can produce vinegar, acetic or nail-polish-remover notes. Oxygen may support some related microbial activity, but volatile acidity is a separate condition. Brettanomyces: A yeast-related condition that can contribute farmyard, leather, medicinal or smoky characters. Heat damage: May produce cooked, stewed or jammy fruit and can accelerate other changes, but heat damage is not identical to oxidation. Normal ageing: A wine can develop savoury or tertiary characters as it matures without being faulty. Sediment: A physical deposit in the bottle, not evidence of oxidation. Wine faults can overlap, so sensory impressions are useful clues rather than laboratory proof. Frequently Asked Questions Is oxidised wine unsafe to drink? Oxidation is primarily a quality and flavour issue. It can make wine unpleasant, but an oxidised taste does not by itself prove that a wine is unsafe. If the wine appears contaminated, has an unusual physical problem or seems otherwise suspect, do not drink it. Does brown wine always mean oxidation? No. Browning can be a clue, especially in a pale wine, but colour is affected by grape variety, production, age and style. Taste and aroma matter too. Does opening a bottle immediately oxidise it? Opening introduces air, but noticeable change depends on the wine, the amount of oxygen, temperature, time and other factors. Opening does not mean every wine is instantly oxidised. Is oxidation the same as ageing? No. Ageing can involve oxygen-related development, but a mature wine is not automatically oxidised or faulty. Whether a developed character is desirable depends on the wine’s style and condition. Can decanting prevent oxidation? No. Decanting increases the wine’s contact with air. It may help some young or closed wines express themselves, but it is not a treatment for unwanted oxidation. Related Learning What is wine? How wine is made What is fortified wine? Winemaking

title: What Is Pinot Gris / Pinot Grigio?
description: Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are names for the same grape. Learn why both appear on labels, how the styles can differ and what Australian drinkers should look for.
text: Highlights Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are two names for the same white-wine grape variety . Pinot Gris is the French name; Pinot Grigio is the Italian name. The grape has greyish-pink or dusky skins, but it is normally made into white wine. Pinot Grigio is often associated with light, crisp and fresh wines. Pinot Gris is often associated with riper, fuller and more textured wines. Those style associations are tendencies, not rules. Australian producers may use either name for different styles. Climate, harvest timing and winemaking choices can matter more than the name on the front label. Quick Answer Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are names for the same grape variety. “Pinot Gris” is French, while “Pinot Grigio” is Italian. Both names refer to the grape’s greyish or dusky skin colour. The variety is usually made as a dry white wine. Depending on where it is grown and how it is made, it can be light, crisp and citrusy, or fuller, riper and more textured. Common flavours include apple, pear, citrus and stone fruit, with some wines showing mineral, spice, creamy or lightly savoury notes. The names can offer a useful clue to style. Pinot Grigio is often linked with earlier-picked, fresh and energetic wines, while Pinot Gris is often linked with riper and more substantial expressions. But this is not a universal rule. In Australia, a producer may use either name for a crisp, rich or textural wine. If you are choosing a bottle, treat “Gris” or “Grigio” as a starting point. Then read the rest of the label or producer description for clues such as crisp , dry , fresh , textured , lees-aged , barrel-fermented or off-dry . One Grape, Two Names The simplest way to understand Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio is to think of them as two languages describing the same grape. Pinot Gris is the French name. Pinot Grigio is the Italian name. Gris and grigio both mean “grey”. The grape’s ripe skins can have a greyish-pink, dusky or coppery appearance. Despite this colour, Pinot Gris/Grigio is normally made into white wine. Grape skin colour does not automatically determine whether a finished wine is red or white; winemaking choices, especially the amount of skin contact, also matter. Pinot Gris belongs to the Pinot family and is related to Pinot Noir. The word “Pinot” is associated with the pine-cone-like shape of Pinot-family grape bunches. Text-first learning component: Same grape, two names Pinot Gris = Pinot Grigio French name | Italian name | same grape variety Do Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio Taste Different? They can, but not because they are different grapes. Over time, the names have developed broad stylistic associations. A wine labelled Pinot Grigio is often expected to be: light to medium-bodied; fresh and crisp; high in perceived acidity; citrusy, mineral or green-apple driven; clean and refreshing. A wine labelled Pinot Gris is often expected to be: riper and fuller; broader or rounder in texture; flavoured with pear, ripe apple or stone fruit; silky, creamy or lightly spicy; sometimes influenced by lees contact, skin contact or oak. These are useful traditions, but they are not fixed definitions. A Pinot Gris can be bright and delicate, while a Pinot Grigio can be rich or textural. The producer, region, vintage and winemaking decisions all matter. That is why it is better to think of Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio as a style spectrum , rather than two sealed categories. Style spectrum: crisp and light → rounded and textured → rich and luscious The label name alone does not determine where a wine sits. What Does Pinot Gris / Pinot Grigio Taste Like? There is no single Pinot Gris or Pinot Grigio flavour profile. The wine may show: lemon or other citrus; green apple; pear; peach or other stone fruit; floral notes; mineral or stony impressions; spice; creamy or savoury texture. Lighter examples are usually driven by freshness. They may feel lean, clean and mouth-watering, with fruit and mineral notes rather than obvious oak. Fuller examples may feel broader and softer. Riper fruit, lees contact, skin contact or barrel fermentation can add weight and texture. Some wines may have a silky or creamy impression even when they are still dry. Is Pinot Gris sweet? Most table-wine examples are dry, but the wine can taste fruity or luscious. A ripe pear flavour is not the same as sweetness from residual sugar. Residual sugar is the sugar left in a wine after fermentation. It can make a wine taste sweet, while fruit ripeness, alcohol and texture can make a dry wine seem rich or soft. If sweetness matters to you, look for terms such as dry , off-dry or sweet , and check the producer’s description where available. Why Do Styles Vary? The same grape can produce noticeably different wines because several decisions shape the finished style. Climate and site Cooler conditions can help a vineyard retain acidity and freshness. Warmer or riper conditions can contribute more body, fruit weight and richness. This is a broad tendency, not a formula: vineyard site, season and picking decisions also matter. Harvest timing Earlier picking generally preserves freshness and lighter fruit character. Later picking can bring more ripeness, concentration and texture. This is one reason the classic light Grigio and fuller Gris associations developed. Skin contact Allowing grape juice to remain in contact with the skins can influence colour, texture and phenolic feel. In Pinot Gris/Grigio, it may contribute a deeper colour or a more textured, savoury style. Lees contact Lees are the sediment left after fermentation, including yeast cells. Keeping wine on its lees can contribute breadth, creaminess or a more rounded texture. Fermentation vessel and oak Stainless steel is often used when a winemaker wants to preserve freshness and fruit character. Barrel fermentation or oak maturation may add texture, spice, toast or vanilla. Oak is optional, not a defining feature of Pinot Gris. Style-influence flow: climate + harvest timing + ripeness + skin contact + lees + oak → final wine style Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio in Australia Australian drinkers may see both names on domestic and imported labels. Pinot Grigio is common on imported Italian wines, while Australian producers may choose either Pinot Gris or Pinot Grigio for their own wines. Australia does not have one universal “Gris style” and one universal “Grigio style”. A bottle’s name can suggest an intention, but it does not guarantee the flavour or texture inside. Relevant Australian contexts include cool or maritime regions such as: Mornington Peninsula; Tasmania; Adelaide Hills; Yarra Valley; Orange. Wine Australia identifies Pinot Gris/Grigio as an important variety in the Mornington Peninsula, where it describes examples as medium-bodied, fruit-driven and mineral in character. These descriptions are broad regional tendencies, not rules for every bottle. Australia also produces Pinot Gris/Grigio in larger inland regions, so the category is not limited to one type of climate or one premium style. Wine Australia’s 2024 variety snapshot recorded 70,757 tonnes crushed in 2024 , while its planting figure of 3,731 hectares used 2015 data. These figures are dated and are not necessary for choosing a bottle, but they illustrate that the variety is established across Australian wine production. How to Choose a Bottle If you prefer a fresh, easy-drinking white, look for descriptions such as: crisp; fresh; bright; mineral; citrusy; light-bodied. If you prefer more weight or texture, look for: ripe pear or stone fruit; rounded; creamy; textured; lees-aged; barrel-fermented; skin contact. Do not assume that “Pinot Gris” automatically means rich or that “Pinot Grigio” automatically means simple and crisp. The producer description, region, vintage and technical notes can give you a better idea of the wine’s style. Serving and Food Pinot Gris/Grigio is generally served chilled. Avoid serving it so cold that its aromas and texture disappear. Crisper styles can work well with seafood, shellfish, salads and lighter dishes. Fuller examples may suit richer seafood, poultry or lightly spiced food. These are starting points rather than strict pairing rules; match the food to the wine’s body, acidity and texture. The Bottom Line Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are two names for the same grape. The names come from French and Italian usage and can suggest different stylistic traditions, but neither name guarantees a particular flavour. Expect anything from a light, crisp and citrus-driven white to a fuller wine with ripe fruit and a more rounded texture. For the most reliable guide, read beyond the grape name and look for the producer’s description of the wine’s freshness, sweetness and texture.

title: What Is Pinot Noir?
description: Pinot Noir is a red grape variety known for fresh acidity, red-fruit flavours and often lighter to medium-bodied wines. Learn what it tastes like, whether it is sweet and where it is grown in Australia.
text: Highlights Pinot Noir is a red grape variety and the name of the wine made from it. It commonly produces light- to medium-bodied red wines , although some examples are fuller and more concentrated. Typical flavours include cherry, strawberry, raspberry, floral, earthy and savoury notes . Pinot Noir usually has fresh acidity and fine to moderate tannin. Most still Pinot Noir is dry , even when it tastes strongly of ripe fruit. Australian Pinot Noir is especially associated with cooler regions , including Tasmania, the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Adelaide Hills. Pinot Noir can be delicate and silky, but it is not automatically pale, weak, sweet or simple. Quick answer Pinot Noir is a dark-skinned wine grape variety used mainly to make red wine. The name “Pinot Noir” can refer to the grape itself or to a bottle of wine made primarily from that grape. Most Pinot Noir is red, dry and light to medium bodied. It often has noticeable acidity, relatively fine tannin and red-fruit flavours such as cherry, strawberry and raspberry. Depending on where it was grown and how it was made, it may also show floral, earthy, savoury or spicy notes. Pinot Noir is strongly associated with cool or temperate climates. In Australia, important examples come from Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia, including the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Adelaide Hills. The most useful thing to remember is that Pinot Noir is a variety with a broad range of styles—not a single fixed flavour formula. One bottle may be pale, bright and silky; another may be darker, richer and firmer. What kind of wine is Pinot Noir? Pinot Noir is a red grape variety. Its name is also commonly used for the still red wine made from it. It is not a region, a brand or a description of sweetness. A wine labelled Pinot Noir tells you primarily which grape variety has been used. Pinot Noir is also an important grape in traditional-method sparkling wine, including Australian sparkling wine. However, when people casually ask for “a Pinot Noir”, they usually mean a still red wine. Compared with deeply coloured varieties such as Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir often produces a paler red wine. Its colour can range from relatively light ruby to deeper ruby or garnet, depending on ripeness, extraction, vintage and winemaking. What does Pinot Noir taste like? Pinot Noir may show flavours such as: cherry; strawberry; raspberry and other red berries; plum in some examples; floral aromas; earthy or forest-floor notes; savoury or spice characters. Cherry and strawberry are common descriptions, but they are not guarantees. Pinot Noir does not always taste earthy, and it does not always taste delicate or fruity. A wine’s flavour depends on its climate, vineyard site, vintage, ripeness and winemaking. The same grape variety can therefore produce noticeably different wines from one region—or even one vineyard—to another. When tasting Pinot Noir, you might notice a lighter texture and red-fruit freshness in one wine, then more concentration, darker fruit or firmer structure in another. Neither style is automatically more “correct”. Is Pinot Noir sweet? Most still Pinot Noir is made as a dry red wine. That does not mean it will taste completely unsweet. Cherry, strawberry and raspberry flavours can create a juicy or sweet-fruited impression even when the wine contains little residual sugar. This is an important distinction: Sweetness refers to sugar in the wine. Fruit flavour describes the aromas and flavours you perceive. A dry Pinot Noir can smell and taste strongly of ripe strawberries without being a sweet wine. Is Pinot Noir light-bodied? Pinot Noir is often light to medium bodied, meaning it may feel less weighty or rich than a full-bodied red such as a powerful Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon. But “light-bodied” does not mean thin, weak or low quality. Pinot Noir can have plenty of flavour and concentration while still feeling relatively graceful in the mouth. Some examples are fuller and firmer, particularly when made from riper fruit or through winemaking choices that build texture and body. A useful beginner summary is: Feature Common Pinot Noir tendency Colour Pale to medium ruby, though variation is considerable Body Often light to medium Acidity Usually fresh and noticeable Tannin Often fine or moderate, but variable Fruit character Commonly red-fruited Texture Delicate and silky to concentrated and firm Sweetness Most still examples are dry These are broad tendencies, not rules for every bottle. Why does Pinot Noir taste different from bottle to bottle? Several factors shape the final wine. Climate Pinot Noir is commonly associated with cool or temperate climates. Cooler conditions can help preserve acidity and red-fruit freshness, while warmer conditions may encourage riper fruit, more body and higher alcohol. That is only a general tendency. Climate does not guarantee a particular colour, alcohol level or body. Vineyard site Elevation, aspect, proximity to water, soils and drainage can affect how quickly grapes ripen and how much water the vines receive. These differences help explain why Pinot Noir can vary within the same broad region. Vintage A growing season may be warmer, cooler, wetter or drier than another. Vintage conditions influence ripeness, acidity, concentration and the decisions made at harvest. Ripeness and harvest timing Picking earlier or later can change the balance between acidity, fruit character, alcohol and texture. Winemakers must decide what style they want from the fruit. Winemaking Techniques such as whole-bunch use, fermentation temperature, extraction, oak and maturation can alter aroma, tannin and texture. They are choices, not requirements for making “real” Pinot Noir. Oak is also not a defining feature of every Pinot Noir. Some winemakers use it to add texture or spice, while others use less new oak so the fruit remains more prominent. Pinot Noir in Australia Australia’s Pinot Noir identity is closely connected with cooler or temperate growing regions. Tasmania, parts of Victoria and the Adelaide Hills are important contexts for the variety. Australian Pinot Noir is not one uniform style. Research comparing wines from regions including Tasmania, the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Adelaide Hills found regional differences in chemical and sensory composition. These differences are useful evidence that place matters, but they do not mean every wine from a region tastes the same. Tasmania Tasmania is one of Australia’s major Pinot Noir regions. Its island position and Southern Ocean influence contribute to a cool climate, while long, sunny and dry autumns can help grapes ripen and develop flavour. Tasmanian Pinot Noir may be light to medium bodied, with red apple, cherry and strawberry characters. Tasmania contains several distinct growing areas, so these descriptions are broad tendencies rather than a tasting rule. Yarra Valley Pinot Noir is the Yarra Valley’s most planted and important grape variety. Differences in elevation and aspect contribute to a range of regional expressions. Yarra Valley Pinot Noir may show cherry, strawberry and plum characters. Some wines are bright and delicate, while others have greater concentration and structure. Mornington Peninsula The Mornington Peninsula is strongly associated with Pinot Noir. Bass Strait, Port Phillip Bay and Western Port contribute maritime influences, while local differences in elevation, aspect and soils create variation across the region. Typical descriptions include strawberry and cherry fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannin. As elsewhere, these are general tendencies rather than a promise about every bottle. Adelaide Hills The Adelaide Hills is an important South Australian region for Pinot Noir. Its cooler conditions also make some fruit suitable for traditional-method sparkling wine. Still red examples may be medium bodied, with ripe cherry and berry characters. The region’s Pinot Noir should not be treated as identical to Tasmanian, Yarra Valley or Mornington Peninsula examples. For more regional detail, see the WineDaddy guides to the Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula . What food goes with Pinot Noir? Pinot Noir’s acidity, red-fruit character and often moderate tannin can make it a flexible food wine. Approachable matches include: roast chicken; pork; salmon; mushrooms; charcuterie; pâté and terrines. These are suggestions, not rules. A fuller Pinot Noir may work with richer food, while a lighter and brighter example may suit simpler dishes. Pinot Noir is generally more enjoyable slightly cool than warm. Avoid serving it overheated, which can make the alcohol feel more obvious and the wine less fresh. Can Pinot Noir age? Some high-quality Pinot Noir can develop with age. Wine Australia notes that the very best examples may age for 10–15 years. That does not mean every Pinot Noir should be cellared. Many bottles are made to be enjoyed while their fresh fruit is prominent. Ageing potential depends on the individual wine, vintage, producer and storage conditions. A final way to think about Pinot Noir Pinot Noir is often described as elegant, silky or delicate, but those words describe only part of its range. It can be light or more concentrated, fruit-driven or savoury, pale or relatively dark, and immediately approachable or capable of developing with age. The common thread is the grape variety—not one compulsory style. If you want deeper information about Pinot Noir’s history, taxonomy, clones, viticulture and technical winemaking, continue to the WineDaddy Pinot Noir grape profile . Related Learning What is wine? title: What Is Reduction in Wine?
description: Reduction in wine can smell like struck match, rubber or rotten egg. Learn what it means, when it may be stylistic, and whether opening the bottle can help.
text: Highlights Reduction is a broad term for sulphur-related wine character, often associated with low-oxygen conditions. It may smell like struck match, flint, rubber, cabbage, onion or rotten egg. Not every reductive aroma is a fault. Subtle flinty notes may be part of a wine’s style. Some temporary reductive aromas soften after opening and swirling. Persistent, unpleasant sulphur character may not improve with ordinary aeration. Reduction is different from oxidation, cork taint and Brettanomyces. One aroma cannot identify a specific chemical compound or winemaking cause. Quick answer: what does reduction mean in wine? Reduction in wine is a sensory and chemical condition associated mainly with volatile sulphur compounds and low-oxygen or “reductive” conditions during winemaking or storage. Depending on the compounds involved, concentration and wine style, reduction may smell of struck match, struck flint, rubber, cabbage, onion, sewage or rotten egg. Some sulphur-related aromas can add complexity or be tolerated in small amounts. Strong or persistent character, however, can overwhelm the wine’s fruit and make it unpleasant. Can air improve it? Sometimes. Opening the bottle, swirling the wine or pouring it into a glass may allow some volatile aromas to escape or change. If the smell fades and the fruit returns, the wine may have had temporary reductive character. Aeration is not a guaranteed cure, though. More persistent sulphur compounds may remain even after the wine has had contact with air. The word “reduction” can also describe a cooking technique involving concentrated wine or sauce. This article uses the wine-tasting meaning. What does reduction smell and taste like? There is no single “reduction aroma”. Common descriptions include: struck match or burnt match flint or smoky mineral character rotten egg rubber cooked cabbage onion or garlic sewage or drains canned corn These descriptions are useful clues, but they are not laboratory diagnoses. For example, a struck-match aroma does not prove that one specific compound is present. The same descriptor can be interpreted differently by different tasters, and aromas can overlap with other wine characters. Hydrogen sulphide is commonly associated with rotten-egg odour. Other sulphur compounds, including methanethiol and ethanethiol, may contribute rubbery, onion-like, cabbage-like or other strongly sulphury aromas. A wine drinker does not need to identify the exact compound to decide whether the aroma is enjoyable, distracting or unpleasant. Why does reduction happen? Reduction is influenced by the way wine handles oxygen and sulphur during fermentation, maturation, packaging and storage. Yeast metabolism, nutrient conditions, lees contact, wine chemistry and the availability of sulphur-containing compounds can all matter. Low-oxygen handling or packaging can allow some reduced sulphur characters to persist or become more noticeable. Closure oxygen transmission can also influence how a wine develops over time. That does not mean a closure alone causes reduction. Australian wines with screw caps can show reductive character, but so can wines under other closures. Reduction is therefore not a uniquely Australian problem. It is a general part of wine chemistry, and Australian research has contributed significantly to understanding volatile sulphur compounds and oxygen management. Is reduction always a fault? No. Context matters. A subtle flinty or struck-flint note may be considered an interesting stylistic character in some white or sparkling wines. A mild sulphur-related aroma may add complexity without hiding the wine’s fruit. The same broad family of aromas can become faulty when it is intense, unpleasant or persistent. Strong rotten-egg, rubbery, onion-like or sewage-like character may mask the wine and make it difficult to enjoy. There is no universal line at which every reductive note becomes faulty. The wine’s style, the intensity of the aroma and your own response all matter. A useful question is not simply “Is this reduction?” but “Is this character adding something, or is it taking over the wine?” Can opening or decanting fix reduction? It may help, but there is no guaranteed timetable or cure. Try a simple comparison: Pour a small amount into a clean glass. Smell it immediately. Swirl gently and smell again. Give it a short interval, then reassess. Notice whether the sulphury character softens and whether fruit becomes easier to smell. If the aroma fades and the wine becomes more expressive, the initial character may have been temporary or mild. If strong rubbery, onion-like, cabbage-like or rotten-egg character remains, ordinary aeration may not fix it. Decanting provides more contact with air, but more oxygen is not always better. An older or delicate wine can lose its freshness if exposed to air for too long. It is usually more useful to test a small amount in a glass before committing the whole bottle to a decanter. Professional winemakers have controlled treatments for some sulphur-related problems. Those cellar techniques are not household remedies, so do not add chemicals or improvised materials to the bottle. Reduction versus other wine faults Reduction is often confused with other wine problems because aroma descriptions overlap. Reduction and oxidation Reduction is generally associated with sulphur-related character and low-oxygen conditions. Oxidation involves oxygen-mediated changes and may produce bruised-apple, nutty, browned, stale or cardboard-like aromas. They are not simply perfect opposites, and a wine can show more than one kind of fault. See What is oxidation in wine? if the live page is available. Reduction and cork taint Cork taint is commonly associated with musty, mouldy, damp-cardboard or wet-newspaper aromas, often alongside muted fruit. It is not the same as sulphur-related reduction. See What is cork taint? if the live page is available. Reduction and Brettanomyces Brettanomyces is a yeast associated with aromas that may be described as farmyard, leathery, medicinal or smoky. Those characters can overlap with some reductive descriptions, but Brettanomyces is a different cause. Reduction and sulphur dioxide Sulphur dioxide is used in winemaking as a preservative and antioxidant. Its smell is not automatically evidence of reduction, and sulphur dioxide and reduction should not be treated as the same thing. A practical checklist for a suspected reductive wine Smell before swirling, then smell again after gentle swirling. Give the wine a little time in the glass rather than judging it from the first sniff. Look for balance: does the aroma soften, or does it continue to dominate? Do not assume that every struck-match, smoky or flinty note is a fault. Do not assume that every sulphury smell is hydrogen sulphide. Do not keep adding air indefinitely in the hope of a guaranteed cure. If the wine remains clearly unpleasant, retain the bottle, closure and proof of purchase and contact the retailer according to its policy. Frequently asked questions Is reduction in wine bad? Not automatically. A subtle flinty or struck-match character may be tolerated or valued in some wines. Strong, unpleasant or persistent sulphur character is more likely to be considered a fault. Does reduction mean a wine has gone off? No. Reduction can be temporary, stylistic or faulty. The important questions are how intense it is, whether it changes with air and whether it masks the wine. Is reduction the opposite of oxidation? They describe different wine conditions, but they are not simply two perfectly opposite states. Reduction is usually discussed in relation to sulphur compounds and limited oxygen; oxidation describes oxygen-mediated changes. Can you fix reduced wine by decanting? Sometimes air helps some volatile sulphur aromas, but decanting is not guaranteed to fix persistent reduction. Test a small amount in a glass first. Do screw caps cause reduction? No closure alone proves the cause. Screw caps influence oxygen transmission, but sulphide-related character can occur under different closure types and depends on the wine’s broader chemistry and history. Can you identify the exact compound by smell? No. Aroma descriptors can suggest a possible reductive character, but sensory observation alone cannot identify the exact compound or winemaking cause. For broader tasting guidance, see How wine is made and What is wine? .

title: What Is Riesling? A Beginner’s Guide to This Aromatic White Wine
description: Riesling is an aromatic white grape that can make dry, off-dry and sweet wines. Learn how acidity, fruitiness and Australian regions shape its style.
text: Highlights Riesling is a white grape variety, not a single sweetness level. It is often aromatic, light- to medium-bodied and high in acidity. Common flavours include lime, lemon, green apple, peach and floral notes. Riesling can be bone-dry, off-dry, sweet or occasionally sparkling. Most Australian Riesling is made in a crisp, dry style. Clare Valley and Eden Valley are important Australian examples, but Riesling is grown in many regions. Some Rieslings can age and develop honeyed, toasty or nutty flavours. Quick answer: what is Riesling? Riesling is a white wine grape variety. The name is also commonly used for wines made primarily from that grape. Riesling is best known for its lively acidity and fragrant character. A young Riesling may smell or taste of lime, lemon, green apple, peach or flowers. Those flavours can appear in a completely dry wine, so Riesling is not automatically sweet. The grape can produce several styles, from bone-dry to off-dry, sweet and dessert wines. In Australia, Riesling is especially associated with crisp, dry wines from regions such as Clare Valley and Eden Valley, although Tasmania, Great Southern, Canberra District and other regions also produce it. The most useful beginner lesson is simple: the word “Riesling” tells you the grape, but not necessarily how sweet the finished wine will be. What does Riesling taste like? Young Riesling is often light- to medium-bodied, fresh and aromatic. Common descriptions include: lime and lemon; green apple; peach; citrus blossom or other floral notes; a clean, mouth-watering finish. These are typical possibilities rather than a fixed checklist. Climate, ripeness, region, winemaking and bottle age all influence the final wine. Riesling’s acidity is one of its defining features. Acidity creates freshness and makes your mouth water, rather like the sensation from biting into a crisp green apple. It can also balance residual sugar, allowing a wine to be sweet without feeling heavy. Riesling is therefore a useful variety for understanding the difference between fruitiness , sweetness , acidity and body : Fruitiness describes aromas and flavours. Sweetness mainly comes from residual sugar left in the wine. Acidity provides freshness and structure. Body describes how light or full the wine feels in your mouth. A wine can smell of ripe peach and still be dry. Another can contain some residual sugar but remain fresh because of its acidity. Is Riesling sweet? Not necessarily. Most Australian Riesling is dry, meaning it contains little perceptible residual sugar. It can still taste intensely of citrus, apple or flowers. Riesling is also made in off-dry, sweet and dessert styles. Off-dry wines contain some residual sugar but may taste balanced rather than obviously sweet. Sweeter styles can be made by harvesting grapes later or by retaining some of the grape’s sugar during fermentation. When choosing a bottle, look for words such as: dry ; off-dry ; sweet ; late harvest ; dessert wine . The grape name alone is not a reliable sweetness guide. If the label is unclear, the producer’s description or a retailer’s tasting note may provide more useful information. For a broader explanation of sweetness, see what is sweet wine? . Why can Riesling taste so different from bottle to bottle? Riesling’s final style is shaped by a chain of decisions and conditions: Climate and site → ripeness and acidity → harvest timing → fermentation and maturation → finished wine. Cooler conditions can help the grapes retain acidity and aromatic freshness. Warmer conditions may encourage riper fruit and a broader texture, although no climate produces exactly one style. Vintage conditions, vineyard site and harvest decisions matter as well. The winemaker’s choices also influence the result. Cool, temperature-controlled fermentation in stainless steel is common for Australian Riesling because it helps preserve fresh fruit and aromatic purity. New oak is not common, although some producers use lees ageing, skin contact or alternative vessels to add texture. Many Australian Rieslings are bottled relatively early to preserve their bright, direct character. A screwcap, also called a Stelvin closure, is very common for Australian Riesling. It can help limit oxygen exposure and preserve freshness, but it is not a guarantee of quality or a particular style. Can Riesling age? Some Rieslings can age very well. Their acidity provides a firm structure that can help the wine remain fresh as it develops. Young Riesling tends to emphasise citrus, apple and floral characters. With bottle age, some examples develop honeyed, lemon-curd, nutty or toasty notes. A distinctive petroleum-like character may also appear in some aged Rieslings, although it is not present in every bottle and is not, by itself, proof that a wine is faulty or superior. Ageing potential varies with the wine, vintage, sweetness, acidity, closure and storage conditions. Not every bottle needs to be cellared, and ageing is not a requirement for enjoying Riesling. Australian Riesling Riesling has an established place in Australian wine. It is grown in several parts of the country and is particularly associated with dry, cool-climate styles. Clare Valley Clare Valley is one of Australia’s major Riesling regions. Wines from the region are often associated with bright acidity, light body and lime or citrus flavours. Some can be enjoyed young, while well-made examples may also develop complexity with age. Eden Valley Eden Valley, within the Barossa Zone, is another important Australian Riesling region. Its elevated vineyard sites are associated with lemon and lime characters, fresh acidity and a steely finish. “Mineral” is sometimes used as a tasting description for these wines; it should not be read as proof that minerals from the soil directly enter the wine and create a specific flavour. Other regions Riesling is also produced in Tasmania, Great Southern, Canberra District, Langhorne Creek, Padthaway, the Riverland and other Australian regions. These examples show why Australian Riesling should not be reduced to one regional style. You can explore broader Australian wine geography through the Australian regions index. Detailed guides to individual Riesling regions may be covered separately. How should a beginner choose a Riesling? Start with the style you want rather than assuming all Riesling tastes the same. For a crisp, refreshing wine, look for an Australian dry Riesling, particularly from a cool-climate region. For a softer or fruitier impression, look for an off-dry description. For dessert or a richer occasion, look for a sweet or late-harvest style. For a more developed experience, look for a bottle with some age, remembering that older does not automatically mean better. A regional name can offer a clue, but it is not a guarantee. The vintage, producer description and stated sweetness style can tell you more. Riesling is usually served chilled. Dry examples can work well with oysters, shellfish, lighter fish, salads and goat’s cheese. Off-dry or sweeter examples may suit spicy dishes, pâté or soft cheese. These are starting points, not rules. Frequently asked questions Is Riesling a white wine? Yes. Riesling is a white grape variety used to make white wines. Is Riesling always dry? No. Most Australian Riesling is dry, but the variety can also produce off-dry, sweet, dessert and occasionally sparkling wines. Is Riesling a sweet wine? It can be, but the grape name does not determine sweetness. Check the label or producer description for clues. What is the difference between Riesling and other white wines? Riesling is commonly recognised for its pronounced acidity and aromatic citrus, apple, peach and floral characters. Its style can still vary considerably with climate, ripeness, winemaking and age. Is Riesling oaked? New oak is uncommon in Australian Riesling. Stainless-steel fermentation is more typical, although some producers use techniques such as lees ageing or alternative vessels to build texture. Can Riesling be aged? Some Rieslings age very well and can develop honeyed, nutty, toasty or lemon-curd characters. Many are also enjoyable young for their fresh citrus and floral character. For more foundational context, start with what is wine? or explore the grape varieties index.

title: What is rosé?
description: Rosé is a wine style, not a single grape or sweetness level. Learn how it gets its colour and how to choose, serve and enjoy it.
text: Highlights Rosé is a wine style with a colour ranging from pale pink and salmon to deeper pink and copper. It is usually made from red grapes, but with much less skin contact than red wine. Rosé is not defined by one grape, region, sweetness level or production method. It can be dry, off-dry or sweet, and pale colour does not automatically mean dry wine. Direct pressing, short skin contact and saignée are three ways to make rosé. Rosé is generally not made by mixing finished red and white wine. Australian rosé is made from many grape varieties and regions. Serve it chilled, then reseal and refrigerate any leftovers. Quick answer Rosé is a wine style known for its pink-to-copper colour and fresh, fruit-driven character. It is most commonly made from red grapes, but the juice spends only limited time with the grape skins. That brief contact gives the wine some colour without the extended extraction associated with most red wine. Rosé is therefore not a single grape variety or a synonym for a sweet wine. A bottle can be dry, off-dry or sweet; pale or deeply coloured; light-bodied or more structured; still or sparkling. The colour usually comes from controlled contact between juice and red grape skins. Winemakers may press the grapes quickly, leave the juice with the skins for a short time, or use a technique called saignée , in which some pink juice is drained from a red-wine ferment and fermented separately. The simplest way to understand rosé is this: it is usually made from red grapes, but handled so that the wine gets less colour and tannin from the skins than a typical red wine. How does rosé get its colour? Grape juice is not always deeply coloured simply because the grapes have dark skins. Much of the pigment that gives red wine its colour is extracted from the skins during winemaking. For rosé, the winemaker controls how much colour and structure are extracted. Less skin contact generally means less colour and less tannin, although grape variety, ripeness, temperature, pressing and other decisions also affect the result. That is why rosé can range from almost onion-skin or peach shades through salmon and bright pink to copper and deeper magenta. Colour can offer clues about how the wine was made, but it does not tell you everything about how it will taste. A pale rosé is not automatically sweeter, drier or better than a darker one. Colour, sweetness, acidity and body are related to winemaking, but they are not the same thing. Three common ways to make rosé Direct pressing With direct pressing , red grapes are pressed soon after arriving at the winery. The juice is separated from the skins early, so it takes on only a small amount of colour. This approach can produce a particularly delicate-looking rosé, but there is no universal colour or flavour outcome. The grape variety and the winemaker’s choices still matter. Short maceration Maceration means leaving juice or crushed grapes in contact with the skins so colour, flavour and phenolic compounds can be extracted. For rosé, that contact is limited. The winemaker separates the juice when the desired colour and structure have been reached. A little more contact may produce a deeper-coloured wine with more texture, but it does not create a fixed style every time. Saignée Saignée —French for “bleeding”—involves draining some pink-coloured juice from a tank of crushed red grapes. The removed juice can then be fermented separately as rosé. The technique is associated with a red-wine ferment, so saignée is not simply another name for all rosé production. Much rosé is made deliberately through direct pressing or short skin contact instead. Is rosé made by mixing red and white wine? Not as a general method. Most rosé is made by controlling colour extraction from grapes, usually red grapes, rather than by pouring finished red wine into finished white wine. Rules around blending differ between countries, wine categories and protected regional designations. Some sparkling-wine categories and regional specifications have their own provisions. It is therefore more accurate to say that red-and-white blending is not the standard explanation for rosé—not that it is universally illegal or that it never occurs in any category. The important beginner distinction is between blending and saignée . Saignée removes juice from a red-wine ferment before that juice is fermented separately. It is not the same as mixing finished red and white wines. Rosé compared with red and white wine Rosé and red wine are both commonly made from red grapes. The main difference is how long the juice remains with the skins. Red wine generally receives longer skin contact, extracting more colour and tannin. Rosé normally receives less, producing a paler wine with less tannic grip. White wine is commonly made by pressing grapes and fermenting the juice with little or no skin contact. Rosé may also be fermented as separated juice, but it usually has some colour and flavour influence from red grape skins. Rosé often shows fresh red-fruit notes such as strawberry, raspberry or cherry. Depending on the grape and winemaking, it may also suggest citrus, melon or flowers. Is rosé sweet? It can be—but it does not have to be. Rosé is made in dry, off-dry and sweet styles. Dry means the wine has little perceived sweetness, although acidity and fruit flavours influence how dry it feels. Sweetness is mainly affected by the amount of residual sugar left in the finished wine and by the balance between sugar and acidity. A pale rosé can be completely dry. A darker rosé can also be dry. If sweetness matters to you, check the label, producer notes or ask the person selling the wine rather than judging by colour. Australian rosé Australian rosé is not one regional or grape variety style. It is made across many regions from varieties including Shiraz, Grenache, Merlot, Nebbiolo and Pinot Noir, among others. That variety gives you a useful starting point when reading a label. A grape name can suggest the kind of fruit or structure you might encounter, but it is not a guarantee. Australian labels may include a grape variety, vintage or Geographical Indication, commonly called a GI , which identifies a wine-growing region. These details are optional rather than requirements for every bottle. Where a single variety, vintage or GI claim is made, Australian labelling rules apply, including the relevant 85 per cent threshold. How to serve and store rosé Chill still rosé before serving. In warm conditions, it may need time in the refrigerator or an ice bucket to reach a refreshing temperature. Avoid serving it so cold that its aroma and flavour disappear. After opening, reseal the bottle and refrigerate it. Still rosé is usually at its freshest over the next few days. Sparkling rosé loses its bubbles more quickly, so use a proper sparkling-wine stopper and drink it sooner. You do not need special glassware. A regular white-wine glass is a useful choice. What food goes with rosé? Rosé is a flexible partner at the table. Try it with salads and grilled vegetables, seafood and shellfish, grilled chicken, charcuterie, picnic foods, fresh or soft cheeses, tomato-based dishes and mildly spiced food. A dry, lively rosé may suit seafood and salads particularly well. A fuller or more deeply coloured example can stand up to grilled foods. Sweeter rosé may work with spicy dishes or fruit-based foods. These are starting points, not rules. In summary Rosé is a broad wine style, not a single grape, region or sweetness level. Its colour usually comes from limited contact between red grape juice and skins. Direct pressing, short maceration and saignée are different ways to achieve that style. Rosé can be dry or sweet, pale or deep, still or sparkling. When choosing one, use the label and producer description rather than assuming colour tells you everything. For the broader foundations, see What is wine? and How wine is made .

title: What is Sangiovese?
description: Sangiovese is an Italian red grape known for bright acidity, savoury character and red-fruit flavours. Learn what to expect in Australian examples.
text: title: What is Sangiovese? description: Sangiovese is an Italian red wine grape known for cherry flavours, lively acidity and noticeable tannin. Learn what Sangiovese wine tastes like and how styles vary. canonical: https://winedaddy.com.au/what-is-sangiovese/ article_type: Educational Guide What is Sangiovese? Highlights Sangiovese is an Italian red wine grape variety, not one single wine style. It is best known for dry red wines with cherry flavours, lively acidity and noticeable tannin. Plum, herbs, spice and savoury notes may also appear, depending on the wine. Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino are famous Sangiovese-based appellations, not definitions of every Sangiovese wine. Australian Sangiovese can be brighter, riper, darker or more savoury depending on its region and how it is made. Its acidity and tannin make it a natural partner for tomato-based dishes, pizza and grilled food. Quick answer Sangiovese is an Italian red wine grape variety strongly associated with Tuscany. It is used to make wines ranging from light and fresh to dark, firm and structured. A typical Sangiovese wine is dry, with flavours of cherry, sour cherry and other red fruits. It often has lively acidity, which gives the wine freshness and a mouth-watering quality, along with noticeable tannin that can feel drying or grippy. Sangiovese is not a fixed recipe. Climate, vineyard site, ripeness, harvest timing, extraction, oak, blending and maturation all influence the finished wine. That is why one bottle may taste bright and savoury while another is richer, darker and more powerful. The variety is famous in Italy through wines such as Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino, but it is also grown and made in Australia. Australian examples are produced in places including the King Valley, McLaren Vale, Riverina, Riverland and the Murray–Darling–Swan Hill area. What does Sangiovese taste like? Sangiovese commonly shows cherry, sour cherry, plum and other red-fruit flavours. Depending on the wine, you may also notice herbs, violet, spice, earth or savoury flavours. Its structure is often as important as its fruit. Acidity gives Sangiovese lift and freshness, while tannin provides grip and a drying sensation. Many examples are medium-bodied, although riper fruit, more extraction, oak maturation or blending can produce a fuller, more structured wine. The finish may be fresh, savoury, tannic or persistent. There is no single tasting profile that applies to every bottle. Is Sangiovese sweet? Most still Sangiovese is dry, meaning it contains little perceptible residual sugar. However, a wine can taste of ripe cherry or plum without being sweet. This is a useful distinction when reading a tasting note: fruitiness describes flavour and aroma; dryness describes sweetness on the palate . A dry Sangiovese can still taste generously fruity. Why does Sangiovese vary so much? The grape’s final style reflects a chain of decisions and conditions. Climate and site Warmer conditions can encourage riper fruit, darker flavours and a fuller impression. Cooler conditions or earlier harvesting may preserve brighter acidity and more red-fruit or herbal character. These are tendencies, not rules. Vineyard elevation, aspect, rainfall, water availability, the season and the producer’s decisions all matter too. A warm region does not automatically produce heavy wine, and a cool region does not automatically produce thin wine. Ripeness and harvest timing Riper grapes can contribute darker fruit, greater body and softer-feeling tannin. Earlier-picked grapes may retain more acidity and show fresher red-fruit flavours. Neither approach is automatically better. The winemaker is balancing freshness, ripeness, tannin and alcohol to create the intended style. Extraction, oak and maturation During red-wine making, contact with grape skins helps extract colour and tannin. More intensive extraction can create a darker, firmer wine, while gentler extraction may preserve freshness and make the wine feel lighter. Oak can add texture and flavours such as spice, toast or vanilla. These are winemaking influences, not inherent Sangiovese flavours. Bottle maturation may soften tannin and bring more savoury, earthy or dried-fruit character, although ageing outcomes vary from wine to wine. Sangiovese may be bottled on its own or blended with other grape varieties. Blending can alter colour, body, aroma, tannin and balance. Sangiovese, Chianti and Brunello One of the easiest ways to understand Sangiovese is to separate the grape from the wine category. Sangiovese is the grape variety. Chianti is a regulated Italian appellation whose wines contain 70% to 100% Sangiovese according to the Chianti consortium’s summary of the rules. Brunello di Montalcino is a specific appellation made exclusively from Sangiovese, locally called Brunello, under defined production and maturation rules. Chianti and Brunello therefore show different expressions of Sangiovese. They do not mean that every Sangiovese wine must taste like either one. Chianti is commonly described as dry, savoury and slightly tannic, with red-fruit and violet notes. Brunello di Montalcino is typically associated with a more robust, structured style and extended maturation. These are appellation-based traditions, not universal characteristics of the grape. Sangiovese in Australia Sangiovese is an established but relatively small variety in Australia. Wine Australia’s 2024 snapshot recorded 5,906 tonnes crushed in 2024. Its planting figure—438 hectares—uses 2015 Australian Bureau of Statistics data, so the two figures refer to different years.
