The largest regional shares listed in that snapshot included Murray–Darling–Swan Hill, the King Valley, Riverina, Riverland and McLaren Vale. These figures describe production context, not a ranking of quality. Australian Sangiovese is not one national style. Depending on the region, season, vineyard material and winemaking, it may be bright and cherry-driven, fuller and darker-fruited, or more savoury and structured. It can be useful to compare Australian and Italian examples, but neither country produces one uniform style. What food goes with Sangiovese? Sangiovese’s acidity can work particularly well with tomato-based foods, while its tannin and savoury character can suit roasted or grilled ingredients. Try it with: tomato-based pasta; pizza; grilled or roasted vegetables; roast or grilled meats; mushroom dishes; and other savoury Mediterranean-style foods. These are suggestions rather than rules. The best match depends on the wine’s weight, tannin and fruit character, as well as the dish. For serving, Sangiovese is generally more refreshing when served slightly cool rather than warm. A lighter, fresher bottle may suit a cooler serving temperature than a fuller, oak-matured example. How to choose a Sangiovese If you are buying Sangiovese for the first time, start by thinking about the style you enjoy: For freshness and red-fruit flavour, look for a lighter or more fruit-driven style. For structure and savoury depth, choose a wine described as firm, concentrated or oak-matured. If you are cooking with tomatoes, acidity is likely to be useful at the table. If you prefer softer wines, be aware that young Sangiovese can have noticeable tannin. The grape name gives you a helpful starting point, but the region, producer and winemaking details on the label can change the experience considerably. For more grape varieties, explore WineDaddy’s grape variety guide . For a broader introduction to wine, see what is wine? . Sangiovese FAQs Is Sangiovese a red or white grape? Sangiovese is a red wine grape variety. Is Sangiovese the same as Chianti? No. Sangiovese is the grape. Chianti is a regulated Italian wine appellation that uses Sangiovese as its principal grape. Is Brunello made from Sangiovese? Yes. Brunello di Montalcino is made exclusively from Sangiovese, which is locally called Brunello. Is Sangiovese full-bodied? It can be, but not every example is. Many Sangiovese wines are medium-bodied and fresh, while riper, more extracted or oak-matured examples may feel fuller and more structured. Is Sangiovese a good food wine? Often, yes. Its acidity and tannin can work well with tomato-based dishes, grilled food, roasted vegetables and savoury meats.

title: What Is Sauvignon Blanc?
description: Sauvignon Blanc is a fresh, aromatic white wine grape variety. Learn what it tastes like, whether it is sweet and how Australian styles vary.
text: Highlights Sauvignon Blanc is a white wine grape variety and the name commonly used for wines made from it. It is often fresh, aromatic and high in perceived acidity, with flavours such as citrus, grapefruit, passionfruit, herbs or grass. Most still Sauvignon Blanc is dry. Fruity or tropical flavours do not necessarily mean the wine contains much sugar. It is not always grassy, sweet, light-bodied or unoaked. Australian examples vary from crisp, aromatic wines to broader Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon blends. Serve it chilled and try it with seafood, salads, goat’s cheese or fresh, herb-led dishes. Quick Answer: What Is Sauvignon Blanc? Sauvignon Blanc is a white wine grape variety. The same name is also commonly used for wines made primarily from that grape. It is best known for producing fresh, aromatic white wines with noticeable acidity. Depending on where the grapes are grown and how the wine is made, you might taste lemon, lime, grapefruit, passionfruit, guava, gooseberry, freshly cut grass, herbs or green capsicum. Most still Sauvignon Blanc is made in a dry style. That does not mean it lacks fruit flavour. A wine can taste strongly of passionfruit or tropical fruit while containing little residual sugar. Fruitiness, sweetness, acidity and body are different parts of the wine. Sauvignon Blanc is often light to medium bodied, but it has a broad range of styles. Stainless-steel fermentation commonly produces a bright, direct and aromatic wine. Riper fruit, barrel fermentation, oak maturation, lees contact or blending with Semillon can create a fuller, rounder or more textural result. In Australia, Adelaide Hills offers one fresh, aromatic expression, while Margaret River is particularly associated with Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon blends ranging from crisp and herbal to richer and more oak-influenced. Tasmania is another useful cool-climate context. These are broad tendencies, not rules for every bottle. What Does Sauvignon Blanc Taste Like? Sauvignon Blanc’s flavour can be easier to understand by separating aroma, acidity, body and sweetness. Aroma and flavour Common descriptions include: lemon, lime and grapefruit; passionfruit and guava; gooseberry; tropical fruit; freshly cut grass; herbs; and green capsicum. Not every bottle shows all of these characters. Some are strongly citrus-driven, while others are tropical, herbal, savoury or more restrained. These descriptions are tasting comparisons, not ingredients added to the wine. Acidity Acidity gives wine freshness and lift. It can make your mouth water and leave the wine feeling lively rather than heavy. Sauvignon Blanc is commonly associated with noticeable acidity, although the impression changes with climate, ripeness, harvest timing and winemaking. Body and finish Body is the sense of weight or fullness in your mouth. Many Sauvignon Blancs are light to medium bodied, but riper fruit, oak, lees contact or Semillon blending can give the wine more breadth. The finish may be crisp and citrusy, herbal, tropical or softly textured. A fresh finish is one reason Sauvignon Blanc works well with lighter foods. Is Sauvignon Blanc Sweet? Usually, no. Most ordinary still Sauvignon Blanc is dry, meaning it contains little perceptible residual sugar. However, ripe fruit flavours can make a dry wine seem sweet. Passionfruit, guava and tropical fruit are aroma and flavour impressions; they are not proof that the wine contains much sugar. A useful way to think about it is: Dryness relates mainly to residual sugar. Fruitiness describes aromas and flavours. Acidity creates freshness and tension. Body describes weight and fullness. A Sauvignon Blanc can therefore be dry, fruity and high in acidity at the same time. Why Does Sauvignon Blanc Vary So Much? The grape responds clearly to both its growing conditions and the choices made in the winery. Climate and ripeness Cool but sunny conditions can help the grapes retain acidity while developing aromatic intensity. Warmer conditions may encourage riper, broader and more tropical flavours, although site, vintage and harvest decisions also matter. Harvest timing changes the balance of flavours. Earlier-picked grapes may retain sharper freshness and greener, herbaceous characters. Longer ripening can encourage riper fruit and reduce some vegetal notes. Winemakers may combine fruit picked at different stages of ripeness to create balance. Sauvignon Blanc can also produce vigorous foliage. Vineyard canopy management and light exposure can influence the balance between green, herbaceous character and riper fruit expression. Fermentation and maturation Stainless-steel fermentation is common. It helps winemakers preserve fresh aromas and a direct, crisp style. Oak is not mandatory, though. Barrel fermentation or oak maturation can add breadth, texture and richness. Lees contact can also contribute a rounder mouthfeel. Some wines are bottled relatively soon after fermentation for a fresh, immediate style. Others are given more time, oak influence or blending to develop a broader shape. Australian Sauvignon Blanc Styles Australia does not have one single Sauvignon Blanc flavour profile. The variety is grown in regions with different climates and is handled in different ways. Adelaide Hills Adelaide Hills is a prominent Australian context for Sauvignon Blanc. Wine Australia describes examples from the region as lively and aromatic, with grapefruit, tropical fruit and crisp acidity. This is a useful style to try if you enjoy fresh, fragrant white wines. Margaret River Margaret River provides a different illustration. Sauvignon Blanc is commonly blended with Semillon, which can add mid-palate weight and texture. Wines may range from light, crisp, lemony and herbal to fuller, more tropical and oak-influenced. This is why Sauvignon Blanc should not be assumed to mean only a lean, unoaked wine. Tasmania Tasmania is another cool-climate Australian context. It helps demonstrate how the variety can be grown in cooler settings where freshness and aromatic definition are important. Individual wines will still vary according to site, vintage and winemaking. A brief comparison with New Zealand can also be useful. New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc is often associated with pronounced passionfruit, grapefruit, grass and capsicum characters, but New Zealand itself produces a range of styles. It should not be treated as the only correct expression of the grape. How Should You Serve Sauvignon Blanc? Serve Sauvignon Blanc chilled or well chilled. An exact serving temperature is not necessary to enjoy a beginner bottle, and the ideal temperature can vary with the wine’s body and style. A very aromatic, light-bodied wine may feel particularly refreshing when well chilled. A fuller, oaked or Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon blend can show more of its texture if it is not served excessively cold. What Food Goes With Sauvignon Blanc? Its acidity and freshness make Sauvignon Blanc a natural partner for lighter, bright-flavoured dishes. Try it with: oysters and other shellfish; fresh white fish; salads; goat’s cheese; lightly prepared chicken or pork; dishes with citrus, herbs or garlic; and fresh vegetables. These are starting points, not rules. A crisp Sauvignon Blanc may suit a simple seafood dish, while a broader Margaret River blend may work better with richer fish, roast chicken or a creamy goat’s cheese preparation. How to Recognise the Style in Your Glass When tasting Sauvignon Blanc, ask four simple questions: What aromas stand out? Citrus, tropical fruit, herbs or green characters? How fresh does it feel? Notice the acidity and mouth-watering finish. How much weight does it have? Light and crisp, or broad and textured? Does it taste sweet, or merely fruity? A tropical aroma can still belong to a dry wine. The main lesson is that Sauvignon Blanc is a grape with a recognisable personality, not a single fixed recipe. It can be crisp, aromatic and herbal, or riper, fuller and more textured. Australian wines are well worth exploring across regions and styles. Related Learning What is wine? How wine is made Red wine vs white wine Explore grape varieties Explore Australian wine regions What does oak do to wine?

title: What Is Shiraz?
description: Shiraz is a versatile red wine grape known as Syrah internationally. Learn what Shiraz tastes like, whether it is sweet and how Australian regions shape its style.
text: Highlights Shiraz is a dark-skinned grape used mainly to make red wine. Syrah is the principal international name for the same grape variety. Australian Shiraz can be medium-bodied and savoury, or rich, full-bodied and dark-fruited. Typical flavours may include blackberry, plum, spice, liquorice, pepper, floral notes and savoury characters. Shiraz is usually made as a dry wine, even when it tastes ripe, rich or jammy. Climate, vineyard site, ripeness and winemaking all help shape the final wine. Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale, Hunter Valley, Heathcote and cooler regions can produce noticeably different styles. Quick Answer Shiraz is a dark-skinned wine grape variety, usually made into red wine. In Australia, Shiraz is the familiar name used on labels and by wine drinkers. Internationally, the same grape is commonly called Syrah . There is no single Shiraz flavour or style. Depending on where the grapes grow and how the wine is made, Shiraz may be medium- to full-bodied, with flavours ranging from red and dark fruit to black pepper, spice, liquorice, flowers and savoury notes. It may feel fresh and peppery, plush and generous, or firm and structured. Australian Shiraz is especially diverse. Warm regions such as Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale are often associated with richer, fuller and darker-fruited wines. More moderate or cooler regions, including Hunter Valley, Yarra Valley and Canberra District, can produce fresher, more aromatic, savoury or peppery expressions. These are broad tendencies, not guarantees. The most useful thing to remember is that “Shiraz” on a label identifies the grape and the Australian naming convention. It does not promise a sweet, heavy, high-alcohol or heavily oaked wine. Shiraz and Syrah: are they the same grape? Yes. Shiraz and Syrah are names for the same grape variety. Syrah is the common international name, particularly in France and regions influenced by French terminology. Shiraz is the established Australian name. Australia adopted and popularised the name during the nineteenth century, and it is now the normal term for the variety on Australian wine labels. The names can be connected with different regional traditions and stylistic expectations, but those comparisons are more detailed than this introduction needs to be. For now, treat Shiraz and Syrah as the same grape with different naming conventions. What does Shiraz taste like? Shiraz can show a wide range of aromas and flavours, including: blackberry, plum, blueberry and black cherry red-fruit notes in some fresher styles black pepper and other spices liquorice violet or other floral aromas earthy, savoury or herbal characters vanilla, toast or spice from oak maturation These are possibilities rather than a tasting checklist. One Shiraz may smell mainly of dark fruit, while another may be floral, peppery or savoury. Shiraz can also feel quite different from one bottle to another. Its body may be medium or full. Its tannins—the drying or grippy sensation in the mouth—may feel firm, fine, silky or plush. Acidity can provide freshness and lift, while alcohol, ripeness and oak can add weight and warmth. Some Shiraz has a distinctive black-pepper aroma. The Australian Wine Research Institute links this character to a grape-derived compound called rotundone , particularly in some cool-climate Shiraz. Not every Shiraz contains enough rotundone to smell peppery, and not every person perceives it in the same way. Why does Shiraz vary so much? The finished wine reflects several influences working together. Climate Warm conditions can encourage riper fruit, richer texture and darker-fruited flavours. Cooler or more moderate conditions can support freshness, aromatic detail, savoury notes and pepper. That does not mean warm-climate Shiraz is always heavy or cool-climate Shiraz is always light. Water availability, vineyard management, harvest timing, vintage conditions and winemaking can all change the result. Vineyard site The vineyard’s aspect, elevation, soil, water conditions and local climate can influence how grapes ripen. Australian research has found that Shiraz from different regions can show measurable chemical and sensory differences, while also finding substantial variation within individual regions. A regional name is therefore a useful clue, not a flavour guarantee. Ripeness and harvest timing Riper grapes may give the wine fuller fruit flavours, more weight and a softer impression of acidity. Earlier-picked grapes may retain more freshness and aromatic lift. Neither approach automatically makes a better wine; they create different styles. Fermentation and extraction During red-wine fermentation, colour, flavour and tannin are extracted from the grape skins. Winemakers can adjust the amount and texture of that extraction through choices involving temperature, time, vessel and cap management. Some Shiraz is fermented with whole bunches, while other wines are made from destemmed grapes. These choices can influence aroma and texture, but neither method is required for an authentic Shiraz. Oak and maturation Oak can contribute flavour, texture and structure. New oak may add vanilla, toast or spice, while older oak can have a subtler influence. Some Shiraz is matured in oak; some uses older vessels; some fresh styles see little or no oak. Oak is common in Shiraz, but it does not define the grape. Australian Shiraz is not one style Shiraz is grown in many Australian wine regions. That gives Australian drinkers a particularly broad range of styles to explore. Barossa Valley is strongly associated with rich, full-bodied and textured Shiraz, often with dark fruit, spice and liquorice-like characters. However, Barossa also produces fresher, more fragrant and medium-bodied wines. It should not automatically be equated with sweetness, high alcohol or heavy oak. McLaren Vale is associated with full-bodied Shiraz, rich fruit and chocolate-like characters. Its Mediterranean-influenced climate contributes to a distinctive regional context, but individual wines still vary. Hunter Valley provides a useful counterexample to the idea that Australian Shiraz is always massive. Its wines are often described as medium-bodied, red-fruited and savoury. Heathcote can produce medium- to full-bodied Shiraz with dark fruit and spice. Yarra Valley and Canberra District are examples of regions capable of more aromatic, savoury, elegant or peppery styles. These descriptions help you form expectations, but they should not be treated as rules. A winemaker, vineyard site and growing season can make two wines from the same region taste quite different. Is Shiraz sweet? Usually, Shiraz is made as a dry red wine. However, ripe fruit flavours can taste sweet, particularly when the wine is rich, jammy or full-bodied. This is an important distinction: Residual sugar means sugar left in the wine. Fruit sweetness is the impression created by ripe fruit aromas and flavours. A dry Shiraz can smell or taste sweet-fruited without being a sweet wine. The exact sweetness of a bottle depends on the individual wine. Is Shiraz always full-bodied? No. Shiraz ranges from medium-bodied to full-bodied. Many warm-region examples are broad, rich and generous, while wines from more moderate regions may feel fresher, lighter on their feet or more savoury. Body is a style characteristic, not a measure of quality. How should a beginner approach Shiraz? Start by comparing wines rather than trying to find one “correct” Shiraz style. A fuller Barossa Valley wine and a medium-bodied Hunter Valley wine can both be recognisably Australian Shiraz while offering very different experiences. Read the region, producer description and alcohol information on the label as clues, not guarantees. Serve the wine according to its individual recommendation; a full-bodied red is generally more enjoyable slightly below a warm room temperature than overheated. A standard red-wine glass is all you need. Most importantly, do not decide whether you like Shiraz based on one bottle. The variety covers a broad landscape of fruit, spice, freshness, tannin and texture. The short version Shiraz is Australia’s familiar name for the Syrah grape. It is usually made into dry red wine and can taste dark-fruited, peppery, floral, savoury, spicy or richly textured. Australian Shiraz is not a single heavy or sweet style: region, climate, ripeness, vineyard conditions and winemaking all shape the result.

title: What is sparkling wine?
description: Learn what creates the bubbles, how sparkling wine is made and why Champagne is one protected regional style.
text: Highlights Sparkling wine is wine containing dissolved carbon dioxide—the gas that creates its bubbles. The bubbles can be created by fermentation in a bottle or tank, or added mechanically through carbonation. Sparkling wine can be white, rosé or red, and range from very dry to sweet. Champagne is a protected regional name, not a generic word for sparkling wine. Traditional-method wines may develop bready or toasty flavours through ageing on yeast sediment. Australia makes sparkling wine in several regions and styles, including sparkling Shiraz. Quick answer Sparkling wine is wine with enough dissolved carbon dioxide to create visible bubbles and a lively, tingling texture when the bottle is opened and the wine is poured. The carbon dioxide can come from fermentation. In the traditional method, a second fermentation happens inside the bottle. In the tank method, it happens in a sealed pressure tank. Some sparkling wines are carbonated by adding carbon dioxide mechanically instead. This means sparkling wine is a broad category, not one single style. It may be white, rosé or red; dry or sweet; light and fruit-driven or richer and more savoury. Champagne is one particular type of sparkling wine: it comes from France’s Champagne region and must meet the region’s rules. Sparkling wine made elsewhere should not be called Champagne. What makes wine sparkling? The bubbles come from dissolved carbon dioxide. When the bottle is opened, pressure falls. The gas then leaves the wine, forming bubbles that rise through the glass. That release is called effervescence . It is the visible bubbling and lively sensation associated with sparkling wine. The useful distinction from still wine is not colour, sweetness or grape variety. It is the presence of noticeable, intentional effervescence. How are the bubbles made? During fermentation, yeast converts sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Usually, much of that gas escapes. For sparkling wine, winemakers retain the gas by carrying out a further fermentation in a sealed environment. Traditional method In the traditional method, the second fermentation takes place in the bottle in which the wine will eventually be sold. The wine may then spend time ageing on lees , the yeast sediment left after fermentation. This can contribute developed flavours and aromas such as toast, biscuit, bread or savoury yeast. “Traditional method” describes how the wine was made. It is not, by itself, a guarantee that one wine is better than another. Tank method In the tank method, the second fermentation takes place in a sealed pressure tank rather than in individual bottles. The wine is then bottled under pressure. This approach is commonly associated with fresh fruit and floral characters, although the final style depends on the grapes, winemaking and ageing. Carbonation Some sparkling wines are made by mechanically adding carbon dioxide to the wine. This is called carbonation . It is a different production approach from creating bubbles through a second fermentation. The method itself is not a complete judgement of quality; it simply tells you where the gas came from. Other methods exist too, including transfer and ancestral approaches. They are useful terms to encounter, but they need not turn a beginner’s definition into a technical production manual. Is sparkling wine the same as Champagne? No. Sparkling wine is the broad category. Champagne is a protected geographical name for qualifying sparkling wine from the Champagne region of France. So these statements are accurate: Champagne is sparkling wine. Not all sparkling wine is Champagne. Australian sparkling wine should not be labelled Champagne. “Champagne” should not be used as a casual synonym for any fizzy wine. Prosecco is another regulated name associated with Italian wine production. It is commonly encountered as a fresh, tank-fermented sparkling style, but the Prosecco DOC denomination also covers semi-sparkling and still wines under its production rules. What styles of sparkling wine are there? Sparkling wine has much more variety than the standard image of a pale, dry drink for celebrations. White, rosé and red Sparkling wine may be white, rosé or red—including Australia’s distinctive sparkling Shiraz style. Colour comes from the grapes and winemaking choices, not from whether the wine is sparkling. Dry through sweet Sparkling wines range from very dry to sweet. Terms such as brut describe sweetness levels rather than the presence or absence of bubbles. Fresh and fruity through richer and savoury Some sparkling wines are light, fresh and fruit-driven. Others have more developed, bready or toasty characters, particularly after time ageing on lees. Bubble size and persistence can vary. They are affected by dissolved carbon dioxide, pressure, temperature, the glass and ageing. Small bubbles alone do not prove that a wine is better. Australian sparkling wine Australia produces sparkling wine across multiple regions and styles. Verified examples include Tasmania, the Adelaide Hills and the Yarra Valley, with traditional-method wines particularly associated with some cool-climate Australian regions. Australia also has a recognised sparkling-red tradition, especially sparkling Shiraz. This is a useful reminder that sparkling wine is not limited to European regions, pale colours or one set of grapes. A simple way to understand the label When you see a bottle of sparkling wine, consider four separate questions: Where is it from? The region may influence the name and style. How was it made? Look for terms such as traditional method or tank method. How sweet is it? Words such as brut provide a clue. What style is it? It may be white, rosé or red, and fresh or more developed. Serve it chilled and pay attention to how the bubbles feel as well as how the wine smells and tastes. A narrow flute is not essential; the glass can influence how aromas and bubbles appear, but the wine remains the main event. The short version Sparkling wine is wine with dissolved carbon dioxide and noticeable effervescence. Its bubbles may come from a second fermentation in a bottle, a second fermentation in a sealed tank or mechanical carbonation. The category includes white, rosé and red wines, from dry to sweet and from fresh to richly developed. Champagne is one protected regional type of sparkling wine—not another name for all sparkling wine. For the wider foundation, see What is wine? and How wine is made .

title: What is sweet wine?
description: Learn what makes wine taste sweet, how residual sugar works and why fruity does not necessarily mean sweet.
text: Highlights Sweet wine tastes sweet because it contains enough residual sugar for you to notice it. Residual sugar is grape sugar left in the wine after fermentation. A wine that smells fruity is not necessarily sweet. Acidity can balance sweetness and make a wine feel fresh rather than heavy. Alcohol warmth, tannin and body are different sensations from sweetness. Sweetness can range from a slight softness to an intensely sugary, concentrated taste. “Sweet”, “off-dry” and “dessert wine” do not always mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Sweet wine is a style characteristic, not a measure of quality. Quick answer Sweet wine is wine with noticeable sweetness, usually because some grape sugar remains after fermentation. This remaining sugar is called residual sugar . During fermentation, yeast converts grape sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. When fermentation continues until almost all fermentable sugar has been used, the wine is generally dry. If fermentation stops or finishes while some sugar remains, the wine can taste sweet. That is only part of the story. A wine’s acidity, alcohol, tannin, aroma and serving temperature all influence how sweet or balanced it seems. A dry wine can smell strongly of peaches, berries or tropical fruit without containing much residual sugar. Conversely, a wine with considerable residual sugar can taste lively and fresh if its acidity balances the sweetness. Sweet wines are made in several ways. Winemakers may stop fermentation early, use grapes with highly concentrated sugars, allow fermentation to finish with sugar remaining, or add a permitted sweet component such as concentrated grape must where the relevant rules allow it. What is residual sugar? Residual sugar is the sugar left in wine after fermentation. Grapes naturally contain sugar. Yeast uses that sugar during fermentation, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide. The more completely fermentation consumes the fermentable sugar, the less sugar remains in the finished wine. A wine with little perceptible sugar is usually described as dry. If enough sugar remains to be noticeable, the wine may be off-dry, medium-sweet or sweet. Residual sugar is a chemical measurement. Perceived sweetness is your sensory experience. Acidity, alcohol, aroma and other components can change how sweet the wine seems. How does wine become sweet? There is no single recipe for sweet wine. Stopping fermentation Fermentation can be stopped before yeast has consumed all the grape sugar. The wine then retains some residual sugar. Fermenting concentrated grapes Grapes harvested very late, dried before pressing or affected by particular conditions can contain more concentrated sugars. Examples include late-harvest wines, botrytised wines, straw wines and icewine or eiswein. These are broad examples rather than one universal production category. Adding a sweet component where permitted Some wines may receive a sweet component, such as concentrated grape must, where the relevant regulations and wine category permit it. This is why it is unsafe to say that sugar can never be added or that all sweet wine is made by stopping fermentation. Sweetness is not the same as fruitiness One of the most common wine misunderstandings is confusing fruity flavour with sweetness. A dry wine can smell of ripe peach, pear, citrus, berries or tropical fruit. These impressions come from aroma compounds and flavour perception, not necessarily from sugar. Fruity: “This smells like strawberries.” Sweet: “This tastes sugar-like on my palate.” Acidic: “This is tart and mouth-watering.” Tannic: “This feels drying or grippy.” Alcoholic: “This feels warming or hot.” Full-bodied: “This feels broad or weighty.” These sensations can appear together, but none is automatically a substitute for another. How sweet can wine be? In everyday wine language, sweetness is often described as a progression: dry, off-dry, medium-sweet and sweet. The boundaries vary. The OIV provides formal definitions based on sugar content and, for some categories, the relationship between sugar and acidity. Its definition of “sweet” begins at 45 grams per litre of sugar. That figure is an OIV classification, not a universal Australian rule. “Dessert wine” is also a broad description, not one single sweetness level. Why acidity matters Acidity gives wine its tart, fresh and mouth-watering quality. In a sweet wine, acidity can balance the sugar and stop the wine feeling flat or heavy. Imagine lemonade: sweetness is more refreshing when enough acidity is present. Wine is more complex, but the same broad idea helps explain balance. Acidity does not remove sugar or make a wine chemically dry. It changes the way sweetness is experienced. Alcohol, tannin and body Alcohol contributes warmth and can add a sense of richness or weight. It is not the same as sweetness. Tannin contributes grip, bitterness and a drying or puckering sensation. Body describes the perceived weight or fullness of a wine. Sugar can contribute to body, but so can alcohol, tannin, acidity, flavour and other components. A full-bodied wine is not automatically sweet. How to taste for sweetness Smell it first. Identify aromas, but do not treat them as proof of sweetness. Take a small sip. Ask whether the wine tastes sugar-like or simply fruity. Notice the middle and finish. Does sweetness remain? Does acidity make your mouth water? Check the texture. Is it drying and grippy, light and fresh, or broad and full? Read the label or technical sheet. Terms such as sweet, off-dry or a residual-sugar figure can help. Australian context Australian drinkers may see terms including dry, medium dry, off-dry, sweet and dessert wine. These may not have identical meanings across every wine or jurisdiction. Australian alcoholic-beverage labelling is governed through the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. That does not mean every Australian wine label must display residual sugar in grams per litre. If you need certainty, check technical information or ask the winery. Does sweet mean better or worse? No. Sweetness is a characteristic, not a quality ranking. A sweet wine can be balanced by acidity, shaped by concentrated fruit and made for a particular occasion. A dry wine can be excellent, ordinary, delicate or powerful. The useful question is whether the wine is balanced and whether its style suits your taste. For the wider foundation, see What is wine? and How wine is made .

title: What Is Sweetness in Wine?
description: Learn what sweetness means in wine, how residual sugar affects the palate, and why a fruity wine can still be technically dry.
text: Highlights Sweetness is the sweet sensation you notice on your palate. Residual sugar—the grape sugar left after fermentation—is its main direct source. A fruity-smelling wine can still be technically dry. “Dry” usually means little perceptible sweetness, not little flavour. Acidity, alcohol, tannin, bitterness, body, texture and temperature all affect how sweet a wine seems. Red, white, rosé, sparkling and fortified wines can all be dry or sweet. Grape variety, colour and region are clues—not guarantees—of sweetness. Quick answer: what does sweetness mean in wine? Sweetness in wine is the perception of sugar on your palate. It mainly comes from residual sugar , which is grape sugar left in the wine after fermentation. During fermentation, yeast converts grape sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. When most of the sugar is fermented, the wine will generally taste dry. When a noticeable amount remains, the wine may taste off-dry, medium-sweet or sweet. But sweetness is not simply a sugar reading. Acidity can make a wine feel fresher and less heavy, while tannin or bitterness can make it seem drier. Alcohol may add warmth or roundness, and fruit aromas can make a wine smell sweet even when it contains little perceptible sugar. That is why a wine can taste fruity yet dry. Dry describes sweetness, not flavour intensity. Sweetness is not the same as fruitiness A wine described as smelling of peach, berries, citrus, ripe melon or honey does not necessarily contain residual sugar. These are comparisons used to describe aromas and flavours—not an ingredient list. For example, a dry Riesling can smell strongly of citrus, green apple or ripe stone fruit. A dry red can show vivid berry or plum character. Those fruit impressions do not prove the wine is sweet. It helps to separate these ideas: Sweetness: a sweet sensation on the palate. Residual sugar: sugar remaining after fermentation. Fruitiness: fruit-like aroma or flavour. Ripeness: a description of grape maturity and resulting character. Alcohol warmth: heat or warmth associated with alcohol. Body: the wine’s perceived weight, fullness and texture. A wine can be fruity but dry, sweet but not obviously fruity, or both sweet and fruity. What you notice What it may indicate Fruity aroma Fruit-like smell, not necessarily sugar Sweet sensation on the palate Possible residual sugar Fresh, mouth-watering finish Acidity may be balancing the wine Drying grip Tannin, especially in red wine Warmth Alcohol, not necessarily sweetness How acidity changes sweetness Acidity is one of the most important factors affecting the impression of sweetness. It gives wine freshness and can make residual sugar feel lighter and less cloying. A wine can contain noticeable sugar and still taste lively when it also has high acidity. The acidity does not remove the sugar; it changes how the wine feels as a whole. Conversely, a wine with lower acidity may seem broader, softer or sweeter. Australian Riesling is a useful example. It can be made in crisp, dry styles or with residual sugar, with acidity helping shape the wine’s freshness and balance. The grape variety does not guarantee one sweetness level. What do dry, off-dry and sweet mean? These terms are useful descriptions, but they are not one universal numerical scale for every wine category and market. Dry: little or no perceptible sweetness. Off-dry: a small but noticeable level of sweetness. Medium-sweet: a moderate, clearly perceptible level of sweetness. Sweet: clearly perceptible sweetness. The precise terminology and boundaries can vary between still wine, sparkling wine and fortified wine, as well as between education systems and markets. Avoid assuming that a single sugar threshold applies to every bottle. Sparkling wine has its own category-specific terms, including Brut, Extra-Dry and Dry. These should not automatically be interpreted through the ordinary meaning of “dry” used for still wine. Australian wine labels and descriptions do not provide one universal sweetness scale that every wine must display. If sweetness matters to your choice, ask the retailer, sommelier or winery for the style of the individual wine. Why can wine seem dry when it contains sugar? Several sensations can make wine seem less sweet: Acidity adds freshness and can balance sugar. Tannin creates grip or a drying sensation, especially in red wine. Bitterness can reduce the impression of sweetness. Alcohol can add warmth or roundness, although it is not sugar sweetness. Texture and body can make sweetness feel lighter, richer or heavier. Temperature changes perception: a warmer wine may show softness or alcohol more prominently, while a chilled wine may seem fresher. Tannin deserves particular attention. In everyday wine language, “dry” usually means low sweetness. A drying mouthfeel, however, is more often associated with tannin. These are different sensations, even though people may use the same word for both. A wine can therefore have some residual sugar and still create a drying or structured impression. Does the colour or grape tell you whether wine is sweet? Not reliably. Red, white, rosé, sparkling and fortified wines can all range from dry to sweet. Grape variety is a clue to possible style, not a guarantee. Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Shiraz and other varieties can be made with different levels of residual sugar. The same is true of regions: a region may be known for particular styles, but its name does not determine the sweetness of every bottle. Australian examples include dry and off-dry Riesling, dry sparkling wine, rosé, and sweet late-picked or fortified styles. The individual wine matters more than its colour, variety or region. For a broader explanation of how sweetness relates to wine categories, see what is sweet wine? . You can also learn the tasting basics in how to taste wine and read about the high-level role of fermentation in how wine is made . How to taste sweetness in wine You do not need to estimate grams of sugar to notice sweetness. Try this simple exercise: Taste the wine at an appropriate serving temperature. Take a small sip and let it move across your palate. Ask whether you notice a sweet sensation, rather than simply a fruity aroma. Notice whether acidity makes the wine feel fresh or mouth-watering. Check whether alcohol feels warm rather than sweet. Notice whether tannin creates grip or drying. Pay attention to the finish: does it feel sweet, fresh, bitter, tannic or clean? Compare it with another wine if you can. A useful question is: “Is this wine actually sweet on my palate, or does it simply smell ripe and fruity?” Your answer may differ from someone else’s. Perceived sweetness is influenced by the wine’s composition and by the taster’s sensitivity, so tasting descriptions are observations rather than personal tests you can fail. Does sweetness matter when pairing wine with food? Yes, at a basic level. A wine generally works well with dessert when it is at least as sweet as the dish. A little sweetness can also help soften the sensation of chilli heat, while acidity keeps the pairing fresh. Sweetness is only one part of a pairing. Acidity, alcohol, salt, bitterness and texture also matter. For a fuller explanation, see how wine pairing works, when available. Frequently asked questions Is dry wine completely free of sugar? Not necessarily. “Dry” generally means little or no perceptible sweetness. It does not always mean that absolutely no sugar remains. Does fruity wine mean sweet wine? No. Fruitiness describes an aroma or flavour impression. A wine can be strongly fruity and still taste dry. Does high alcohol mean a wine is sweet? No. Alcohol can create warmth, roundness or softness that some people interpret as sweetness, but alcohol is not residual sugar. Is Riesling always sweet? No. Australian Riesling can be crisp and dry, off-dry or made in a richer style with residual sugar. Check the individual wine rather than relying on the grape name alone. Is a drying red wine sweet? Not necessarily. A drying sensation is often caused by tannin. That is different from sweetness, which is the perception of sugar on the palate.

title: What Is Tempranillo?
description: Tempranillo is a Spanish red grape that can make juicy young wines or complex oak-aged styles. Learn what Australian drinkers should expect.
text: title: "What Is Tempranillo? Taste, Style and Australian Examples" description: "Tempranillo is a Spanish red-wine grape known for dry wines with red and dark fruit, fresh acidity and noticeable tannin. Learn what it tastes like and how Australian examples can differ." canonical: " https://winedaddy.com.au/what-is-tempranillo/ " article_type: "Educational Guide" What Is Tempranillo? Highlights Tempranillo is a red-wine grape variety , not one fixed style of wine. It is strongly associated with Spain, especially Rioja and Ribera del Duero. Tempranillo wines are usually dry, with red and dark fruit, fresh acidity and noticeable tannin. Oak and ageing can add vanilla, spice, leather or savoury flavours, but these are not guaranteed. Australian Tempranillo can range from fresh and elegant to dark, full and spice-driven. Fruit flavours such as cherry and plum do not mean the wine is sweet. Quick answer Tempranillo is a red grape variety from the Iberian Peninsula, best known through Spanish wines. It commonly produces dry red wines with flavours of cherry, plum, blackberry and other red or dark fruits. Fresh acidity gives the wine lift, while tannin can add a drying or grippy sensation. The style can change considerably. A fresher example may be medium-bodied, bright and red-fruited. A riper, more extracted or oak-matured wine may be fuller, darker, firmer and more savoury. That is why “Tempranillo” tells you the grape, but not exactly how every bottle will taste. Tempranillo is also grown and made in Australia. Australian examples may show the same broad grape identity while reflecting their region, climate, vintage and winemaking choices. What does Tempranillo taste like? A useful starting point is cherry, plum and other red or dark fruit , supported by acidity and tannin. Depending on the wine, you might also notice blackberry, strawberry, spice or savoury flavours. Oak maturation can contribute flavours such as vanilla, toast, cedar or spice. With bottle age, some wines develop more earthy, leathery, tobacco-like or dried-fruit characters. These are influences of winemaking and maturation as much as expressions of the grape itself. Tempranillo can be medium- to full-bodied. “Body” describes how weighty or full the wine feels in your mouth. A lighter-feeling Tempranillo may be fresh and energetic, while a richer example may feel broader and more powerful. Is Tempranillo sweet? Most still Tempranillo is dry. Its ripe fruit flavours can make it seem rich or fruit-sweet, but fruitiness is not the same as residual-sugar sweetness. If a wine tastes of cherry, plum or blackberry, that does not mean sugar has been added or that the wine is sweet. Dryness describes the amount of perceptible residual sugar; fruit flavour describes what your nose and palate sense. Is Tempranillo tannic? Tempranillo often has noticeable tannin, although the texture varies. Tannin can make your mouth feel slightly dry, grippy or firm, particularly in a young, extracted or oak-matured red. Ripeness, extraction, blending and bottle age all influence that sensation. Some Tempranillos feel polished and supple; others are more structured and drying. Tempranillo in Spain Spain is central to Tempranillo’s identity. Rioja and Ribera del Duero are two important Spanish contexts for the variety, but Tempranillo is not the same thing as Rioja. Rioja is a wine region; Tempranillo is a grape. You may also encounter regional names such as Tinta del País , Tinto Fino and Tinta de Toro . Spanish official material also records names including Cencibel and Ull de Llebre . These names are associated with Tempranillo in particular regional or technical contexts. They should not automatically be treated as completely different grapes, nor as guarantees of one particular flavour profile. The name Tempranillo is commonly linked to the Spanish word temprano , meaning “early”, referring to the variety’s tendency to ripen relatively early. That does not mean every Tempranillo ripens early in every vineyard: climate, site and growing conditions still matter. Why Tempranillo wines vary The grape provides a starting point, but the finished wine is shaped by several decisions and conditions: Climate and site: warmer conditions can encourage riper fruit and greater body, while cooler conditions or earlier harvesting may preserve freshness and red-fruit character. Ripeness and harvest timing: riper grapes may produce darker fruit and more weight; earlier-picked grapes may feel brighter and more energetic. Extraction: more contact with grape skins can increase colour and tannin. Gentler extraction may produce a softer, lighter-feeling wine. Oak: oak can add vanilla, toast, spice or cedar, as well as influence texture. Oak is a winemaking choice, not an unavoidable flavour of Tempranillo. Blending: Tempranillo may be bottled as a varietal wine or blended with other grapes. Blending can alter the wine’s colour, body, freshness, tannin and spice. Ageing: time can soften tannin and allow savoury, earthy, leather-like or dried-fruit notes to emerge. Not every Tempranillo is intended for long ageing. This is why two wines made from the same grape can feel quite different in the glass. Tempranillo in Australia Tempranillo is grown and made in Australia, although it remains a relatively small variety in the national wine sector. Wine Australia’s 2025 variety snapshot records 5,263 tonnes crushed in 2025 . It also records 7 hectares planted , but that planting figure is based on 2015 ABS data , so it should not be read as a 2025 or 2026 planting total. The snapshot lists the Riverland, Riverina, Murray–Darling–Swan Hill Victoria, Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale among the leading production contexts for Tempranillo. These figures describe production, not quality rankings. Australian Tempranillo is not one fixed national style. Wine Australia describes warm-region examples as potentially powerful, dark-fruited and spice-driven while retaining balancing acidity. It also identifies cooler Adelaide Hills examples as potentially fresher and more elegant. In practical terms, an Australian bottle may be bright and medium-bodied, or dark, full and structured, depending on its site and how it was made. What should you eat with Tempranillo? Tempranillo’s acidity, tannin and savoury possibilities can work well with substantial, savoury food. Try it with grilled or roasted meats, roast vegetables, tomato-based pasta, mushrooms, savoury rice or bean dishes, and firm or mature cheeses. These are starting points rather than rules. A lighter, fresher Tempranillo may suit different food from a fuller, oak-matured example. For serving, try Tempranillo slightly cool or at a cool room temperature. The best approach depends on the wine’s body and structure. You do not need to know its region or ageing history before enjoying it: taste the wine, notice whether it feels fresh, firm, soft or rich, and serve it in a way that makes those qualities enjoyable. Is Tempranillo worth trying? If you enjoy dry red wine with fruit, freshness and some structure, Tempranillo is a useful variety to explore. Look beyond the grape name and consider the style suggested by the label or wine description: fresh and elegant, or fuller and oak-influenced. The most important thing to remember is that Tempranillo is a grape, not a flavour checklist. Spain provides its best-known identity, while Australian producers interpret it through a different range of regions and conditions. Frequently asked questions Is Tempranillo a red or white wine? Tempranillo is a red-wine grape variety and is most commonly used to make dry red wine. Is Tempranillo similar to Shiraz? Both can make full-flavoured red wines, but they are different grape varieties. Tempranillo’s acidity, tannin, fruit profile and oak treatment vary from wine to wine, so a direct comparison should not be assumed. Does Tempranillo need to be aged? No. Some structured wines may develop complexity with age, but many Tempranillos are made to be enjoyed young. Ageing potential depends on the individual wine. Can Tempranillo be blended? Yes. It can be made as a varietal wine or used in a blend. Blending may change the wine’s body, colour, acidity, tannin and flavour. Where does Tempranillo grow in Australia? Wine Australia’s 2025 snapshot identifies production contexts including the Riverland, Riverina, Murray–Darling–Swan Hill Victoria, Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale. Other Australian regions are also exploring the variety. Related learning Explore Australian grape varieties What is wine? How wine is made Australian wine regions What is Shiraz? What is Cabernet Sauvignon?

title: What Is Terroir? How Place Influences Wine
description: Terroir describes how place, climate, site, soil, vine and people interact to shape wine. Learn what the term usefully means.
text: Route: /what-is-terroir/ Audience: Australian wine drinkers and beginners Highlights Terroir describes how a place—and the people working there—can influence a wine’s character. It includes climate, weather, soil, geology, slope, elevation, water availability, biology and vineyard decisions. Terroir is not simply soil , and wine does not literally taste like the rocks beneath a vineyard. The same grape variety can produce different wines in different places. Vintage, farming and winemaking can make the expression of a site clearer, quieter or quite different. A Geographical Indication identifies where a wine comes from; it does not guarantee one fixed flavour profile. Terroir is a useful way to understand wine, but it is not a mystical guarantee of quality or authenticity. Quick answer: what does terroir mean? In wine, terroir means the combined influence of a particular place and the people working there on the character of a wine . The place may include its climate, seasonal weather, soil, underlying geology, slope, elevation, aspect, drainage, water availability and local biological conditions. The people part includes choices such as grape variety, rootstock, vine spacing, canopy management, irrigation, harvest timing, fermentation and maturation. These influences interact. Climate affects how quickly grapes ripen. Soil and geology can affect drainage and how much water vines can access. Elevation and aspect can change temperature, sunlight and exposure. Farming and winemaking then influence how those grapes become wine. Terroir does not mean that every wine from one region tastes the same. Nor does it mean you can taste soil or minerals directly in a glass. It is better understood as a framework for asking how place and practice help shape a wine. What does terroir include? Climate and weather Climate is the longer-term pattern of conditions such as temperature, rainfall, sunlight and wind. Weather is what happens in a particular season or year. Both matter. Temperature and sunlight influence ripening. Rainfall affects water supply and disease pressure. Heat, frost, wind and unusual rain can alter the growing season and harvest timing. These conditions may influence acidity, sugar accumulation, flavour development, tannins and the eventual structure of a wine. A vineyard’s recurring climate can contribute to a recognisable sense of place, but each vintage is different. A particularly cool, hot, wet or dry year may make a site seem different from one year to the next. Soil and geology Soil is the material in which vines grow. Geology refers more broadly to the underlying rock, landforms and geological history of a place. Soil and geology can influence drainage, water storage, fertility, rooting depth and vine vigour. Those effects may then influence grape development. The pathway is indirect: soil affects the vine’s growing conditions, the vine develops grapes, and those grapes are transformed through winemaking. That is why “terroir means soil” is too narrow. It is also why claims that wine literally tastes like the minerals or rocks beneath a vineyard are misleading. Soil is one part of a larger system. A future guide to what soil does in wine can explore those mechanisms in more detail. Topography Topography is the shape of the land. It includes slope, elevation, aspect—the direction a slope faces—and exposure to wind and sun. A vineyard at higher elevation may experience different temperatures from one nearby at lower elevation. A slope may drain cold air more effectively than a flat site. Aspect can affect sunlight, while hills and surrounding landforms can influence wind and frost exposure. This is one reason a broad wine region can contain many smaller growing environments. A regional name is not the same thing as one uniform vineyard. Water availability Water availability reflects rainfall, groundwater, drainage, soil water-holding capacity and irrigation. In some Australian regions, irrigation is an important part of growing grapes because rainfall is limited or variable. Irrigation is a human management decision, but it responds to the conditions of the site. Its effect depends on factors such as timing, amount, soil, rootstock, vine age and climate. This makes irrigation a useful reminder that terroir is not a simple battle between “natural” conditions and human intervention. Place and management work together. Biology and local ecology The living environment around a vineyard may also be relevant. Soil organisms, vineyard plants, insects, vines and microorganisms can interact with the physical environment. However, biological influences are difficult to isolate. Microbial populations can vary between regions, vintages, vineyards and wineries, and cellar conditions and fermentation choices also matter. It is safer to say that biology may contribute to terroir than to claim that a vineyard’s microorganisms create a guaranteed flavour. How can place influence the taste and structure of wine? Place does not pour a flavour directly into the bottle. Instead, it helps shape the conditions in which vines grow and grapes ripen. For example, a site’s climate and water supply can influence the timing of ripening. That can affect the balance between acidity, sugar, flavour development and tannin development. Soil, drainage and root access to water can influence vine growth. Slope and aspect can alter temperature and sunlight. Disease pressure and wind can affect vineyard decisions and harvest timing. The finished wine is the result of all these influences passing through the vine and then through the winery. That is why terroir is best described with words such as influence , contribute and help explain , rather than determine . Why can the same grape taste different in different places? A grape variety provides genetic potential, but it does not grow in a vacuum. Pinot Noir, Chardonnay or Shiraz may ripen differently depending on the climate, water supply, soil, elevation and exposure of the vineyard. The grower may also choose different rootstocks, canopy practices or harvest dates. The winemaker may use different fermentation, extraction, oak or blending decisions. To compare the influence of place fairly, try comparing wines made from the same variety and a similar vintage, with broadly similar winemaking. If one wine is heavily oaked and another is unoaked, or if one is harvested much later, the differences may have more to do with technique or ripeness than site. The role of people in terroir Definitions of terroir vary. Some traditional uses focus mainly on natural site conditions. In broader modern wine discussions, terroir often includes the interaction between place and human practice. Important decisions can include: which variety, clone and rootstock to plant; vine spacing and row orientation; canopy and disease management; crop levels and irrigation; harvest timing; fermentation and skin contact; maturation vessels; blending. These choices can reveal, modify or conceal site differences. Wine Australia’s research into Barossa terroir, for example, examined climate, soil, vines, grape chemistry, sensory results and management. It found that water and nitrogen applications could modify grape composition. That does not make place irrelevant; it shows that a regional pattern is shaped by how a vineyard is farmed. Winemaking is related to terroir but is not identical to it. Fermentation, oak, extraction and blending can add their own strong signatures. A wine may communicate something about its site, while also communicating a winemaker’s choices or a producer’s house style. Australian examples: one region is not one flavour Australian wine regions show why terroir should not be reduced to a regional stereotype. Wine Australia’s research into Barossa Shiraz examined regional, subregional and vineyard-management effects. Some subregional patterns could be identified, while management practices also influenced grape chemistry. The lesson is not that Barossa Valley and Eden Valley wines each have one guaranteed taste. It is that regional and subregional patterns can exist alongside variation between sites, seasons and farming approaches. The Peel region in Western Australia provides another useful example. Its broad area includes coastal, inland and higher-elevation environments, with differences in rainfall, temperature, breezes, groundwater and geology. Coastal areas include limestone sands and fluvial sediments, while inland and elevated areas include older granite and gravel soils. A single regional name therefore covers a range of growing conditions. Macedon Ranges illustrates how elevation, cool conditions, frost risk, slope exposure, wind protection and soil can combine to influence where particular varieties grow successfully. The region is described as Australia’s coolest mainland wine region, but even there, one vineyard site is not interchangeable with every other. These examples demonstrate variation; they do not create fixed tasting rules. A GI can identify geographic origin without guaranteeing a uniform sensory profile. Terroir, variety, vintage, winemaking and GI: what is the difference? Term What it means Terroir The interacting influence of place and practice on wine character Grape variety The genetic type of grape, such as Chardonnay or Shiraz Vintage The growing and harvest year Winemaking The cellar decisions that turn grapes into wine Geographical Indication A recognised geographic origin used for Australian wine labelling Tasting note Language describing perceived aromas, flavours, texture or structure A GI tells you where the wine comes from within an approved geographic framework. It does not promise that every wine from that area tastes the same, nor does it prove that a particular bottle expresses terroir more authentically than another. Why is terroir difficult to prove or isolate? Researchers can compare vineyards, climates, soils, grape chemistry and sensory results. They may find recurring relationships between place and wine characteristics. But terroir is not one ingredient that can be separated neatly in a laboratory. Climate, vintage, soil, vine material, farming, disease pressure, harvest timing, fermentation, maturation and blending overlap. Management can change the result, and the same site can produce different wines under different conditions. That does not make terroir meaningless. It means the term works best as a nuanced explanation of interacting influences, not as a single score or fingerprint. How to think about terroir when tasting wine When you encounter the word on a tasting note or hear it at a cellar door, ask: What place is being discussed? A country, GI, region, subregion or vineyard? Which factors might matter there? Climate, elevation, aspect, soil, water or exposure? What else shaped the wine? Variety, vintage, harvest timing, fermentation, oak or blending? Is the claim cautious? “Can contribute to” is more credible than “guarantees”. Can I compare similar wines? Same variety and similar vintage make place easier to consider. You do not need to identify terroir perfectly to enjoy it. Think of it as a question: What did this place make easier or harder for the vine and winemaker to do? Frequently asked questions Is terroir just soil? No. Soil is one component. Terroir can also include climate, weather, geology, topography, water availability, biology and human decisions. Can you taste the soil in wine? Not literally. Soil can affect drainage, water access, fertility and vine growth, which may contribute indirectly to grape and wine characteristics. The wine is not a direct flavour sample of the soil. Does terroir determine wine quality? No. Terroir may influence style and regional character, but quality also depends on grape condition, farming, winemaking, storage and the drinker’s preferences. Does a wine region guarantee a particular taste? No. A GI identifies origin, but regions contain different sites,

title: What Is Volatile Acidity in Wine?
description: Learn what volatile acidity means in wine, how acetic acid and ethyl acetate smell, when VA is acceptable or faulty, and how it differs from ordinary wine acidity.
text: Highlights Volatile acidity, often shortened to VA , refers to volatile acids in wine, mainly acetic acid. Acetic acid can smell like vinegar and taste sharp or sour. A related compound, ethyl acetate, can add nail-polish-remover, glue or solvent-like aromas. VA is different from the normal acidity that gives wine freshness and structure. Small amounts of VA are normal and may add lift or complexity. Excessive or persistent VA can overwhelm fruit and make a wine taste unbalanced. A vinegar or solvent smell is a clue, not proof of a particular fault or compound. Quick answer: is volatile acidity always a fault? No. Volatile acidity is not automatically a fault. In wine science, volatile acidity is an analytical measure of volatile, steam-distillable acids. It is dominated by acetic acid , the compound associated with vinegar-like aroma and sharpness. A related compound called ethyl acetate can add aromas similar to nail-polish remover, acetone, glue or solvent. Small amounts of these compounds can occur naturally during fermentation. They may be barely noticeable, or may contribute a little aromatic lift in some wines. But when volatile acidity becomes strong, persistent or out of balance, it can suppress the wine’s fruit and make it smell vinegary, taste harsh or seem solvent-like. At that point, it is generally considered a wine fault. The important question is not simply whether VA is present. It is how much there is, how noticeable it is, and whether it suits the wine’s style . What does volatile acidity smell and taste like? The most familiar description is vinegar . A wine with noticeable acetic acid may smell sharp, vinegary or pickled, and can taste sour or prickly on the palate. If ethyl acetate is also present, the aroma may lean towards: nail-polish remover; acetone; glue; solvent; a pungent, lifted smell that masks the fruit. These descriptions are useful tasting clues, but they are not a laboratory test. Similar aromas can have different causes, and tasters vary in their sensitivity. A single sniff cannot tell you the wine’s exact chemical composition, concentration or microbial cause. A practical approach is to pour a small amount into a clean glass, smell it before and after swirling, and notice whether the character remains intrusive. This can help you describe your experience, but only analysis can establish the actual VA concentration. Acetic acid and ethyl acetate are not the same thing These two terms are often grouped together in discussions of volatile acidity, but they are chemically different. Acetic acid is the main contributor to measured VA. It is associated mainly with vinegar-like aroma and sharp, sour flavour. Ethyl acetate is an ester, not an acid. It can strongly influence how VA is perceived, particularly by adding nail-polish-remover or solvent-like character. That distinction matters because saying “VA is vinegar” is an oversimplification. VA is a broader analytical category, while acetic acid is its main component and ethyl acetate is a separate compound that can intensify the sensory impression. How is VA different from normal wine acidity? Normal wine acidity is often what makes a wine taste fresh, crisp and lively. It contributes sourness, balance and shape to the palate. These acids are commonly described as fixed or non-volatile acidity . Volatile acidity refers mainly to a different group of volatile acids and is often noticed through aroma as well as taste. A simple comparison is: Normal fixed acidity Volatile acidity Helps give wine freshness and structure Refers to volatile acids, mainly acetic acid Usually noticed as crispness or sourness on the palate Often noticed as vinegar-like aroma or sharpness Is not automatically a fault Small amounts may be normal; excessive amounts may be faulty Not every sharp-tasting wine has excessive VA. High ordinary acidity, tannin, carbon dioxide or the wine’s style can also create a brisk or edgy impression. For more on how wine is made and how fermentation shapes wine, see how wine is made and winemaking . Why does volatile acidity develop? Small amounts of acetic acid can be produced by yeast during alcoholic fermentation. Other yeasts and bacteria may also contribute under particular conditions. One important cause of elevated acetic acid is acetic-acid bacteria . These bacteria use oxygen and can convert alcohol into acetic acid. This means VA can become a risk when wine, juice or grapes are exposed to air while spoilage organisms are present. Conditions that may contribute include: damaged or diseased fruit; fermentation stress; oxygen exposure; poorly sealed tanks, barrels or containers; excessive ullage, meaning too much air space; warm or poorly protected storage; microbial growth during fermentation, maturation or storage. Oxygen is important, but oxygen exposure alone does not mean a wine will develop high VA. Microorganisms, the condition of the fruit and the wine’s handling all matter. Brettanomyces and lactic-acid bacteria can also be involved in some circumstances, but VA is not the same thing as Brettanomyces. Brettanomyces is more commonly associated with earthy, leathery, medicinal or smoky characters, although it may contribute acetic acid in certain conditions. When is VA acceptable, and when is it a fault? Wine is not chemically blank. A sound wine normally contains small amounts of volatile compounds, including acetic acid. Whether a small amount is acceptable depends on the wine and the person drinking it. A little volatility may be tolerated when it is integrated with the wine’s fruit, texture and balance. In some wines, it may be experienced as lift or complexity. That does not mean VA is generally desirable, or that more is better. VA is more likely to be considered a fault when it: dominates the aroma; clearly smells of vinegar or solvent; makes the palate harsh or sour; masks the wine’s fruit; persists after the wine has been poured and reassessed; feels inconsistent with the wine’s intended style. A delicate, fruit-driven wine may show an intrusive fault at a level that another taster finds interesting in a more robust or unusual style. Sensory thresholds vary with the wine, its sweetness, alcohol, aroma intensity and the individual taster. What is the Australian legal limit? Wine Australia identifies a legal maximum of 1.5 grams per litre of volatile acidity , excluding sulphur dioxide and expressed as acetic acid, for Australian wine. This figure is a regulatory ceiling , not a universal sensory threshold. A wine below that figure is not automatically guaranteed to taste sound, and a drinker cannot determine compliance simply by smelling or tasting a glass. Legal standards, analytical measurements and personal taste are related but not identical questions. Australian wine drinkers may encounter the term VA in wine-show judging, cellar-door conversations, hospitality training, winemaking courses and tasting notes. It is useful language for describing a wine’s character, but it should not be treated as a diagnosis from one aroma. How is VA different from other wine faults? Several wine faults can produce strong or unusual aromas, but they are not interchangeable. Oxidation may produce bruised-apple, nutty, stale or browned characters. It can occur alongside VA, but it is a separate process. Reduction is associated with sulphur compounds and may smell like struck match, rubber, rotten egg or cabbage. Cork taint is commonly associated with musty, damp-cardboard or mouldy aromas. Brettanomyces may produce leathery, farmyard, medicinal or smoky characters. It is not another name for VA. Sulphur dioxide can smell sharp or match-like in some conditions, but it is not volatile acidity. Wine faults can overlap, and sensory descriptors are not proof of one particular compound. The most useful response is to describe what you notice without claiming more certainty than the glass allows. Frequently asked questions Is volatile acidity the same as vinegar? Not exactly. Acetic acid, the main component of VA, is associated with vinegar. But VA is a broader analytical measure, and ethyl acetate may add solvent-like aromas. Can decanting fix volatile acidity? Do not rely on decanting to remove established VA. Opening a wine may change how its aromas are perceived, but aeration does not reliably remove acetic acid or ethyl acetate and may expose the wine to more oxygen. Does volatile acidity mean a wine is unsafe? The useful wine question is usually about quality and balance, not diagnosis from aroma. A vinegar or solvent smell may indicate a sensory problem, but it does not establish the wine’s safety, legality or exact cause. How should I describe a wine that seems high in VA? You might say that it smells vinegary, sharp or solvent-like, and that the aroma dominates the fruit. That is more accurate than claiming to know the exact concentration or microorganism responsible.

title: What Is Wine Aroma?
description: Learn what wine aroma means, how smell contributes to flavour, where aromas come from and how to identify them with a simple tasting method.
text: Highlights Wine aroma is the smell you perceive from wine, both in the glass and while drinking it. Smell contributes greatly to what we commonly call flavour. Taste is only one part of the experience. Wine aromas can be broadly associated with the grape, fermentation, maturation or ageing. Descriptions such as “peach”, “pepper” or “vanilla” are comparisons to familiar smells—not usually ingredients added to the wine. You do not need to identify precise aromas straight away. Start broad, then become more specific. Aroma intensity and aroma quality are different things: a stronger-smelling wine is not automatically better. Your description does not have to match somebody else’s. Memory, experience, health and surroundings all influence perception. Quick answer: what is wine aroma? Wine aroma is the smell perceived from wine. You notice it when you smell wine in the glass, and also when you drink it. During drinking, volatile aroma compounds can travel from the mouth towards the nose, contributing to the experience people usually call flavour. This is why a wine can smell one way in the glass and seem different once you taste it. A simple way to explore aroma is to smell the wine before swirling, notice a broad impression, swirl it gently, then smell again. You might begin with “fruity” or “spicy” before recognising something more specific, such as citrus, red berries or black pepper. There is no need to find the exact descriptor used by a critic or winemaker. Aroma, taste and flavour are not the same These words are often used interchangeably, but they describe different parts of tasting: Aroma or smell is what your olfactory system perceives through your nose. Taste refers to sensations such as sweetness, acidity, bitterness and saltiness. Flavour is the combined impression of taste, aroma and mouth sensations such as texture, warmth and astringency. When you smell wine directly from the glass, this is sometimes called orthonasal perception . When aromas travel from your mouth towards your nose while drinking, it is called retronasal perception . You do not need to memorise these terms to enjoy wine. They simply explain why smelling matters, and why the wine’s impression can change between the nose and the palate. For the broader tasting sequence, see how to taste wine . Where do wine aromas come from? Wine aroma is created by many compounds and processes. For beginners, three broad groups are useful. They overlap, so they should not be treated as rigid compartments. Primary or grape-related aromas Primary aromas are broadly associated with the grape and the character of the fruit. They may remind you of: citrus, apple or pear; peach or apricot; red or black fruit; flowers; fresh herbs or leafy notes; capsicum; spice. These are examples, not rules. A grape variety can show different aromas depending on climate, ripeness, region, vintage, winemaking and bottle age. An Australian wine label may provide useful context, but a grape variety or region does not guarantee one fixed aroma profile. You can explore individual styles in WineDaddy’s guides to Shiraz , Pinot Noir and Chardonnay , without expecting every bottle of those varieties to smell the same. Fermentation-derived aromas Fermentation and related post-fermentation processes can contribute aromas such as fresh ferment, estery fruit, bread, dough, brioche, butter, cream or savoury lees-like notes. This does not mean every wine will show these characters. The result depends on the wine and how it was made. For a broader introduction to the production process, see how wine is made . Maturation or ageing-derived aromas Maturation in oak, other vessels or the bottle can contribute or develop aromas such as vanilla, toast, cedar, spice, dried fruit, nuts, leather, earth and savoury notes. These categories can overlap. For example, a spicy impression may be connected to the grape, fermentation, oak or ageing—or to more than one of them. An aroma descriptor alone cannot prove a wine’s grape variety, region or production method. Aroma descriptors are comparisons When a tasting note says a wine smells like peach, blackberry, rose, pepper, vanilla or toast, it is using a familiar smell as a reference point. It does not usually mean that peach, blackberry, rose or pepper was added to the wine. It means the wine reminds the taster of that smell. Different people may choose different comparisons for the same wine. One person might notice red berries; another might think of cherries or a particular berry dessert. Neither person necessarily has the “wrong” answer. If you are new to wine, begin with broad families: fruity; floral; herbal; spicy; savoury; earthy; oaky; neutral or restrained. Only move to a precise descriptor when it feels genuinely recognisable. How to identify wine aroma at home You can practise with an ordinary clean wine glass. You do not need special equipment or a professional vocabulary. 1. Create a reasonably neutral setting Strong perfume, smoke, food, cleaning products and even freshly brewed coffee can compete with the wine’s aroma. If you have a cold or blocked nose, your perception may also be reduced. 2. Smell before swirling Hold the glass securely and take a gentle sniff. Notice the broad impression first. Is it fresh, fruity, floral, herbal, spicy, savoury, earthy or restrained? Do not force yourself to identify a particular fruit immediately. 3. Swirl gently A careful swirl increases contact between the wine and air and may make some aromas easier to notice. If swirling feels awkward, keep the glass on a stable surface and move it gently. Vigorous swirling is unnecessary, and swirling does not automatically improve every wine. 4. Smell again Ask what has changed. The wine may seem more expressive, or you may notice a new layer. Move from broad to specific: “fruit” might become “citrus”, “red fruit” or “dark fruit”; “spice” might become “pepper” or “baking spice”. 5. Taste and notice the retronasal aroma Take a small sip and notice whether the wine seems similar or different in your mouth. Some aromas may become clearer as the wine warms slightly, moves around the mouth or is swallowed. 6. Separate description from judgement First describe what the wine reminds you of. Then consider whether you find it pleasant, unusual, restrained or intense. Aroma intensity means how strongly you perceive the smell. It is separate from aroma character, which describes what the smell resembles. A highly intense aroma is not automatically a sign of quality, and a delicate aroma is not automatically a weakness. At an organised tasting, spitting is normal, and you do not need to finish every pour. Tasting is about observing the wine, not consuming a particular amount. Why can two people smell the same wine differently? Aroma perception varies between people. Our sensitivity, physiology, memories and previous experiences all influence how we interpret smells. Your perception can also be affected by: the wine’s temperature; glass shape and cleanliness; the amount of wine in the glass; time exposed to air; the bottle’s condition; surrounding odours; recent food, coffee, smoking or toothbrushing; congestion or illness; expectations created by the label, price or region; familiarity with particular smells. This is why aroma descriptions are useful observations rather than universal verdicts. Practice can make you more familiar with common references, but you do not need to smell exactly what someone else smells to taste wine successfully. Is an unusual aroma a fault? Not necessarily. An aroma can be distinctive without being faulty, and an intense or familiar aroma does not automatically prove that a wine is well made. Earthy, savoury, oaky or nutty notes may be part of a wine’s style, depending on the context. Other smells may suggest a wine fault, but identifying a fault requires more than noticing that an aroma seems unusual. Detailed discussions of cork taint, oxidation and other faults belong on their own pages. The useful beginner rule is simple: describe the aroma first, then consider its context. Do not turn one smell into an instant quality score. Frequently asked questions Does wine aroma mean the same thing as wine flavour?
