No. Aroma is perceived through smell, while flavour combines aroma with taste and mouth sensations. Aroma contributes substantially to flavour, but it is not the whole experience. Do wine aromas come from added fruit or spices? Usually not. Words such as “lemon”, “berry”, “vanilla” and “pepper” are familiar comparisons used to describe what the wine reminds someone of. Do I need to identify exact aromas to understand wine? No. Start with broad impressions such as fruity, floral, herbal or spicy. Specific vocabulary becomes easier with practice, but enjoyment does not depend on naming every aroma. Does a stronger aroma mean a better wine? No. Aroma intensity is a description of strength, not an automatic quality judgement. A wine can be delicate, expressive, complex or simple in different combinations. Why does wine smell different after swirling? Gentle swirling increases the wine’s contact with air, which may make some aromas easier to perceive. The effect varies between wines, and swirling is not compulsory. Keep exploring Wine aroma is one part of the wider tasting process. Once you are comfortable noticing smell, you can explore other aspects such as body, acidity, tannin, sweetness, finish, balance and complexity. Each describes a different part of the wine’s overall experience.

title: What Is Wine Body?
description: Wine body describes how heavy, full or textured wine feels in your mouth. Learn to recognise light-, medium- and full-bodied wine and avoid common misconceptions.
text: Highlights Wine body is the perceived weight, fullness and texture of wine in your mouth. A light-bodied wine feels relatively delicate; a full-bodied wine feels broader and more substantial. Light, medium and full are useful descriptions, not rigid categories or quality grades. Body is not the same as alcohol, sweetness, acidity, tannin, colour or flavour intensity. The easiest way to assess body is to notice how much presence and texture the wine has across your palate. Grape variety is a clue, not a guarantee: Australian Chardonnay, Shiraz and Pinot Noir can all be made in different styles. Quick Answer: What Does Wine Body Mean? When someone describes a wine as light-bodied , medium-bodied or full-bodied , they are describing how the wine feels in the mouth. A light-bodied wine tends to feel delicate, lean and less substantial. A medium-bodied wine sits between light and full, with moderate weight and fullness. A full-bodied wine generally feels broad, dense, enveloping or more substantial across the palate. “Weight” is a sensory comparison, not the physical weight of the wine. Body does not mean that a wine is thick like syrup, either. It is a combined impression created by the wine’s texture, fullness and presence. Body is one part of wine structure. Alcohol, residual sugar, acidity, tannin, flavour concentration and winemaking can all influence how body is perceived. None of them defines body on its own. The categories are best understood as points on a spectrum. A wine can sit between light and medium, or medium and full. Two people may also describe the same wine slightly differently. That is normal: body is a sensory impression rather than a single laboratory measurement. Light-, Medium- and Full-Bodied Wine Light-bodied wine A light-bodied wine may feel: delicate or slender; relatively lean; easy-moving across the palate; less dense or coating; refreshing rather than weighty. Light-bodied does not mean bland, weak or low quality. A light wine can have vivid aromas, strong flavour or lively acidity. Many Australian Pinot Noir, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc styles are often light- to medium-bodied, but the variety alone cannot predict the result. Medium-bodied wine A medium-bodied wine generally feels more substantial than a light-bodied wine without seeming especially heavy. It may offer a comfortable middle ground between freshness and weight. Many Australian Chardonnays can be medium-bodied, as can some Pinot Noir, Grenache and Shiraz styles. Medium-bodied is not a lesser category. It is simply a description of the wine’s palate presence. Full-bodied wine A full-bodied wine may feel: broad or weighty; dense or concentrated; enveloping; substantial in texture; persistent across the palate. Some Australian Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon styles can be full-bodied, while richer Chardonnay styles may also have considerable body. A full-bodied wine can be dry, sweet, tannic, acidic, smooth or warm. “Full-bodied” does not automatically mean sweet, hot or better. How to Recognise Body When Tasting You do not need specialist equipment to make a useful assessment. Try this: Pour the wine and take a small sip. Let it move naturally across your mouth. Ask whether it feels delicate, moderate or substantial. Notice the texture. Is it crisp, smooth, creamy, dense, firm or light? Pay attention to how much presence remains after swallowing or spitting. Compare it with another wine served at a similar temperature. It is easier to recognise body comparatively than absolutely. For example, you might write: “This Pinot Noir is medium-bodied: more substantial than the Riesling, but less dense than the Shiraz.” As you taste, keep separate notes for other sensations. Notice warmth as alcohol, sweetness as sweetness, freshness or tartness as acidity, and drying grip as possible tannin. Strong aromas or flavours should also be recorded separately from body. What Wine Body Is Not Body is not alcohol Alcohol can contribute warmth, volume and palate presence. It is often associated with fuller wines, but high alcohol does not automatically mean full body. A wine can taste hot or warming without feeling especially full. Conversely, a wine can feel full because of its texture, concentration, sugar or tannin without tasting strongly alcoholic. A useful distinction is: Alcohol: the warmth or heat you may feel. Body: the overall impression of weight, fullness and texture. Body is not sweetness Residual sugar can add roundness and fullness, but sweetness and body are different attributes. A dry Australian Shiraz can be full-bodied. A sweet wine can also feel relatively light in structure if it has low alcohol, high acidity or a delicate texture. Never assume that full-bodied means sweet. Body is not acidity Acidity usually brings freshness, tartness and a mouth-watering sensation. It can make a wine feel brisk or leaner, but it does not simply remove body. A wine can be both high in acidity and full-bodied. Some richer Chardonnays, sparkling wines and sweet wines combine noticeable freshness with substantial palate weight. Body is not tannin Tannin creates drying, firm or grippy sensations, especially in many red wines. It can add structure and make a wine seem more substantial, but tannin is not body itself. A wine may be full-bodied and tannic, or light- to medium-bodied with noticeable tannin. Cabernet Sauvignon can show this distinction clearly: tannin may provide grip while alcohol, flavour concentration and texture contribute to body. Body is not colour Dark colour does not automatically mean full body, and pale colour does not automatically mean light body. Colour is a visual clue affected by grape variety and winemaking. A pale Pinot Noir can have moderate body, while a dark wine can still feel lean if it has high acidity and limited alcohol or extract. A pale sweet wine may feel full because of its sugar and texture. Body is not flavour intensity A wine can have powerful aromas or flavours while feeling light-bodied. Aromatic Riesling is a useful example: it may smell intensely of citrus or flowers but still feel delicate in the mouth. The distinction is simple: Flavour intensity: how strongly the flavour or aroma registers. Body: how much weight, fullness and presence the wine has in your mouth. What Influences Perceived Body? Body comes from the interaction of several features rather than one ingredient. Alcohol can add warmth, volume and fullness, although heat should be considered separately. Residual sugar can add sweetness, roundness and a fuller texture. Acidity changes freshness and balance, affecting how weight is perceived. Tannin and other phenolic material can add grip and structure. Flavour concentration and extract may increase the impression of substance. Winemaking can influence texture and body through choices involving ripeness, extraction, fermentation, oak, lees contact, blending and residual sugar. Serving conditions can change perception. A warmer wine may show alcohol more strongly, while a chilled wine may seem fresher and less broad. Glycerol is sometimes described as the reason wine feels full, but its contribution at normal table-wine concentrations may be limited or context-dependent. It is safer to think of body as a whole-wine impression. Australian Wine Examples Australian wines vary with region, climate, vintage, ripeness, alcohol level and winemaking. These are tendencies, not rules: Pinot Noir: often light- to medium-bodied, particularly in cooler-climate styles, but can become more substantial. Riesling: often light- to medium-bodied, with acidity providing freshness. Sauvignon Blanc: commonly light- to medium-bodied, though ripeness and winemaking can add texture. Chardonnay: ranges from lean and light-bodied to rich and full-bodied. Shiraz: can range from medium-bodied cool-climate styles to full-bodied, ripe and concentrated warm-climate styles. Cabernet Sauvignon: often medium- to full-bodied, with tannin contributing structure. Pinot Gris or Pinot Grigio: can range from light and crisp to broader and more textural. The grape name is a useful starting point, not a promise about body. The wine in your glass is also shaped by where and when it was made, how ripe the grapes were and the winemaking choices used. A Simple Way to Use Body When Choosing Wine Body is most useful as a comparison tool. If a menu describes a wine as light-bodied, expect a relatively delicate palate presence. If it describes one as full-bodied, expect something broader and more substantial. That description does not tell you everything. Consider body alongside acidity, tannin, sweetness, flavour and finish. For the broader tasting process, see How to taste wine . You can also explore how winemaking affects a wine’s character in How wine is made , or compare body tendencies through Pinot Noir , Shiraz , Chardonnay , Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc . Wine Body FAQs Is full-bodied wine better than light-bodied wine? No. Body describes style, not quality. A light-bodied wine may be exactly what suits the occasion, food or drinker. Does high alcohol mean a wine is full-bodied? No. Alcohol can contribute to body, but it may also create warmth or heat. Body is the broader impression of weight, fullness and texture. Does dark wine have more body? Not necessarily. Colour and body are separate observations. Can white wine be full-bodied? Yes. Rich Chardonnay, some sweet wines and some sparkling wines can have substantial body. Is Pinot Noir always light-bodied? No. Pinot Noir is often light- to medium-bodied, but style varies with region, vintage, ripeness, alcohol and winemaking. How can I describe body if I am new to wine? Start with a comparison. Ask whether the wine feels lighter, similar to or fuller than another wine. “Light”, “medium” and “full” are enough; you do not need specialist vocabulary.

title: What Is Wine Finish?
description: Wine finish is what remains after you swallow or spit. Learn how to recognise short, medium and long finishes, describe their character and understand why longer is not always better.
text: Highlights Wine finish is what remains after you swallow or spit the wine out. It includes lingering flavour, aroma, acidity, sweetness, tannin and mouthfeel. A finish can be short, medium or long—but there are no universal time limits. Finish describes both how long sensations last and what those sensations are like. A long finish is not automatically better than a short one. A simple pause after swallowing or spitting can help you recognise a wine’s finish. Quick answer: what does “finish” mean in wine? Wine finish is the collection of flavours, aromas, tastes and mouthfeel sensations that remain after wine leaves your mouth. You might notice fresh citrus, red fruit, spice, savoury notes, oak, sweetness, tannin, bitterness or alcohol warmth. The finish describes both the character of those sensations and how long they persist. For example, a wine might have a short, clean finish if its flavours fade quickly but neatly. Another might have a long, spicy finish if recognisable spice and fruit remain well after the sip. When wine professionals talk about finish, they may also use the words length , persistence or aftertaste . These terms overlap in everyday wine writing. Finish is often the broader term because it can include flavour, aroma and mouthfeel—not just the last taste. How do you taste a wine’s finish? Finish is assessed after you swallow or spit the wine out. Try this: Take a small sip and hold it briefly across your palate. Swallow or spit. Pause before taking another sip. Notice what remains. Consider how quickly those sensations fade. Describe their character: fruity, fresh, spicy, savoury, sweet, drying, warm or bitter. Ask whether the persistence is pleasant, neutral or distracting. You do not need a stopwatch. The aim is to make a clear observation, not to produce a laboratory measurement. Ask yourself: What is the last recognisable flavour? Does freshness or acidity remain? Is there lingering fruit or spice? Does tannin leave a drying grip? Does the wine feel hot, bitter or overly sweet? Does the finish feel clear and tidy, or muddled? Taste again if you are unsure. A repeatable impression is more useful than trying to sound technical. Short, medium and long finish Tasting notes commonly describe finish as short , medium or long . Short: the recognisable sensations fade relatively quickly. Medium: the sensations remain for a noticeable but moderate period. Long: recognisable sensations continue for a relatively extended period. These are useful descriptive categories, not universal scientific scores. There is no agreed rule that a short finish lasts a particular number of seconds or that a long finish must exceed a fixed threshold. Different tasting systems and research methods may assess persistence differently. The category is only part of the description. A long finish dominated by harsh bitterness or excessive alcohol is not necessarily a positive feature. A shorter finish may be entirely appropriate for a light, fresh style. What can contribute to a wine’s finish? Finish is a whole-wine impression, so it rarely has one simple cause. Several parts of the wine may contribute: Acidity can leave freshness, tartness or a mouth-watering sensation. Tannin can leave drying, gripping or textural sensations, particularly in red wine. Sweetness can leave a rich or sweet impression. Alcohol can contribute warmth or heat. Flavour and aroma compounds can remain as fruit, floral, herbal or spicy impressions. Oak may contribute lingering toast, vanilla, cedar, coconut or spice-like notes. Concentration and texture may give the wine more sensory presence after the sip. These elements interact. High alcohol, abundant tannin, oak or concentration does not guarantee a long or enjoyable finish. The wine’s overall composition—and how it is perceived by the individual taster—matters. Finish is not the same as intensity or body These wine terms are related, but they answer different questions. Intensity asks: How strong is the sensation? Finish asks: What remains after the sip, and how long does it last? A wine can be powerful and aromatic but fade quickly. Another can seem restrained at first yet leave a persistent, precise impression. Body describes the wine’s perceived weight or fullness in your mouth. Finish describes what remains afterwards. A full-bodied wine does not automatically have a long finish, and a lighter-bodied wine can still be persistent. Finish is also different from balance and complexity . Balance describes how the wine’s components work together. Complexity describes the range and interaction of its sensory characteristics. A long finish may contribute to an impression of quality, but it is not the same thing as balance or complexity. Does a long finish mean better wine? Not necessarily. A long finish can be a positive feature when pleasant, clear and well integrated sensations continue after the sip. But persistence alone is not a complete measure of quality. Bitterness, excessive alcohol warmth, coarse drying tannin, intrusive oak or cloying sweetness can also linger. The useful question is not simply, “How long does it last?” It is also, “What is lingering, and do I enjoy it?” Likewise, a short finish does not automatically mean a wine is poor. Some wines are designed to be light, fresh and immediately drinkable. Quality depends on the whole experience, including balance, concentration, texture, freshness and suitability to the style. A long finish also does not reliably prove that a wine will improve with age, cost more or receive higher scores. How Australians may see finish described Australian tasting notes may use phrases such as: “good length”; “persistent”; “lingering”; “clean finish”; “long aftertaste”. You might find that an Australian Riesling leaves a fresh citrus or mineral-like impression, that a Chardonnay finishes with acidity, fruit, oak or texture, or that a Shiraz leaves fruit, spice, tannin or warmth. These are possible observations, not guarantees. No Australian variety or region has one fixed finish profile. The same wine may also seem different depending on its serving temperature, the food you have eaten, the glass, tasting order and your own sensitivity. Frequently asked questions Is finish only the last flavour in wine? No. Finish can include flavour, retronasal aroma, taste and mouthfeel. The last recognisable flavour is one part of the experience. Is finish the same as aftertaste? The terms overlap. “Aftertaste” usually refers to a taste or sensation that remains, while “finish” is often used more broadly for the whole post-swallow or post-spit experience. Can white wine have a long finish? Yes. White wine can leave persistent acidity, citrus, floral, mineral-like, oak, texture or other sensations. Finish is not limited to red wine. How can I describe a finish? Combine a duration with a character: “short and fresh”, “medium with savoury spice” or “long with fruit and fine tannin”. This is more useful than calling every persistent sensation “good length”. The simplest way to remember it Finish is what remains after the wine is swallowed or spat out. Judge both duration and character . A long finish can be rewarding, but the best finish is not necessarily the longest one—it is the one that remains pleasant, clear and suited to the wine. Related reading: What is wine? and What is Shiraz? .

title: What is wine?
description: Wine is fermented grape juice, but grapes, vineyard conditions, fermentation and winemaking choices create an enormous range of colours, flavours and styles.
text: Highlights Wine is a beverage made by fermenting grapes or grape juice, usually with yeast. Yeast converts grape sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Wine production is not one fixed recipe. Grape variety, ripeness, climate, site, skin contact and winemaking decisions influence the finished wine. Red, white, rosé, sparkling, sweet and fortified are characteristics or approaches that can overlap. Quick answer Wine is an alcoholic beverage made primarily from grapes or grape juice through alcoholic fermentation. Yeast consumes fermentable grape sugars and produces alcohol and carbon dioxide, along with other compounds that contribute to the wine’s character. The finished wine may then be matured, clarified, stabilised, blended, carbonated, fortified, bottled or packaged, depending on the style. Its colour, aroma, flavour and texture are influenced by the grape variety, ripeness, vineyard conditions, skin contact and decisions made during and after fermentation. On this page From grape to bottle Why wines differ Main types of wine Australian context Terms that need care FAQs From grape to bottle Wine production begins in the vineyard, but the journey from grape to bottle can vary considerably. There is no single sequence that every producer or style follows. A simplified journey Grow → harvest → sort → crush, destem or press as appropriate → manage skin contact → ferment → mature and treat as appropriate → bottle or package. Growing and harvesting grapes Grapes are an agricultural raw material, so the wine’s story begins with how they grow. Grape variety, weather, climate, vineyard site and ripeness all affect the fruit that arrives at the winery. Harvest timing is a decision rather than a universal rule. A producer may balance sugar, acidity, flavour development, colour, tannin and the intended wine style. Crushing, destemming and pressing Grapes can be crushed or destemmed, pressed as whole bunches, or left partly or wholly intact. Pressing separates juice from solid grape material. Crushing breaks the fruit and releases juice, while destemming removes some or all of the stems. These steps are not mandatory in every wine. Skin contact and maceration Grape skins contain colour compounds and other phenolic material. Maceration means keeping grape solids and liquid in contact so compounds can be extracted. The amount and timing of skin contact can change colour, flavour, texture and structure. Red wines are commonly fermented or macerated with their skins. Many white wines are pressed and fermented with relatively little skin contact. Rosé generally limits colour extraction from red-grape skins. Some white grapes are fermented on their skins, producing amber or orange-coloured wines. Visual coming later: the grape-to-bottle journey A learning diagram will show how production choices branch by wine style. Fermentation Fermentation turns grape juice into an alcoholic beverage. Yeast converts fermentable grape sugars into ethanol , the main alcohol in wine, and carbon dioxide. It also produces other compounds that contribute aroma and flavour. Some wines use selected yeast cultures, while others rely on spontaneous fermentation from yeast present in the grapes or winery environment. The beginner-level idea is simple: alcohol is generally created during fermentation rather than added to ordinary wine. Maturation and other treatments Fermentation is not necessarily the end of winemaking. Wine may be held in stainless steel, concrete, oak, glass-lined tanks or other vessels. It may spend time with lees , the solids that settle after fermentation, including yeast cells and other grape or fermentation material. Wine may also be clarified, filtered, stabilised or blended. Maturation does not automatically mean oak ageing. Oak is one possible vessel or influence, not a requirement. Carbonation, fortification and packaging Some wines contain dissolved carbon dioxide, giving them bubbles. Fortified wines have alcohol added during or after fermentation. Fortified wine is not automatically sweet: sweetness and fortification are separate characteristics. Finally, wine is bottled or otherwise packaged and may be stored before release. Why do wines look and taste different? Wine’s character usually comes from several influences working together rather than one factor acting alone. Grape variety, ripeness, climate and site Different varieties have different combinations of sugars, acids, colour compounds, tannins and aroma precursors. As grapes mature, these components change. Temperature, sunlight, rainfall, altitude, exposure and other site conditions also influence vine growth and grape development. The same variety can therefore produce different wines in different vineyards or under different winemaking approaches. Skin contact, fermentation and maturation Skin contact is one of the clearest reasons wines differ in colour and structure, but its effects depend on timing, temperature and duration. Fermentation conditions, vessel, oxygen exposure, time and post-fermentation treatments can all affect character. Oak and lees contact may influence flavour, texture and integration. Neither guarantees better wine. Blending Blending combines wines or components, including grape varieties, vineyard parcels or vessels. It is not evidence of poor quality, just as a single-variety wine is not automatically superior. It is one way to shape balance and style. Sweetness, acidity, tannin, body and alcohol Sweetness is mainly associated with residual sugar left after fermentation. Acidity contributes freshness and tension. Tannin can contribute grip or a drying sensation. Body is an overall impression of weight or fullness. Alcohol can contribute warmth, weight and balance. A wine can smell strongly of ripe fruit without being sweet. These structural elements interact in how the wine feels. Visual coming later: why wines differ A future explainer will map grape, place and winemaking influences to colour, aroma, flavour and texture. The main types of wine These categories are useful for orientation, but they are not one complete universal legal classification. Colour, sweetness, carbonation and fortification describe different dimensions, so categories can overlap. Type What it means Usual production distinction Red Commonly red, purple or ruby. Usually made with red grapes and skin fermentation or maceration. White Commonly pale yellow, straw, greenish or gold. Often pressed and fermented with limited skin contact. Rosé Pink or salmon-coloured. Usually limited colour extraction from red-grape skins. Sparkling Contains dissolved carbon dioxide that produces bubbles. Bubbles may arise from fermentation in bottle or tank, or another permitted process. Sweet Noticeable sweetness, generally associated with residual sugar. Sugar remains through the production approach used. Fortified Alcohol level has been increased by adding alcohol. Alcohol is added during or after fermentation. A wine can be white and sweet, red and sparkling, or fortified and sweet. “Sparkling” describes bubbles while “sweet” describes a characteristic mainly associated with residual sugar. “Dry” generally means low or barely perceptible residual sugar. It does not necessarily mean non-fruity, highly acidic or better quality. Visual coming later: wine style dimensions A comparison will show how colour, bubbles, sweetness and fortification overlap. A short Australian context Wine in Australia is both an agricultural product and a cultural beverage. Australian readers will also encounter practical information on wine labels. Under Food Standards Australia New Zealand requirements, beverages containing 0.5% alcohol by volume or more must include alcohol-content information; beverages over 0.5% must include a statement of standard drinks; and alcoholic beverages over 1.15% must generally carry the prescribed pregnancy-warning label, subject to the Food Standards Code and applicable exceptions. These are label requirements, not a complete explanation of Australian wine law. Regulatory details can change, so check current FSANZ guidance when using label information. Terms that need care Natural wine “Natural wine” does not have one universally accepted definition. It should not automatically be described as wine with nothing added, or as healthier, more authentic or better. Traditional “Traditional” may refer to a method, region, vessel or historical practice. It is not, by itself, a guarantee of quality or minimal intervention. Old World and New World These broad informal groupings can oversimplify the diversity of wine regions and producers. They are not necessary to understand the basic definition of wine. Amber or orange wine Amber or orange wine is generally made from white grapes using red-wine-style techniques, including fermentation with skins, seeds and sometimes stems. It is not simply white wine that has accidentally oxidised. FAQs Is wine just grape juice with alcohol added? Usually, no. Yeast converts fermentable grape sugars into alcohol during fermentation. Fortified styles can involve alcohol being added during or after fermentation. Does all wine contain grapes? Wine is primarily associated with grapes and grape juice, and the OIV’s technical framework defines it through fermentation of fresh grapes or grape must. Legal definitions may vary between jurisdictions. Why is red wine red? Red wine is commonly fermented or macerated with grape skins, extracting colour compounds and other phenolic material. Can white wine be made from red grapes? Yes. If the juice has little contact with the dark skins, it can remain pale. Is rosé made by mixing red and white wine? Methods vary. Rosé generally involves limiting colour extraction from red-grape skins, often through short skin contact or direct pressing. What makes a wine sparkling? Dissolved carbon dioxide creates the bubbles. It may come from fermentation in a bottle or tank, or another permitted process. Is sweet wine the same as fruity wine? No. Wine can smell or taste fruity without noticeable sweetness. Sweetness is mainly associated with residual sugar. Is fortified wine always sweet? No. Fortification and sweetness are separate characteristics. What does “dry” mean? It generally means low or barely perceptible residual sugar. It does not necessarily mean non-fruity or highly acidic. What is orange or amber wine? It is generally wine made from white grapes using red-wine-style skin fermentation, which can give deeper colour and a different texture. Sources International Organisation of Vine and Wine — International Code of Oenological Practices OIV — Alcoholic fermentation Australian Wine Research Institute — Skin contact AWRI — Amber wine AWRI — Lees contact FSANZ — Labelling of alcoholic beverages WineDaddy summarises authoritative material in plain English. Regulatory information should be checked against current guidance.

title: When Should Wine Be Decanted?
description: Learn when decanting can help wine, when it may do little, and how to decant young, old and sediment-bearing bottles safely.
text: title: "When Should Wine Be Decanted?" description: "Learn when decanting helps wine, when it is unnecessary, and how to decant around sediment without relying on rigid timing rules." canonical: " https://winedaddy.com.au/when-should-wine-be-decanted/ " article_type: "Educational Guide" When Should Wine Be Decanted? Highlights Decant wine for one of two reasons: to remove sediment or to give some wines more contact with air. Most everyday filtered wines can be served straight from the bottle. Young, powerful reds may become more expressive with air, but this is not guaranteed. Older wines can contain sediment, yet delicate older wines may fade if exposed to too much air. Sediment is generally harmless; it is a natural deposit that can be unpleasant in the glass. Taste the wine first when possible. A small pour can tell you whether decanting is worthwhile. You do not need a special decanter: a clean jug or larger wine glass can sometimes do the job. Quick answer Wine should be decanted when there is a clear purpose. The first purpose is sediment removal . Mature red wines, vintage Port and some minimally filtered or bottle-aged wines can develop a deposit. Carefully pouring the wine into another clean vessel leaves that sediment behind. The second purpose is aeration : increasing the wine’s contact with air. This may help a young, robust, tannic wine that tastes tight, austere or muted. But air does not automatically improve wine. A delicate older wine may lose aroma and flavour if it is exposed for too long. So, decant a mature wine when sediment is expected, try decanting a small amount of a young, powerful wine if it seems closed, and serve most fresh everyday wines directly. The best decision depends on the individual bottle, not simply its colour, grape variety or country of origin. Decanting has two different jobs Decanting means pouring wine from its original bottle into another clean vessel. That simple action can serve two quite different purposes. Removing sediment Sediment is natural material that can settle in a bottle over time. It is more likely in mature reds capable of bottle ageing, vintage Port and wines made with little or no filtration. Sediment is generally harmless. It does not mean the wine is faulty or spoiled. However, it can taste bitter, astringent or gritty, and many people would rather leave it in the bottle than find it in their glass. For sediment, decanting is a practical serving step rather than a way to change the wine’s character. The aim is to separate the clear wine from the deposit and serve it soon afterwards. Giving wine more contact with air Aeration is the process of increasing a wine’s contact with air. Pouring wine into a decanter exposes more of it to air than simply removing the closure, because more of the wine’s surface is exposed. Some young, full-bodied reds become more expressive after aeration. Their aromas may become easier to notice and their tannins may seem less closed-in. Other wines show little change, while some lose definition as they spend time in the decanter. That is why “let the wine breathe” is not a universal instruction. Treat aeration as an experiment: taste the wine, give it some air if it seems likely to benefit, and keep checking its progress. A simple decanting decision What is in your glass or bottle? What to do Why Mature red, vintage Port or wine with visible or expected sediment Decant carefully Separate the wine from its deposit Young, robust, tannic or full-bodied red that seems tight or austere Try a small amount first It may become more expressive with air Most fresh, filtered everyday wines Serve directly Decanting is usually unnecessary Delicate or fragile older wine Handle gently; decant briefly only if needed Excessive air may make it fade Rosé or most sparkling wine Usually serve directly Decanting is not normally needed These are useful starting points, not laws. A mature Australian Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon may contain sediment, while a young filtered red may not. Australian wine does not follow one decanting convention; the particular wine’s age, structure, filtration and condition matter more. For more background, see what wine is , red wine versus white wine , what Shiraz is and what fortified wine is . Which wines are most likely to benefit? Mature reds with sediment If a bottle has meaningful age, particularly a red designed to develop in bottle, sediment becomes more likely. Vintage Port is a clear example. Some mature Australian reds, including Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon, may also have a deposit, but age and winemaking choices—not the Australian label alone—are what matter. If sediment is the reason for decanting, do it shortly before serving. There is no benefit in leaving a sediment-bearing wine in a decanter for hours simply because it is old. Young, powerful reds Young reds with plenty of tannin, concentration or structure are the strongest candidates for an aeration trial. This can include some full-bodied Australian reds, but not every Shiraz or Cabernet needs decanting. Pour a small amount into a glass first. If the wine seems closed, severe or muted, swirl it and taste again after several minutes. If it becomes more open, you might decant the rest. If it is already expressive, serve it directly. Delicate older wines Older does not mean “needs more air”. A fragile wine can be beautiful but vulnerable to prolonged exposure. It may become less aromatic or lose its shape in the decanter. If an older wine has sediment, decant it gently and serve it soon. If it has no sediment, consider leaving it in the bottle and allowing it to develop gradually in the glass. How to decant wine Check the bottle. Consider its age, whether it was minimally filtered and whether sediment is visible. Stand it upright if sediment is expected. This gives the deposit time to settle towards the bottom. Handle an older bottle gently and avoid unnecessary movement. Open it carefully. Try not to shake or agitate the wine. Use a clean vessel. A decanter is convenient, but a clean, neutral-smelling jug or carafe can work for casual service. Residual detergent, dust or odours can affect the wine. Pour slowly and steadily. Hold the bottle near a phone torch or another small light so you can see sediment approaching the neck. Stop before the sediment enters the vessel. Leaving a little wine behind is preferable to pouring the deposit into the clean wine. Taste and monitor. For aeration, do not rely on a fixed timer. Check how the wine smells and tastes as it changes. A larger wine glass can also be enough for a wine that simply needs a little room to open. It gives you a chance to observe the wine without committing the entire bottle to a decanter. How long should wine be decanted? There is no single correct decanting time. For sediment removal, decant shortly before serving. For aeration, begin with a small pour and reassess after several minutes. A young, robust wine may tolerate more air, while a delicate older wine may decline quickly. Simply opening the bottle and leaving it untouched is not the same as decanting. Only a small amount of wine in the bottle neck is exposed to air. It can be a gentler approach for a delicate wine, but it is not a reliable substitute when the goal is to expose more wine quickly. If the wine is improving in the glass, let it develop there. You do not need to pour the entire bottle into a decanter. What about white, rosé, sparkling and fortified wine? Most white wines do not need decanting, although some older or complex whites may benefit from careful handling. White-wine crystals or deposits are not automatically a sign of a fault. Rosé is generally served directly. Sparkling wine is not normally decanted by beginners. Specialist practices exist, but decanting can affect the wine’s bubbles and presentation. Vintage Port is the main fortified-wine example where decanting may be important because of sediment. Not every Port or fortified wine needs to be decanted. You can learn more about the category in what fortified wine is . What decanting cannot fix Decanting is not a cure for a faulty wine. It does not reliably repair cork taint, oxidation, volatile acidity or a wine that is otherwise spoiled. Air may sometimes make certain reductive aromas less noticeable, but that is not the same as fixing the wine. If a bottle smells or tastes wrong, more oxygen may do nothing—or may accelerate its decline. Decanting should be used for a serving purpose, not as a general rescue technique. The simplest rule to remember Ask two questions: Could this wine contain sediment? If yes, decant carefully and stop before the deposit reaches the clean wine. Does this young wine seem closed or severe? If yes, try a small amount with air and watch how it develops. If the answer to both questions is no, serve the wine directly. Decanting is a useful option, not a ceremony every bottle has to pass through. Frequently asked questions Does every red wine need to be decanted? No. Most everyday red wines can be served directly. Decanting is most useful when a red has sediment or when a young, robust wine seems likely to benefit from air. Does decanting make wine taste better? Not always. Some wines become more expressive, while others lose aroma and flavour definition with too much air. Taste before and during decanting where possible. Is sediment a sign of bad wine? No. Sediment is usually a natural deposit, particularly in some mature or minimally filtered wines. It may be unpleasant to drink, but it does not automatically mean the wine is faulty. Can I decant wine without a decanter? Yes. A clean jug or carafe can be practical for sediment removal or aeration. For some wines, pouring into a larger glass and swirling is enough. Should old wine be decanted for longer? No. Older wine may contain sediment, but delicate older wines can fade with prolonged aeration. Decant gently and briefly when sediment removal is the main purpose.

title: Why Wine Prices Vary — And Whether Expensive Wine Is Better
description: Wine prices reflect grapes, farming, winemaking, packaging, freight, taxes, reputation and demand. Learn how to judge wine value without assuming expensive means better.
text: Highlights Wine prices reflect far more than the liquid in the bottle. Grapes, vineyard land, labour, yield, winemaking, packaging, freight, taxes and retail costs can all contribute. Scarcity, reputation and demand can raise a price even when they are not direct production costs. Two wines made from the same grape variety can have very different prices. A higher price may signal extra cost or desirability, but it does not guarantee better quality or greater enjoyment. Value depends on your taste, occasion and budget—not just the number on the shelf. Quick answer Wine costs more or less because its final price combines production costs with commercial decisions. Vineyard location, grape prices, farming, labour, yield, weather risk, winemaking, maturation, packaging, transport, taxes, distribution and retail margins may all play a part. A wine can also cost more because it is scarce, comes from a highly regarded place, has a strong reputation or is in demand. Those factors may reflect real desirability, but they are not the same as the cost of making the wine. So, does a higher price mean better wine? Not necessarily. Price can provide clues about production, scarcity or reputation, but it is an imperfect guide to quality—and an even less reliable guide to whether you will personally enjoy the wine. What goes into the price of a bottle? A useful way to think about wine pricing is as a chain: Vineyard and grapes → winemaking and maturation → packaging → freight and storage → taxes and commercial costs → retail price Not every wine involves these stages in exactly the same way, and their relative importance varies. Wine Australia’s export-pricing guidance, for example, treats grape costs, processing, oak, holding, wastage, packaging, freight, commissions, taxes, exchange rates and retail margin as separate pricing inputs. That does not provide a universal breakdown of a bottle’s shelf price. It does show why the price of wine cannot be explained by the grapes alone. Grapes, vineyards and farming Grape prices vary according to variety, region, vintage, supply, demand and fruit quality. A winery might buy grapes from another grower or use fruit from its own vineyards, but either way the vineyard represents costs. These can include: land and water; pruning and canopy management; machinery and fuel; labour; pest and disease control; irrigation; harvesting; winery transport; and the risks of frost, drought, heat, smoke or disease. Yield matters too. If a vineyard produces fewer grapes, the costs of managing the site may be spread across less fruit. That can increase the cost assigned to each bottle. But low yield is not a guarantee of quality. A statement such as “low-yield” describes one production factor; it does not automatically tell you whether the wine will suit your taste. Australian grape supply changes from year to year. Wine Australia’s 2026 National Vintage Report estimated a national crush of 1.27 million tonnes—19% below the 2025 vintage—and an estimated weighted average value of purchased grapes of $570 per tonne. These are dated industry estimates, not a standard cost per bottle or a quality score. Winemaking and time Winemaking choices can add costs through equipment, labour, storage and materials. Sorting fruit, using particular fermentation vessels, blending, testing, bottling and managing wastage all require resources. Maturation can also tie up space and money. A wine held in oak or stored for longer before release may involve: barrel or vessel costs; cellar space; labour and monitoring; insurance and inventory costs; and wine lost through evaporation or other handling. That may help explain a higher price, but expense is not the same as preference. Oak-aged wine is not automatically better than unoaked wine; it is simply made in a different way. The same applies to hand work, long ageing and other techniques. Their value depends on how successfully they contribute to the style—and whether you enjoy that style. For more context, see how wine is made . Bottles, labels and packaging The bottle itself is part of the product cost. So are the closure, capsule, label, carton, bottling and transport packaging. Bottle weight and design can vary, while labels may need to be produced for different markets. Packaging can be functional, protective, aesthetic or part of a brand’s presentation. It can therefore affect price without proving anything about the wine’s quality. A more elaborate bottle may make a wine feel special, but it is still worth asking whether the thing you value is the wine, the presentation, the occasion—or some combination of the three. Freight, distribution and where you buy Before a bottle reaches you, it may travel from vineyard to winery, then to a warehouse, distributor, retailer or restaurant. Storage, insurance, handling and delivery can all add commercial costs. Australia’s geography makes freight relevant, particularly when wine moves between regions and states or travels to export markets. But distance alone does not determine price. Shipment size, contracts, routes, storage arrangements and the sales channel matter too. The same wine may therefore have different prices at a cellar door, bottle shop, supermarket, online retailer or restaurant. Promotions, local competition, stock levels and the retailer’s business model can change the price at a particular moment. Australian taxes: WET and GST Australian wine prices generally reflect applicable taxes as well as production and supply-chain costs. Wine Equalisation Tax (WET) is a value-based tax on assessable wine dealings. The Australian Taxation Office currently states that WET is charged at 29% of the wholesale sale value , subject to rules, exemptions, rebates and credits. It is not simply 29% of every bottle’s shelf price. Goods and Services Tax (GST) is generally 10% on taxable supplies . GST and WET are separate taxes, and their interaction depends on the transaction. Different alcoholic products and commercial circumstances can also have different treatment. The practical point is simple: taxes affect the price you see, but tax is not the same thing as the producer’s cost or a retailer’s margin. Avoid trying to reverse-engineer a bottle’s price using a universal tax formula. Scale, scarcity and reputation Production scale can affect unit costs. A larger winery may spread equipment, administration, bottling and distribution costs over more bottles. A smaller producer may make fewer bottles and have less purchasing power, although it may also operate with different sourcing and production choices. Scarcity can raise a wine’s price when supply is limited relative to demand. That scarcity might come from a small vineyard, a difficult vintage, limited production, restricted distribution or an allocation system. Reputation can matter too. Buyers may be willing to pay more for a well-known producer, region, vineyard, variety or vintage because they expect a particular experience. This expectation can be commercially meaningful even when it is separate from the direct cost of making the wine. Reputation and scarcity can influence price without guaranteeing technical quality. A limited wine is not automatically better; it is simply less available. Why the same grape can have different prices Imagine two Australian Chardonnay wines. They may use the same grape variety but differ in: vineyard location and land costs; grape yield and fruit price; harvesting and sorting; fermentation vessels; oak use; time in storage; bottle and label; production scale; freight and sales channel; reputation and demand. One may be made in large volumes for broad distribution. Another may come from a small site, be made in limited quantities and spend longer in the winery. Both can be well made, but their costs, positioning and intended styles may be different. The grape name is therefore a starting point—not a complete explanation of the price. Does expensive wine mean better quality? A higher price is not a guarantee of better wine. Some research suggests price can act as a quality signal, particularly when buyers have limited information. Other research, including blind-tasting studies, finds weak, absent or non-linear relationships between price and enjoyment. Knowing that a wine is expensive can also shape expectations and influence how people assess it. That does not mean price is meaningless. A higher price may reflect more expensive fruit, longer maturation, scarcity, reputation or demand. It means price is only one clue, and a fairly imperfect one. It helps to separate five ideas: Cost: what it takes to produce and sell the wine. Price: what you are asked to pay. Reputation: what the market expects from the wine. Quality: how successfully the wine meets a relevant standard or intention. Value: how worthwhile it feels to you at that price. A $25 wine can be excellent value for a weeknight meal. A more expensive bottle might offer value to someone who prioritises rarity, a particular region or a special occasion. Neither judgement is universal. How to judge value when buying wine Try this approach: Choose a style first. Think about grape variety, colour, sweetness, body or occasion before looking for the highest price. Compare like with like. Similar wines are easier to compare than unrelated bottles with different vintages, sizes and origins. Use the label for context. Variety, region, vintage, producer and alcohol information can help set expectations. See how to read a wine label if that page is available. Consider the occasion. A wine for cooking, a casual meal, a gift and a celebration may have different value. Treat reviews as information. Look for clues about style and structure, but remember that your preferences may differ. Use price as one signal, not a verdict. It may reflect scarcity or reputation, but it cannot predict your enjoyment. Check the conditions of comparison. Vintage, promotions, retailer, location and stock can all change the price. Wine prices are moving targets. A price observed in one bottle shop, state or month may not be a fair comparison with another bottle, vintage or channel. The best value wine is not automatically the cheapest or most expensive. It is the wine that gives you the experience you want, at a price that feels worthwhile. Frequently asked questions Why is one wine more expensive than another if they use the same grape? The wines may differ in vineyard costs, yield, fruit quality, labour, winemaking, oak, maturation, packaging, scale, freight, reputation or demand. The grape variety alone does not determine the price. Does a heavier bottle mean better wine? No. A heavier or more elaborate bottle may cost more or reflect a presentation choice, but it does not guarantee higher quality. Are expensive wines always better? No. Higher prices can reflect real costs, scarcity or reputation, but price does not reliably predict every drinker’s quality judgement or enjoyment. Why can the same wine have different prices? Retailer pricing, promotions, location, restaurant mark-ups, stock levels, vintage and sales channel can all change what buyers are asked to pay. Is Australian wine taxed at 29%? WET is currently 29% of the wholesale sale value for assessable dealings, subject to relevant rules, exemptions, rebates and credits. That is not the same as saying 29% is added directly to every shelf price. GST is a separate tax generally charged at 10% on taxable supplies.

title: Wine and Cheese Pairing: How to Choose a Wine for Any Cheese Board
description: Learn how to pair wine and cheese by matching salt, creaminess, texture, intensity and maturity with wine acidity, sweetness, tannin and body. Includes practical pairings for fresh, soft, washed-rind, hard, aged and blue cheeses.
text: Highlights Pair wine and cheese by comparing their strongest features, not by following rigid rules. Salt, creaminess, texture, rind, age and flavour intensity all affect the match. Fresh cheeses usually suit fresh, lighter wines; creamy cheeses often enjoy acidity or bubbles. Sweet or fortified wines are excellent starting points for salty, intense blue cheese. Tannic reds can be powerful with delicate or salty cheeses, so choose them carefully. A dry wine can still taste fruity. Dryness describes sweetness, not the absence of fruit flavour. There is no single perfect wine for every cheese. The best pairing is the one that tastes balanced and enjoyable to you. Quick answer: how do you pair wine and cheese? Start by identifying the cheese’s main character. Is it fresh and tangy, creamy, pungent, firm, salty or intensely savoury? Then choose a wine that either matches that intensity or provides a useful contrast. Fresh, mild cheeses generally work with crisp whites such as Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc or Pinot Gris, as well as fresh sparkling wine. Creamy cheeses often benefit from acidity and bubbles, which create freshness between bites. Firm or aged cheeses can support wines with more flavour, structure or development, including Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon or fortified wine. Blue cheese is a classic opportunity to try a sweet wine. Sweet Riesling, a late-harvest style or fortified wine can balance the cheese’s salt and intensity. That does not make sweet wine the only correct choice: a fresh sparkling wine or dry Riesling may suit a milder blue cheese or a particular cheese-board accompaniment. The important point is that grape variety alone does not decide the pairing. A fresh Chardonnay and a rich, oaky Chardonnay can behave very differently. The same is true of Pinot Noir, Shiraz and Riesling. Look for the wine’s acidity, sweetness, tannin, body, alcohol and flavour intensity. Match the wine to the cheese style Fresh cheese Fresh cheeses are usually soft, moist and mild, with a lactic or tangy character. Think of ricotta, cream cheese, fromage blanc or fresh chèvre. Try these with: Riesling Sauvignon Blanc Pinot Gris Fresh sparkling wine A fresh, lightly chilled Chardonnay The aim is freshness rather than power. A heavily tannic red, high-alcohol wine or strongly oaked wine can overwhelm a delicate cheese. Herbs, citrus, olive oil or honey can change the result, so taste the cheese with its accompaniments before making a final decision. Fresh goat cheese is often a useful match for crisp white wine, but “goat cheese” is not a complete flavour description. Age, texture and added ingredients still matter. Soft-ripened or bloomy-rind cheese Brie- and camembert-style cheeses have a soft interior and a surface rind. They can be creamy, buttery and mild, although a mature example may be much more aromatic. Try: Australian sparkling wine Fresh Chardonnay Light Pinot Noir Riesling Sparkling wine provides a lively contrast to creaminess. Acidity in a still wine can play a similar role by keeping the combination from feeling heavy. Pinot Noir can work when it is relatively light and fresh, but a very tannic or alcoholic red may dominate the cheese. Washed-rind cheese Washed-rind cheeses are matured with the rind washed in brine, wine, beer, brandy or another liquid. Their aroma can be much more pungent than their actual flavour. Because these cheeses can be savoury and aromatic, they need a wine with enough flavour presence. Try: Medium-bodied Chardonnay Pinot Noir Sparkling wine Medium-bodied Shiraz An aromatic white wine Do not assume that a pungent rind requires a heavy red. The cheese may be soft, salty and delicate on the palate, making a high-tannin or high-alcohol wine feel harsh. Freshness and proportion matter more than simply choosing the biggest wine available. Semi-hard and hard cheese Firm cheeses have more chew and can range from mild to strongly savoury. Examples include cheddar- and gouda-style cheeses, along with parmesan-style cheeses. Try: Chardonnay Pinot Noir Shiraz Cabernet Sauvignon Sparkling wine The cheese’s age and saltiness are important. A young, mild cheese may suit a fresher wine, while a mature, savoury cheese can stand up to more structured Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon. Sparkling wine offers a different route, combining freshness with enough texture for a salty, firm cheese. Hard cheese does not automatically require red wine. A fresh white, sparkling wine or fortified wine may be more enjoyable depending on the cheese and the rest of the board. Aged cheese As cheese matures, it often becomes firmer, more concentrated and more savoury. That can make it a better partner for a wine with greater flavour intensity or structure. Try: Structured Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon Developed Chardonnay Pinot Noir Fortified wine Sparkling wine for contrast Tannin needs to be proportionate. A rich, firm, savoury cheese may make a structured red feel more integrated, but cheese does not simply “cancel” tannin. If the wine leaves your mouth feeling dry and bitter, choose a softer red or a fresher wine. Blue cheese Blue cheeses can be salty, creamy, crumbly, pungent and intense. This is where sweetness often becomes especially useful. Try: Sweet Riesling Late-harvest wine Fortified wine Sparkling wine Dry Riesling with a milder blue Sweetness can balance the salt and intensity of blue cheese, particularly when the wine also has enough acidity to stay lively. A dry wine can work too, especially with a milder blue, but it may taste harder beside a very salty cheese or sweet accompaniment. Dry does not mean flavourless A dry wine can smell and taste strongly of fruit. “Dry” refers mainly to perceived sweetness; it does not mean that the wine lacks apple, citrus, stone-fruit or berry character. This distinction matters on a cheese board. A fruity dry Riesling may provide flavour without adding sweetness, while a sweet Riesling adds both fruit character and noticeable sweetness. The latter may be a better choice for salty blue cheese or a board with intense savoury flavours. The reusable visual VIS-002 — “Dry does not mean flavourless” can help illustrate this distinction. How to build a mixed cheese board Choose three or four contrasting cheeses. For example, combine a fresh or soft cheese with a semi-hard cheese, an aromatic washed-rind cheese and a blue or aged cheese. Decide whether you want one wine or a progression. One fresh, moderate wine is simplest. Two or three wines allow you to move from delicate flavours to stronger ones. Taste from mild to intense. Start with fresh and soft cheeses, then move towards washed-rind, aged and blue cheeses. Taste without strong accompaniments first. Honey, fruit paste, chutney, pickles, nuts, crackers and cured meats can change the balance. Establish how the wine and cheese work together before adding them. Reserve sweetness for the strongest flavours if needed. A sweet or fortified wine can be saved for blue cheese or a particularly salty, intense cheese. For one versatile wine, fresh sparkling wine, Riesling or moderate Chardonnay is often a sensible starting point for a board built around mild to medium cheeses. If the board centres on aged or blue cheese, add a second, more structured or sweeter wine rather than forcing one bottle to do everything. What to do when the pairing tastes wrong It tastes harsh or drying The wine may have too much tannin, alcohol or acidity for the cheese. Try a softer red, a fresher white or sparkling wine. You can also retaste with a richer, firmer cheese and remove sharp pickles or vinegar-heavy accompaniments. It tastes flat The cheese or accompaniment may be more intense than the wine. Try a wine with more acidity or flavour, or pair sparkling wine with a rich creamy cheese. Removing chutney, honey or fruit paste may also restore balance. It tastes bitter or metallic Strong tannin, alcohol, oak, salt or savoury accompaniments may be contributing. Try a lower-tannin Pinot Noir, fresh Chardonnay or sparkling wine, or retaste with a less intensely savoury cheese. It tastes too sweet The cheese may be too mild for the wine, or sweet accompaniments may be amplifying the sweetness. Try a drier, higher-acid wine, remove the sweet condiments or choose a saltier, more intense cheese. For more background on the structure behind these choices, see How wine pairing works and How to taste wine . You can also explore sparkling wine , sweet wine , fortified wine , Pinot Noir , Shiraz , Chardonnay , Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio , Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling . Frequently asked questions What is the best wine for a cheese board? There is no single best wine. Fresh sparkling wine, Riesling or moderate Chardonnay can be versatile starting points, while sweet or fortified wine is useful for salty blue or aged cheese. Is red or white wine better with cheese? Neither is always better. White and sparkling wines are often useful with fresh or creamy cheese, while softer or structured reds may suit firmer, aged cheeses. The wine’s style matters more than its colour. Does cheese always go with red wine? No. Many cheeses work beautifully with white, sparkling, sweet or fortified wines. Red wine can taste drying or dominant with fresh, salty or delicate cheeses. Why does sweet wine work with blue cheese? Sweetness can balance the salt and intensity of blue cheese. Acidity helps keep the wine fresh rather than heavy. Can I pair one wine with several cheeses? Yes. Choose a wine with freshness, moderate body and enough flavour to remain present without overwhelming the mildest cheese. A small progression of wines gives you more flexibility.

title: Wine and Seafood Pairing: What Wine Goes Best With Seafood?
description: Learn how to pair wine with oysters, fish, prawns, shellfish, salmon, fried seafood and spicy seafood by considering preparation, sauce, richness and texture.
text: Highlights There is no single best wine for all seafood. Match the whole dish: seafood, cooking method, sauce, seasoning and richness. Fresh white wines and sparkling wine are reliable starting points for delicate, raw or fried seafood. Fuller Chardonnay, rosé and selected light reds can suit grilled, smoked or oily seafood. A little sweetness can work well with chilli-forward seafood. Sauce and preparation can matter more than the seafood species. Pairing suggestions are starting points, not rules. Quick answer The best wine for seafood depends on how the seafood is prepared. For raw oysters, delicate white fish and lightly seasoned shellfish, start with a fresh, high-acid wine such as Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris or sparkling wine. Fried seafood often works with sparkling wine or a crisp white because freshness and bubbles provide contrast to oil, salt and crunch. Richer dishes need a different approach. Grilled or roasted fish may suit textured Chardonnay, dry rosé or a light Pinot Noir. Salmon and other oily fish can support Chardonnay, Riesling, rosé, sparkling rosé or Pinot Noir, depending on the sauce and cooking method. For chilli-forward seafood, try a fresh wine with some sweetness, such as an off-dry Riesling. The most useful question is not “What wine goes with prawns?” It is: “What is the strongest feature of this prawn dish?” Garlic butter, chilli, smoke, cream, lime or soy may influence the pairing more than the prawns themselves. A simple way to choose Before choosing a bottle, look at four things: How is it cooked? Raw, steamed and poached dishes are usually more delicate. Frying, grilling, roasting and smoking add richness or intensity. What is the sauce? Lemon, vinegar, tomato and herbs point in a different direction from cream, butter, soy or chilli. How rich is the dish? Oily fish, fried coatings, butter and cream generally need freshness, bubbles or a wine with enough body. How intense is the flavour? A subtle wine can disappear beside smoke, char or a strongly seasoned sauce. Then choose the wine’s style before its grape name. A fresh Australian Chardonnay and a rich, heavily oaked Chardonnay may behave very differently at the table. Wine matches for common seafood dishes Raw oysters Start with brut sparkling wine, dry Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc or crisp Pinot Gris. Oysters are delicate and briny, and are often served with lemon, vinegar or mignonette. Freshness and bubbles can complement their saline character without overwhelming them. The garnish matters: a creamy or spicy dressing may make a different style more suitable. Delicate white fish For simply steamed, poached or lightly pan-cooked fish, try Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, fresh Chardonnay or dry sparkling wine. These wines provide freshness while allowing the fish to remain the focus. Avoid assuming that all white fish needs the same wine, though. A delicate fillet with lemon is a different pairing from the same fish with a rich cream sauce or smoky barbecue seasoning. Grilled or roasted fish Grilling and roasting add char, savoury flavour and sometimes extra richness. Consider a textured Chardonnay, fuller dry Riesling, a Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon style, dry rosé or light Pinot Noir. A lemon-and-herb dressing may favour a fresher wine. Butter, cream, smoke or a strongly seasoned glaze can support more body and flavour intensity. Battered or fried seafood Sparkling wine, Sauvignon Blanc, dry Riesling, Pinot Gris or dry rosé are useful starting points for battered fish, prawns and other fried seafood. Here, the batter, oil, salt and crisp texture may matter more than the fish species. Acidity can make the dish feel more refreshing, while sparkling wine adds another source of lift. This is why a fresh bottle can work so well with fish and chips, particularly with lemon or vinegar. Prawns, crab and lobster Prawns, crab and lobster can suit Riesling, Chardonnay, sparkling wine, Sauvignon Blanc or Pinot Gris. The choice depends on what accompanies them. Citrus, herbs and chilli may favour a fresh aromatic white. Garlic butter, mayonnaise or grilling can support a fuller Chardonnay or sparkling wine with enough texture. Wine Australia also identifies Australian Riesling and Chardonnay as useful partners for fish, shellfish and crustaceans, including prawns, lobster and crab. Mussels and other shellfish For mussels and shellfish, consider dry Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, sparkling wine, Pinot Gris or fresh Chardonnay. A light, acidic broth usually suits a fresh white or sparkling wine. Cream may call for a more textured Chardonnay that still has freshness. Tomato, garlic or chilli can shift the choice again, so pair with the broth or sauce rather than the shellfish alone. Salmon and other oily fish Salmon can support Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, dry or off-dry Riesling, sparkling rosé or dry rosé. Oily fish generally has enough richness to stand alongside wines with more texture and flavour. Preparation remains decisive: raw salmon with soy and ginger is not the same pairing as smoked salmon with crème fraîche, or grilled salmon with a sweet glaze. Smoked seafood Smoke increases flavour intensity, so a very delicate wine may disappear. Try sparkling wine, Riesling, Chardonnay, dry rosé or, where the dish is rich enough, a light Pinot Noir. Freshness and bubbles can stop the combination feeling heavy. A fuller wine may work with strongly smoked or oily seafood, but firm tannin is still best treated cautiously. Tuna and richer fish Tuna and other richer fish can suit Pinot Noir, dry rosé, medium-bodied Chardonnay or sparkling rosé. A light red may also work when the fish is grilled or strongly seasoned. Raw tuna with sesame and soy, seared tuna with a pepper crust and barbecued tuna with a savoury glaze are different dishes. Let the preparation decide how much body, freshness or tannin the wine can carry. Chilli-forward seafood For chilli prawns, spicy fish or seafood with chilli and lime, try Riesling with some sweetness, fresh Sauvignon Blanc, sparkling wine, dry rosé or aromatic Pinot Gris. Some sweetness can soften the perception of chilli and help the wine remain balanced beside sweet-and-sour or spicy sauces. It does not remove the heat. High alcohol and firm tannin may make chilli feel more aggressive, so they are risky default choices. What about red wine with seafood? Red wine is not automatically forbidden, but it needs the right dish and style. A lighter, lower-tannin Pinot Noir may suit grilled salmon, tuna, smoked seafood or a strongly flavoured preparation. Powerful, tannic reds are more likely to dominate delicate seafood or create a drying sensation. Research has also identified fishy aftertaste in specific wine-and-dried-scallop combinations, but that does not mean every red wine clashes with every seafood dish. If you prefer red wine, choose a lighter style, serve it slightly cool and match it with seafood that has enough richness, smoke or seasoning to meet it. If you are unsure For a mixed seafood table, bring a fresh sparkling wine or dry Riesling. These styles are versatile with oysters, prawns, shellfish, fried seafood and many lightly seasoned dishes. If the meal is grilled, buttery or creamy, choose a fresh but fuller Chardonnay. If it is especially spicy, consider a Riesling with some sweetness. If it is rich, smoky and substantial, a light Pinot Noir may be worth trying. Remember that a dry wine can still taste fruity. Fruit aroma is not the same as sweetness, so a dry Riesling or Sauvignon Blanc may smell richly of citrus or tropical fruit without tasting sugary. The best pairing is the one you enjoy Pairing advice is there to make choosing easier, not to police your dinner. Taste the wine with the dish and notice what happens. If the wine tastes harsh, hot or bitter, try something with less alcohol or tannin and more freshness. If it disappears, choose a wine with more body or flavour intensity. The seafood may be the headline, but the sauce, preparation and your own preference often write the ending.

title: Wine and Spicy Food Pairing: How to Choose the Right Wine
description: Learn how to pair wine with chilli-hot food by matching sweetness, acidity, alcohol, tannin, body and bubbles to the complete dish.
text: Highlights There is no single best wine for every spicy dish. With strong chilli heat, fresh, fruit-driven, moderate-alcohol wines are often comfortable starting points. A little sweetness can soften the impression of heat, but it does not remove or “neutralise” capsaicin. Acidity refreshes rich, creamy and coconut-based dishes. High alcohol, firm tannin and heavy oak can make chilli dishes feel hotter or harsher. Slightly off-dry Riesling is a useful first choice, but sparkling wine, rosé, aromatic whites and selected reds can also work. Pair the whole dish—not just the chilli level—with the wine. Quick answer: what wine goes best with spicy food? A slightly off-dry Riesling is one of the most useful starting points for chilli-hot food. Its freshness, fruit character and gentle sweetness can balance heat without making the wine feel heavy. But the best choice depends on the dish. For fresh chilli and herbs, try Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc or another aromatic white. For salty or fried spicy food, sparkling wine can provide refreshing acidity and bubbles. Rosé suits many grilled or moderately spicy dishes. A fruit-driven red with moderate tannin can work with smoky, grilled or tomato-based food. In general, be cautious with wines that are very high in alcohol, strongly tannic or heavily oaked. Chilli heat can make their warmth, dryness or bitterness feel more obvious. The important question is not simply “How spicy is it?” Also consider whether the dish is sweet, salty, acidic, creamy, coconut-based, fried, smoky or rich. Chilli heat is different from aromatic spice “Spicy” can describe several different sensations. Fresh chilli, dried chilli and chilli oil create pungent heat. Black pepper, Sichuan peppercorn, ginger, mustard, cumin, coriander and five-spice can add warmth, fragrance, bitterness or complexity without producing the same chilli burn. That distinction matters. A fragrant curry with little chilli heat may suit a broader range of wines than a dish dominated by fresh bird’s-eye chilli or chilli oil. Start by identifying the main sensation: Chilli-hot: look for freshness, fruit and moderate alcohol. Aromatic and herbal: aromatic whites can echo the dish’s fragrance. Sweet and spicy: some wine sweetness can keep the pairing balanced. Smoky and grilled: a fruit-driven rosé or moderate-tannin red may work well. How wine characteristics affect spicy food Sweetness A wine with some residual sugar can make chilli heat feel less stark and can match a sweet-and-spicy sauce. It does not need to taste like dessert wine: “slightly off-dry” is often enough. Do not confuse sweetness with fruit flavour. A dry Riesling can smell and taste strongly of lime, apple or other fruit while containing little or no perceptible sweetness. Australian Riesling ranges from crisp, dry styles to off-dry and sweeter examples, so check the individual wine rather than relying on the grape name alone. If the dish is strongly sweet, a completely dry wine may seem sharp or austere beside it. If the dish is savoury and not sweet, an obviously sweet wine may feel mismatched. Alcohol Alcohol creates warmth in the mouth. Chilli creates a separate burning sensation, and the two can combine to make a wine feel hotter or more aggressive. That is why moderate- or lower-alcohol wines are often safer with intense chilli heat. This is a tendency, not a rule: a balanced, fruity wine can be enjoyable even when it is not especially low in alcohol. Acidity Acidity gives wine freshness. It can refresh the palate between bites of creamy, coconut-based, buttery or fried spicy food. Try fresh Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, sparkling wine or rosé when richness is part of the dish. However, a very sharp wine may seem sour beside food that is already highly acidic because of lime, vinegar, tamarind or pickles. Tannin Tannin gives wine grip and a drying, sometimes astringent texture. Strong chilli heat can make a firm, tannic wine feel more drying, bitter or aggressive. This makes heavily structured Cabernet Sauvignon or powerful, tannic Shiraz risky choices with very hot food. Red wine is not automatically wrong, though. Look for ripe fruit, moderate tannin, balanced alcohol and restrained or integrated oak. Body, fruit and bubbles Body is the impression of weight or fullness in the mouth. It is not the same as alcohol, sweetness or grape variety. A very light wine may disappear beside a strongly flavoured dish, while an overly concentrated wine may overwhelm it. Fruit intensity can help a wine remain expressive beside chilli without necessarily making it sweet. Carbonation adds another kind of refreshment. Sparkling wine can work particularly well with salty, fried or rich spicy food. Bubbles do not remove chilli heat or oil, but they can make the combination feel lively and refreshing. Serving a suitable white, rosé or sparkling wine chilled can also improve refreshment. Chilling cannot repair a wine that is too tannic, alcoholic, oaky or sweet for the dish. Choose a wine by dish style Fresh chilli, herbs and lime For chilli-heavy salads, fresh chilli seafood, herb-led noodles or chilli-and-lime dishes, try: Riesling; Sauvignon Blanc; an aromatic white; fresh rosé; sparkling wine when the heat is moderate. These styles can provide freshness and aromatic lift. Avoid automatically choosing a high-alcohol red or heavily oaked wine. Sweet-and-spicy dishes For chilli jam, sweet soy, honey-chilli food, hot barbecue sauce or a gochujang-style glaze, consider: off-dry Riesling; fruit-driven rosé; a sparkling wine with generous fruit character; a soft, moderate-alcohol red; an aromatic white with noticeable fruit. The wine should have enough sweetness or fruit presence to avoid tasting hard beside the sauce. Creamy or coconut-based curries Riesling and aromatic whites can bring freshness to coconut-based curries. A fresh Chardonnay may also work, while a fuller Chardonnay can suit dishes where cream, coconut or roasted flavours dominate. The hotter the curry, the more useful moderate alcohol and some sweetness may become. The richer the sauce, the more acidity and body matter. Salty, fried or rich spicy food Sparkling wine is a natural style to consider with fried chicken, chilli-coated prawns, salty snacks or rich appetisers. Fresh rosé and lively whites can also work. With very intense chilli heat, choose a sparkling wine with enough fruit and avoid assuming that the driest style will always be most comfortable. Smoky or grilled chilli food For grilled prawns, spicy barbecue, roasted meat or smoky chilli dishes, try: fruit-driven rosé; a moderate-tannin Shiraz; a fresh, lighter red; medium-bodied Chardonnay, particularly with poultry or creamy accompaniments. Australian Shiraz is not one fixed style. Alcohol, tannin, oak, ripeness and body can vary considerably, so choose the bottle’s style rather than the variety name alone. When can red wine work? Red wine is more likely to work when the dish includes smoke, char, tomato, roasted meat, lentils, beans or a savoury glaze, and when the chilli heat is moderate rather than extreme. Choose a red with: moderate alcohol; ripe fruit; moderate tannin; freshness; limited or integrated oak. Be cautious with young, strongly tannic Cabernet Sauvignon, very high-alcohol Shiraz and heavily oaked reds. These may feel hot, dry or bitter beside intense chilli, strong vinegar or salty chilli oil. Troubleshooting a difficult pairing If the combination tastes hotter , try a wine with lower alcohol, more fruit or a little sweetness. If it tastes flat , the wine may lack aromatic intensity or acidity. A fresher Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc or sparkling wine may help. If it tastes bitter or drying , reduce tannin and heavy oak. Try rosé, a white wine or a softer red. If the wine tastes too sweet , choose a drier style or reduce the sweet element of the dish. If it tastes too sharp , look for a rounder, fruitier wine and consider whether the food already contains substantial lime, vinegar or other acidity. The most useful pairing skill is adjustment. Taste the wine with the food, notice what becomes more intense, and change one variable at a time. FAQs Is Riesling always sweet? No. Australian Riesling is commonly dry, but off-dry and sweeter styles are also available. Read the label or ask for the wine’s sweetness level. Can you drink Shiraz with spicy food? Yes, particularly with smoky, grilled, tomato-based or moderately spicy dishes. Choose a fruit-driven Shiraz with moderate tannin and alcohol rather than the most powerful style. Is sweet wine best with chilli? Not automatically. Some sweetness can balance heat, but acidity, alcohol, tannin, body, fruit intensity and the dish’s richness matter too. Does chilling wine remove chilli heat? No. Chilling can make a suitable wine feel more refreshing, but it cannot fix excessive alcohol, tannin, oak or an unsuitable level of sweetness. What is the safest wine to bring to a spicy dinner? A fresh Riesling—especially one that is slightly off-dry—is a practical starting point. Sparkling wine or fresh rosé can also be flexible choices, depending on the food.

title: Wine and Steak Pairing: What Wine Goes Best with Steak?
description: Learn how to pair wine with steak by considering the cut, cooking method, char, sauce and richness. Includes Australian Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir and alternatives.
